countries.name: Chile
countries.tagline: A ribbon of vineyards between the Andes and a cold ocean, where phylloxera never arrived and a lost Bordeaux grape was found hiding in plain sight.

stats.note: SAG Catastro Vitícola 2024: 116,962 ha of wine grapes plus 9,287 ha of pisco grapes (OIV 2025 counts 154,000 ha including table grapes). Production: SAG 2026 harvest, 949.5 million litres excluding pisco wine. Rank: OIV 2025, where Chile made 8.4 mhl (8th).

countries.overview:
Chile is a wine country shaped by walls. To the east the Andes rise above 6,000 m; to the west the cold Humboldt Current chills the Pacific; to the north lies the Atacama, the driest desert on Earth; to the south, ice fields and fjords. Inside that box, a strip rarely wider than 180 km and more than 1,300 km long from Copiapó to Chiloé, sits one of the most naturally protected vineyards in the world. Phylloxera, the root louse that destroyed Europe's vineyards in the late 19th century, has never established itself here, so most Chilean vines still grow on their own roots, and Chile's quarantine rules for plant material remain among the strictest of any wine country.

The geography also explains the climate. Between the Andes and the lower coastal range runs the Central Valley, a sun-soaked Mediterranean trough with dry summers and winter rain. Cold air drains off the mountains each night and the Pacific sends fog and wind through every gap in the coastal hills, so days are warm but nights are cool. That combination gives ripe fruit with real acidity and keeps disease pressure low. For most of the 20th century the industry worked the irrigated valley floor; since the 1980s it has moved outwards, east into the Andean foothills and west towards the coast, and Chileans now describe their wines by those bands as much as by valley: *Costa*, *Entre Cordilleras* and *Andes*.

Chilean wine has two founding stories. The first is colonial: Spanish conquistadors and missionaries brought the vine from Peru in the 1550s, and for three centuries Chile drank País, the grape known elsewhere as Mission or Listán Prieto, grown on dry hills in Maule and Itata. The second is French: from 1851, when Silvestre Ochagavía brought Bordeaux vines and a French winemaker to Santiago, the mining and banking elite planted Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Malbec and a then-common Bordeaux grape called Carmenère on estates around the capital. Phylloxera hit France soon after, so Chile kept vines that Europe lost, including Carmenère, which disappeared from Bordeaux and survived in Chile disguised as Merlot until the ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot identified it at Viña Carmen on 24 November 1994.

Modern Chilean wine dates from 1979, when Miguel Torres brought stainless steel and temperature control to Curicó, and from the export boom of the late 1980s and 1990s. Foreign investment followed: Lafite's Los Vascos, Mouton Rothschild's partnership with Concha y Toro in Almaviva, Robert Mondavi's with Errázuriz in Seña, and the Marnier-Lapostolle family in Apalta. In 2004 the Berlin Tasting placed Viñedo Chadwick 2000 and Seña 2001 above first-growth Bordeaux in a blind panel, a stunt that permanently changed Chile's image.

Today Chile is one of the world's largest exporters by volume, and its industry is in an uncomfortable transition. The national vineyard has shrunk from about 145,000 ha in 2020 to 126,000 ha in SAG's 2024 census, as falling global demand forces growers to pull out bulk vineyards, and 2026 production recovered to about 950 million litres after very short 2024 and 2025 crops. At the same time the country's most interesting wines have never been more diverse: Limarí Chardonnay grown on limestone, Leyda and Casablanca Sauvignon Blanc, Puente Alto Cabernet of real longevity, Carmenère that is finally ripe without being green or jammy, old-vine Carignan from Maule, and País and Cinsault from 100-year-old dry-farmed bush vines in Itata. The Chilean wine map keeps moving south too: a 2025 decree created DOs for the Chiloé archipelago and for Easter Island.

history.title: The vine crosses from Peru
history.text: Spanish conquistadors and missionaries bring Vitis vinifera south from the Viceroyalty of Peru; local tradition credits Francisco de Aguirre with some of the first plantings. The grape is the 'common black grape' later called País, the same Listán Prieto that became Mission in California and Criolla Chica in Argentina.

history.title: País and Moscatel on the dry hills
history.text: Jesuits and settlers spread vineyards through the Central Valley and the south around Concepción and Chillán. Wine for Mass and for the colony is made in clay *tinajas*; sweet wines from País and Moscatel, sometimes boiled to concentrate them, are the colonial style. In 1795 Lima imports 5,000 botijas of wine from Concepción.

history.title: Ochagavía brings Bordeaux to Santiago
history.text: Silvestre Ochagavía Echazarreta imports French vines (Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Malbec, Carmenère and others) and a French winemaker to his estate south of Santiago. The Bordeaux model becomes the template for Chile's elite estates.

history.title: The great Maipo estates
history.text: Cousiño Macul (1856), Errázuriz at Panquehue (1870), Santa Carolina (1875), Santa Rita (1880) and Concha y Toro at Pirque (1883) are founded, mostly by families enriched by silver, copper and banking.

history.title: Phylloxera spares Chile
history.text: As phylloxera devastates European vineyards, Chile's isolation keeps the louse out. French winemakers and vine material arrive, and Chile preserves pre-phylloxera Bordeaux varieties on their own roots, including Carmenère.

history.title: Miguel Torres arrives in Curicó
history.text: The Catalan producer buys land in Curicó and introduces stainless steel tanks and temperature-controlled fermentation, kicking off Chile's technical modernisation.

history.title: Casablanca is planted
history.text: Pablo Morandé plants vines in the Casablanca Valley, opening the first cool coastal region and Chile's white-wine era.

history.title: Decree 464 and the rediscovery of Carmenère
history.text: On 14 December 1994 Decree 464 creates Chile's viticultural zoning of regions, subregions, zones and areas, effective 1995. Weeks earlier, on 24 November, Jean-Michel Boursiquot identifies Carmenère among the 'Merlot' vines at Viña Carmen; SAG recognises the variety officially in 1998.

history.title: Almaviva and the icon era
history.text: Concha y Toro and Baron Philippe de Rothschild launch Almaviva in Puente Alto; Seña (Errázuriz and Mondavi) and Don Melchor complete Chile's first generation of icon wines.

history.title: The Berlin Tasting
history.text: Eduardo Chadwick organises a blind tasting in Berlin where Viñedo Chadwick 2000 and Seña 2001 finish ahead of Lafite, Margaux and Latour.

history.title: Old vines, Costa, Entre Cordilleras, Andes
history.text: The VIGNO association promotes old dry-farmed Maule Carignan; Itata's País and Cinsault are rediscovered; Decree 464 is amended to add the Secano Interior special DO and the Costa, Entre Cordilleras and Andes label complements.

history.title: Four new DOs
history.text: Apalta, Los Lingues, Licantén and Lo Abarca become DOs, the first defined by vineyard identity rather than municipal boundaries.

history.title: Chiloé and Rapa Nui
history.text: Decree 27, published 14 May 2025, creates a Chiloé subregion and a Rapa Nui-Isla de Pascua area, citing climate change as a reason vines now succeed further south.

history.title: Secano Interior extended, Los Lingues upheld
history.text: Decree 4 (published 14 July 2026) adds seven Biobío communes to the Secano Interior DO; in June the Supreme Court rejects a trademark holder's attempt to annul the Los Lingues DO.

countries.classification:
Chile's appellation system is a geographic map with almost no rules about how wine is made, created by Decree 464 of 14 December 1994 (in force from 1995) and administered by the Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero (SAG). It nests four levels: six viticultural Regions (Atacama, Coquimbo, Aconcagua, Valle Central, Sur, Austral), Subregions (mostly the valleys: Elqui, Limarí, Casablanca, Maipo, Rapel, Curicó, Maule, Itata and so on), Zones inside some subregions (Leyda, Cachapoal, Colchagua, Teno, Lontué, Claro, Loncomilla, Tutuvén) and Areas, which usually match one or more communes. Because the units follow municipal lines rather than soil or climate, a single area can stretch from valley floor to Andean summit.

A DO wine must contain at least 75% of grapes from the named place (85% is the norm for export), at least 75% of a named variety and vintage, and up to three regions or subregions can be blended on a label. Approved varieties are listed in the decree, which was widened in 2024 with dozens more. Quality terms (Reserva, Gran Reserva and so on) rest mostly on alcohol above the legal minimum and oak, not on ageing time or yield, so they tell you little.

Three later layers matter more to the wine nerd. Since a 2011 amendment (first used on labels around 2012), wines may add *Costa*, *Entre Cordilleras* or *Andes* if at least 85% of the wine comes from areas declared to have that condition, a much better clue to style than the valley name. The special DO *Secano Interior* (País and Cinsault from dry-farmed land in Maule, Ñuble and Biobío) recognises the old-vine heritage, extended in 2026. And since 2018 small DOs can be drawn around a recognised place or famous vineyard: Apalta, Los Lingues, Licantén and Lo Abarca. Chiloé and Rapa Nui joined in 2025. Producer associations add their own rules, most notably VIGNO for old-vine Maule Carignan.
countries.climate_soils:
Almost all of Chile's vineyards sit between 30°S and 38°S, the latitude of North Africa and southern Spain, but the climate is far cooler than that suggests. The Humboldt Current brings Antarctic water up the coast, producing coastal fog (*camanchaca*) and afternoon winds that are channelled inland through gaps in the coastal range. The Andes add nightly katabatic winds and huge day-night swings, while the coastal range shelters the Central Valley and casts a rain shadow. Rainfall rises steeply from north to south: under 100 mm in Elqui and Limarí, about 300 to 350 mm in Maipo, 600 to 700 mm in Colchagua and Maule, over 1,000 mm in Itata and Bío-Bío and around 1,300 mm in Malleco. Summers are dry everywhere, so disease pressure is low, irrigation from Andean snowmelt is usual in the north and centre, and dry farming is possible in the south.

Soils follow the geology of three bands. The coastal range is old granite, weathered into sandy *maicillo* with clay subsoils, with patches of slate (Empedrado), schist and rare limestone (Limarí's Talinay and Quebrada Seca, Lo Abarca). The Central Valley floor is deep alluvium, gravels and clays laid down by Andean rivers such as the Maipo, Cachapoal, Tinguiririca and Maule. The Andean piedmont adds colluvial fans and volcanic material, most famously the stony terraces of Puente Alto. The east-west contrast inside a single valley is often bigger than the north-south one between valleys.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: Chile's most planted grape and its benchmark red; 27.5% of DO wine in 2026. Puente Alto, Pirque and the Andean foothills of Maipo give the classic style of cassis, graphite and a mint or eucalyptus edge.

grapes.name: Carmenère
grapes.note: The lost Bordeaux grape, identified among Chilean 'Merlot' in 1994 and now Chile's signature; best in warm, clay-rich sites such as Peumo, Apalta and Colchagua's valley floor, where it ripens fully and loses its green pepper note. 7.8% of DO wine in 2026.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: Second largest DO volume (17.6% in 2026); the coastal valleys (Casablanca, Leyda, San Antonio, Paredones, Limarí) give a saline, citrus style. Some older Chilean 'Sauvignon' is actually Sauvignonasse (Friulano).

grapes.name: País
grapes.note: Chile's colonial grape (Listán Prieto, Mission, Criolla Chica), planted from the 1550s and still on dry-farmed hills of Maule, Itata and Bío-Bío; reborn as light, earthy reds, rosés and sparkling wines.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: Much of Chile's historic 'Merlot' was Carmenère; true Merlot, planted since the late 1990s, is a major volume grape (12.2% of DO wine in 2026).

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Grown from Limarí to Malleco; the limestone of Limarí and the cool coastal valleys give a tense, mineral style.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.note: Old dry-farmed bush vines in Maule's secano, planted after the 1939 earthquake to add colour and acidity, now championed by VIGNO.

grapes.name: Cinsault
grapes.note: Itata's grape: juicy, light, red-fruited reds from old own-rooted vines on granite.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.note: From warm Colchagua to the cool coast and high Elqui, where it shows pepper and violets.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Coastal sites of Casablanca, Leyda, Limarí and the cool south; increasingly serious.

grapes.name: Moscatel de Alejandría
grapes.note: Old Itata and Bío-Bío vines for dry and orange whites; in Elqui and Limarí a pisco grape.

grapes.name: Malbec (Cot)
grapes.note: Pre-phylloxera Malbec survives in old Maule and Colchagua vineyards; 3% of DO wine.

countries.name: Argentina
countries.tagline: Malbec at altitude: desert oases fed by Andean snowmelt, from the Tropic of Capricorn to the Patagonian wind.

stats.note: Vineyard: INV, all grape vines at 31 Dec 2024 (Malbec report 2025). Production: INV 2026 annual report, 9,700,421 hl (down 9.9% on 2025). Rank: OIV 2025, where Argentina made 10.8 mhl, 6th in the world.

countries.overview:
Argentina makes wine in the desert. Almost every vineyard lies in the rain shadow of the Andes, in irrigated oases strung along rivers of snowmelt between the Tropic of Capricorn in Jujuy and 45°S in Chubut. Rainfall is often 200 mm a year or less, the sun shines on more than 300 days, and the only reason a vine can grow is a canal network whose oldest channels follow Huarpe and Inca irrigation. Height does the work that latitude does in Europe. Vineyards run from about 500 m on the eastern plains of Mendoza to 1,500 m in the Uco Valley and above 3,000 m in the Calchaquí valleys of Salta, among the highest commercial vineyards on Earth. Every 100 m of altitude costs roughly 0.6°C, so the higher sites keep acidity and freshness while the intense ultraviolet light thickens grape skins.

The vine came from Chile and Peru with Spanish priests and conquistadors in the 1550s: to Santiago del Estero in 1557, to Mendoza after its founding in 1561, to San Juan soon after. For three centuries the country drank wine from Criolla grapes, the Listán Prieto family that Chile calls País. The modern story begins in 1853, when Domingo Faustino Sarmiento's Quinta Normal in Mendoza, run by the French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget, brought French varieties including Malbec. The railway from Buenos Aires reached Mendoza in 1885, carrying Italian and Spanish immigrants west and their wine east, and by the early 20th century Argentina had one of the largest wine industries in the world, built on cheap table wine for a nation that drank about 90 litres a head in the 1970s.

That model collapsed in the 1980s, along with consumption, hyperinflation and much of the old Malbec vineyard. The rebirth of the 1990s came from looking outward: foreign capital and flying winemakers, drip irrigation, yield control, new oak, and above all a few producers who bet on altitude and on Malbec. Nicolás Catena planted the Adrianna vineyard at about 1,450 m in Gualtallary in 1992, when locals thought it was too cold to ripen anything. French investors arrived in the Uco Valley (Clos de los Siete, Cheval des Andes), and by the 2000s Argentine Malbec, plush, violet-scented and affordable, had become one of the wine world's great export stories.

Malbec is now the most planted grape in the country, 47,064 ha in 2024 according to INV, 23.5% of the national vineyard and present in 18 of 20 wine provinces. It is joined by Bonarda (Douce Noir of Savoie), Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, the pink-skinned Criolla Grande and Cereza that still fill boxes and demijohns, and Torrontés Riojano, the floral white born in Argentina from Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica. Phylloxera is present, but in a weak form held back by sandy soils and flood irrigation, so most vineyards remain ungrafted.

The frontier of the 2010s and 2020s is precision. Mendoza's Uco Valley has been carved into district IGs drawn on geology (Paraje Altamira, Los Chacayes, San Pablo, Pampa El Cepillo), producers map calcareous crusts and river stones parcel by parcel, and new IGs keep appearing in the high north, the Andean valleys of San Juan, Patagonia and even the Atlantic coast of Buenos Aires. At the same time the domestic industry is shrinking: the 2026 harvest of 18.6 million quintals was among the lowest on record, wine output fell to 9.7 million hectolitres, and the national vineyard has lost tens of thousands of hectares in a decade. Argentines still drink more wine than anyone else in the Americas, about 21 litres per adult in 2025 according to the OIV, and wine has been the national drink by law since 2013.

history.title: First vines at Santiago del Estero
history.text: Vine cuttings from Chile are planted at Santiago del Estero, the oldest Spanish town in Argentina; tradition credits the priest Juan Cedrón (or Cidrón). The grape is the Criolla family, ancestor of Criolla Chica and cousin of Chile's País.

history.title: Mendoza is founded
history.text: Pedro del Castillo founds Mendoza on 2 March 1561. Spanish settlers extend the Huarpe irrigation canals, and vineyards spread through Cuyo; San Juan follows from 1562. Wine and aguardiente travel by cart and mule to Buenos Aires, Córdoba and the silver city of Potosí.

history.title: Jesuit estancias
history.text: Jesuit estancias around Córdoba, such as Caroya, make wine for their colleges until the order's expulsion in 1767; the estancias are now a UNESCO World Heritage site.

history.title: Pouget, Sarmiento and Malbec
history.text: Following Domingo Faustino Sarmiento's plan, the project for Mendoza's Quinta Normal de Agricultura is presented to the provincial legislature; its director, the French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget, brings French vine varieties including Malbec. The date is now celebrated as Malbec World Day.

history.title: The railway reaches Mendoza
history.text: The Buenos Aires to Mendoza railway opens, championed by governor Tiburcio Benegas, owner of El Trapiche. Italian and Spanish immigrants pour into Cuyo, and wine for the booming capital becomes Mendoza's industry.

history.title: Nicola Catena plants Malbec
history.text: Italian immigrant Nicola Catena plants his first Malbec vineyard in Rivadavia, Eastern Mendoza, founding the family firm that his grandson Nicolás would turn into Argentina's best-known fine-wine house.

history.title: Wine in Patagonia
history.text: Humberto Canale plants vines in the Alto Valle of Río Negro, beginning commercial Patagonian viticulture.

history.title: INV and Chandon
history.text: Law 14.878 creates the Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura to regulate the industry; the same year Moët & Chandon chooses Argentina for its first winery outside France.

history.title: Boom and bust
history.text: Per-capita consumption peaks near 90 litres a year in the 1970s; then consumption falls, inflation soars and vast areas of old vines, Malbec included, are uprooted or grafted to high-yielding pink grapes.

history.title: Modernisation and altitude
history.text: Economic stabilisation brings foreign investment and flying winemakers. Nicolás Catena plants the Adrianna vineyard at about 1,450 m in Gualtallary (1992); Michel Rolland and partners begin Clos de los Siete in Vista Flores (1998); the Uco Valley boom starts.

history.title: Law 25.163: IP, IG and DOC
history.text: The national law creates Argentina's appellation system of Indicación de Procedencia, Indicación Geográfica and Denominación de Origen Controlada, regulated by Decree 57/2004; the large IG list follows in 2002.

history.title: Wine becomes the national drink; Paraje Altamira
history.text: Law 26.870 declares wine Argentina's national drink. The same year INV recognises Paraje Altamira, the first Uco district IG drawn after soil-pit studies, opening the era of geology-based IGs.

history.title: Zuccardi Valle de Uco
history.text: The Zuccardi family opens its stone winery at Paraje Altamira, built from the alluvial rocks of its own vineyards; it is later named the World's Best Vineyard three years running.

history.title: New IGs from Patagonia to Jujuy
history.text: INV recognises El Hoyo (Chubut), Tamberías, Hilario and Sorocayense (Calingasta), Tandil (Buenos Aires), Valle de Pucará (Salta), Alto Agrelo (Luján de Cuyo) and Valles Templados (Jujuy).

history.title: A short harvest
history.text: INV reports an 18.6 million quintal grape harvest, among the lowest on record, and 9.7 million hl of wine; Argentina also sets the rules for protecting Mercosur partners' wine GIs under the 2019 Bento Gonçalves agreement.

countries.classification:
Argentina's appellation law is Law 25.163 of 1999, regulated by Decree 57/2004 and administered by the Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura (INV). It creates three tiers. An *Indicación de Procedencia* (IP) is for table and regional wines with at least 80% of grapes from the named area. An *Indicación Geográfica* (IG) is for quality wines from a region, locality or area no larger than a province (or an established interprovincial zone) whose character is mainly due to its origin; grapes must be grown and the wine made in the area. A *Denominación de Origen Controlada* (DOC) requires that quality be due 'exclusively or essentially' to the place, natural and human factors combined, with a regulatory council and production rules.

In practice, the IG is what matters. INV's register held 110 IGs and 2 DOCs in 2023, and at least eight more IGs have been added since (El Hoyo, Tamberías, Hilario, Sorocayense, Tandil, Valle de Pucará, Alto Agrelo, Valles Templados). They nest loosely: interprovincial regions (Cuyo, Patagonia, Valles Calchaquíes, Valles del Famatina), provinces (Mendoza, San Juan, Salta), departments (Luján de Cuyo, Tupungato, Cafayate) and districts or *parajes* (Agrelo, Los Chacayes, Paraje Altamira, San Pablo). Many department IGs were registered in bulk in 2002, while the district IGs of the 2010s and 2020s were drawn on soil, geology and climate studies. Since INV Resolution 56/2024, wineries in an area with a department or provincial IG can use it automatically. Gualtallary, Argentina's most famous district, has long been labelled under a provisional 'mención precaria' while its boundaries are argued over.

Only two DOCs exist, Luján de Cuyo (Malbec-focused, the only one in regular use) and San Rafael (2007). Varietal labels require 85% of the named grape. Under INV rules, 'Reserva' and 'Gran Reserva' are tied to minimum ageing periods, but they do not imply a particular origin.
countries.climate_soils:
The climate is continental desert modified by altitude. Mendoza averages around 200 mm of rain a year, most of it falling in summer thunderstorms that bring hail (*la piedra*), the industry's great hazard, which is why many vineyards sit under anti-hail nets. The Zonda, a hot, dry foehn wind off the Andes, can damage flowering in spring. Day-night temperature swings of 15 to 20°C are normal, and low humidity keeps fungal disease rare, so organic farming is easy. In the north, the Calchaquí valleys add extreme altitude and ultraviolet light; in Patagonia, latitude, constant wind and long summer days take over; and on the Atlantic coast of Buenos Aires, the ocean.

Soils are young and alluvial: fans of stones, gravel, sand and silt washed out of the Andes by rivers and flash floods. Near the mountains the fans are coarse, with rounded boulders often coated in white calcium carbonate (caliche), which drains fast and stresses the vine; further from the mountains the material becomes deep sand and silt, fertile and easy to irrigate. That gradient, more than latitude, explains why Uco Valley and Luján de Cuyo Malbec taste so different from Eastern Mendoza's. Organic matter is very low everywhere, and the sandy soils are one reason phylloxera never became the catastrophe it was elsewhere.

grapes.name: Malbec
grapes.note: Argentina's signature: 47,064 ha in 2024 (INV), 23.5% of all vines and the most planted variety, from Salta to Patagonia. Brought from France via Pouget's Quinta Normal in 1853; it thrives in the high Andean light, giving dark, violet-scented, plush wines.

grapes.name: Bonarda
grapes.note: Argentina's second red, genetically the Douce Noir of Savoie (Charbono in California), not the Bonarda of Piedmont. Juicy and soft; old-vine Bonarda from Eastern Mendoza and San Rafael is a cult value red.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: Planted throughout Cuyo and Salta; firmer and more herbal at altitude, often blended with Malbec.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.note: The rising star of Uco and Gualtallary since the 2010s, with fresh herbal lift on calcareous soils.

grapes.name: Criolla Grande and Cereza
grapes.note: Pink-skinned Criolla grapes of colonial descent, still major in the East and San Juan for bulk wine, juice and concentrate.

grapes.name: Criolla Chica
grapes.note: Listán Prieto, the original colonial grape (Chile's País, California's Mission), revived by small producers in Salta, Calingasta and Mendoza for light, earthy reds.

grapes.name: Torrontés Riojano
grapes.note: Argentina's own aromatic white, a natural cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica; at its best in Cafayate and the Famatina valley. Torrontés Sanjuanino and Mendocino are separate, lesser varieties.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.note: Especially associated with San Juan's warm Tulum and Pedernal valleys.

grapes.name: Pedro Giménez
grapes.note: A widely planted white for everyday wine and concentrate, distinct from Spain's Pedro Ximénez.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: From Gualtallary and San Pablo come some of South America's most precise Chardonnays; also the backbone of Mendoza sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Old vines in Río Negro (Chacra, Noemía's neighbours) and high Uco sites; the main red for traditional-method sparkling.

grapes.name: Semillon
grapes.note: Old-vine Semillon in Uco (La Consulta) and Río Negro is a revived treasure.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.note: Grown in Salta's Calchaquí valleys, where altitude softens its tannins.

countries.name: Uruguay
countries.tagline: An Atlantic-cooled pocket between the River Plate and the ocean, where a Basque pioneer's Tannat became a national identity.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figures for 2023: 5,848 ha of grapes and 50,224 t of wine (about 0.5 mhl), from a drought-hit vintage; INAVI had reported about 6,000 ha in production and roughly 70 million litres a year in 2022 (La Mañana, Jan 2022). Not in the OIV 2025 top 20

countries.overview:
Uruguay is South America's Atlantic wine country. Where Argentina and Chile grow grapes in deserts under the Andes, Uruguay grows them on low, rolling hills a few kilometres from the River Plate estuary and the ocean, at 30 to 35°S, in a humid temperate climate with about 1,000 mm of rain a year spread through every season. The landscape looks more like Bordeaux or the French Basque country than like Mendoza, and that resemblance is the key to its story.

The founding figure is Pascual Harriague, a Basque immigrant from France who planted Tannat near Salto in the north of the country around 1870, using vines brought from Concordia across the Uruguay river. Locals called the grape 'Harriague'. Almost at the same time Francisco Vidiella planted European vines at Colón, near Montevideo, and made the first harvest there in 1883. Italian, Basque and Spanish families built the industry that followed, and by the 1950s Uruguay had about 19,000 ha of vines, many of them hybrids for a thirsty home market.

The modern era began in the late 1980s, when the coming Mercosur trade bloc threatened to flood Uruguay with cheaper Argentine and Brazilian wine. The response, led by INAVI (the national wine institute, created in 1987), was to pull out hybrids, plant clean vinifera stock and bet on quality and on one grape. Tannat, a tough, tannic red from Madiran in south-west France, became Uruguay's signature. Grown in a wetter, more maritime climate and often made with softer extraction, Uruguayan Tannat is rounder and more approachable than Madiran, with dark plum, blackberry and a savoury edge. In 2022 Uruguay had about 1,575 ha of Tannat, about 27% of its vineyard, the largest share of any country.

The industry is small and family-based: more than 1,200 mostly small vineyards and, by INAVI's 2022 figure, about 6,000 ha in production, down from 8,000 ha a quarter-century earlier. Most production is in Canelones and Montevideo, but the most exciting growth is east, in Maldonado's granite hills near Punta del Este, where Bodega Garzón and others make Albariño, Pinot Noir and fresh Tannat, and north, in Rivera's red sands on the Brazilian border. Uruguay declared wine its national drink in 2014. Exports remain modest, mostly to Brazil and the United States, while the home market drinks most of the wine.

history.title: Colonial vines
history.text: Spanish settlers plant vines, probably Moscatel, alongside olives in the Banda Oriental, for table grapes and family wine.

history.title: Los Cerros de San Juan
history.text: Uruguay's oldest commercial winery is founded in Colonia department.

history.title: Harriague plants Tannat in Salto
history.text: Basque immigrant Pascual Harriague plants Tannat cuttings, brought from Concordia in Argentina, near Salto in the north. The grape is known locally as 'Harriague' for decades.

history.title: Vidiella's first harvest at Colón
history.text: Francisco Vidiella harvests his European vines at Colón, near Montevideo, on 25 February 1883, an event remembered as the first national harvest festival. Folle Noire becomes known locally as 'Vidiella'.

history.title: First wine law
history.text: Uruguay's first wine law (17 July 1903) regulates 'natural wine'; quality controls and production census follow in 1904.

history.title: INAVI created
history.text: Law 15.903 creates the Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura, based in Las Piedras, Canelones; the Vino de Calidad Preferente category follows in 1993, as hybrid vineyards are replaced with vinifera.

history.title: Maldonado's first vines
history.text: Alto de la Ballena plants the first modern vineyard in Maldonado, opening Uruguay's Atlantic frontier.

history.title: Wine becomes the national drink
history.text: Decree 171/014 declares Uruguayan wine, in all its styles, the national drink and requires labels to say so.

history.title: Bodega Garzón
history.text: Alejandro Bulgheroni's Bodega Garzón opens its winery near Pueblo Garzón in Maldonado and is named New World Winery of the Year by Wine Enthusiast in 2018.

countries.classification:
Uruguay has no formal denomination of origin system. Wine law, administered by INAVI under laws 15.903 (1987) and 18.462 (2009), divides wine into two main categories: *Vino de Calidad Preferente* (VCP), quality wine from Vitis vinifera, bottled in containers of 75 cl or less, with registered labels; and *Vino Común* (VC), table wine often sold in demijohns or cartons. Under MERCOSUR rules a varietal or vintage claim requires at least 85% of the named grape or year.

Geographic names on labels follow the country's 19 administrative departments (Canelones, Maldonado, Colonia and so on), and producers may use a finer place name if all grapes come from it. The industry and INAVI's promotion group departments into informal regions, commonly six: Metropolitana (Canelones, Montevideo, San José), Oceánica (Maldonado, Rocha, Lavalleja), Litoral Sur (Colonia, Soriano), Litoral Norte (Salto, Paysandú, Artigas), Centro (Durazno, Florida, Tacuarembó) and Norte (Rivera). These groupings have no legal force, and Uruguay notified only the national name for protection in the Mercosur GI agreement. Uruguay was the first South American country to ban foreign place names such as 'Champagne' on domestic labels, in 1993.
countries.climate_soils:
Uruguay's climate is humid and temperate, closer to Bordeaux than to Mendoza. Average temperatures are around 17°C, rainfall around 1,000 to 1,100 mm a year spread across all seasons, and sea breezes from the River Plate and the Atlantic cool nights and summer afternoons. That humidity is the great challenge (rot and mildew, vintage variation) and the reason thick-skinned Tannat was the grape that survived best. The south and east are coolest; the northern border departments of Rivera, Salto and Artigas are warmer and more continental.

Geologically, Uruguay is ancient: the Precambrian crystalline shield outcrops as granite and gneiss in the eastern hills of Maldonado and Lavalleja, while the Metropolitan region has heavy, fertile clays and clay-loams, sometimes with calcareous layers. Rivera has deep red sands derived from sandstones, very free-draining, and the western littoral has sedimentary soils shaped by the Uruguay river. INIA's soil inventory identifies dozens of soil types under vine, a lot of diversity for so small an industry.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.note: The national grape: about 1,575 ha in 2022, roughly 27% of the vineyard. Brought by Pascual Harriague around 1870; softer and rounder than Madiran, often blended with Merlot, Cabernet Franc or Pinot Noir.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: The second red, prized for softening Tannat in blends.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.note: Increasingly important for fresh, herbal reds, especially in Maldonado and Canelones.

grapes.name: Albariño
grapes.note: First planted by Bodega Bouza around 2002; now a signature white of the Atlantic coast and, by INAVI's count, about 128 ha in 2024.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: A leading white, bright and saline in coastal sites.

grapes.name: Marselan
grapes.note: A Cabernet Sauvignon x Grenache cross that has found a second home in Canelones.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Becoming a speciality of Maldonado's cooler, granitic hills and of sparkling wines.

grapes.name: Moscatel (Muscat Hamburg) and Ugni Blanc
grapes.note: Large areas remain for rosé and table wine, though INAVI is encouraging reconversion.

countries.name: Brazil
countries.tagline: Italian immigrants' hill-country sparkling wine, tropical vineyards that harvest twice a year, and 'winter wines' made by reversing the seasons.

stats.note: Vineyard: IBGE 2024 via Embrapa (all grapes, including table and juice grapes). Production: OIV 2025 (2.8 mhl, 15th; +81% on the frost- and flood-hit 2024).

countries.overview:
Brazil is a giant that makes a modest amount of wine, and most of it is not what you might expect. Of about 84,000 ha of vines (IBGE 2024), the majority are American and hybrid grapes such as Isabel, Bordô and Niágara, grown for juice, table grapes and sweet *vinho de mesa*. Fine wine from Vitis vinifera is a smaller but fast-improving slice, concentrated in the far south, and Brazil's best calling card is sparkling wine.

The story is Italian. From 1875 the Brazilian empire settled immigrants from Veneto, Trentino and Lombardy on the forested basalt plateau of the Serra Gaúcha in Rio Grande do Sul, around Bento Gonçalves, Garibaldi, Caxias do Sul and Flores da Cunha. They planted vines on small family plots and built cooperatives such as Aurora (1931); their descendants (Valduga, Miolo, Salton, Pizzato and many more) still run much of the industry. The Serra is humid, with summer rain, so early-ripening Chardonnay and Pinot Noir for traditional-method *espumante* and the aromatic Moscato of Farroupilha became its strengths. Brazil's first geographical indications were born here: Vale dos Vinhedos became an IP in 2002 and Brazil's first wine DO in 2012, and Altos de Pinto Bandeira became the second DO, for traditional-method sparkling wine only, in 2022.

Brazil also breaks the rules of viticulture. In the semi-arid Vale do São Francisco, at 9°S on the border of Pernambuco and Bahia, irrigated vines never go dormant, and growers prune to produce two or more harvests a year, making fruity reds, whites and Muscat sparkling wines in the tropics. In Minas Gerais and São Paulo, the *dupla poda* (double pruning) technique developed by Epamig moves the harvest to the dry, cool winter (June to September), creating 'vinhos de inverno', winter wines of Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc that received their own IG, Sul de Minas, in 2025. Meanwhile the high plateau of Santa Catarina around São Joaquim, at 900 to 1,400 m, makes cool-climate wines under snow-dusted winters, and the Campanha Gaúcha on the Uruguayan border produces sunny reds on sandy soils.

Brazilians drink about 4.4 million hl of wine a year (OIV 2025), much of it imported from Chile, Argentina and Portugal, but local sparkling wine has won a large share of the home market. Vintages swing wildly: the catastrophic floods of 2024 in Rio Grande do Sul cut fine-wine production in the state by about half, and national output rebounded by about 80% in 2025, according to the OIV.

history.title: Portuguese vines
history.text: Portuguese settlers try vines in São Vicente (São Paulo) from the 1530s; Jesuit missions later plant vines in the south, but tropical humidity and disease defeat colonial viticulture.

history.title: Isabel arrives
history.text: The American grape Isabella (Isabel), resistant to fungal disease, is introduced to Rio Grande do Sul and becomes the foundation of Brazilian grape growing.

history.title: Italian colonisation of the Serra Gaúcha
history.text: The first Italian immigrants, from Veneto, Trentino and Lombardy, settle the Serra Gaúcha, founding the colonies of Conde d'Eu (Garibaldi), Dona Isabel (Bento Gonçalves) and Caxias. Wine for family and church follows.

history.title: Cooperativa Aurora
history.text: Sixteen families found the Aurora cooperative in Bento Gonçalves, now Brazil's largest wine cooperative.

history.title: Multinationals and vinifera
history.text: Moët & Chandon, Martini & Rossi and other multinationals invest in the Serra Gaúcha, spreading Vitis vinifera and modern sparkling-wine techniques.

history.title: Brazil's first geographical indication
history.text: On 19 November 2002 INPI grants Vale dos Vinhedos an Indicação de Procedência, the first GI for any product in Brazil, to the producers' association Aprovale.

history.title: Vale dos Vinhedos DO
history.text: On 25 September 2012 Vale dos Vinhedos becomes Brazil's first wine Denominação de Origem, built on Merlot and Chardonnay.

history.title: IGs spread
history.text: INPI recognises Campanha Gaúcha (2020), Vinhos de Altitude de Santa Catarina (2021), Altos de Pinto Bandeira DO for sparkling wine (2022), Bituruna (2022) and Vale do São Francisco, the first tropical wine IG in the world (2022).

history.title: The great flood
history.text: Floods in Rio Grande do Sul in 2024, after heavy rain in late 2023, hit the vineyards of the Serra Gaúcha; fine-wine production in the state falls by about half.

history.title: Winter wines win a GI
history.text: INPI grants the IP Sul de Minas for 'vinhos de inverno', double-pruned wines harvested between June and September, Brazil's 13th wine GI.

countries.classification:
Brazilian wine geographical indications are granted by INPI (the national industrial property institute) under Law 9.279 of 1996, with technical support from Embrapa Uva e Vinho. There are two kinds. An *Indicação de Procedência* (IP) protects a place known for a product; a *Denominação de Origem* (DO) requires that the wine's qualities be due essentially to the place, natural and human factors combined. Each has a *caderno de especificações técnicas* with permitted varieties, yields, area of production and processing, and a numbered seal; many IPs require 85% of grapes from the area, and wines are tasted by a regulatory council.

As of 2025 Brazil had 13 wine GIs: two DOs (Vale dos Vinhedos 2012, Altos de Pinto Bandeira 2022) and IPs for Vale dos Vinhedos (2002, still active), Pinto Bandeira (2010), Altos Montes (2012), Monte Belo (2013), Farroupilha (2015), Campanha Gaúcha (2020) in Rio Grande do Sul, Vales da Uva Goethe (2012) and Vinhos de Altitude de Santa Catarina (2021) in Santa Catarina, Bituruna (2022) in Paraná, Vale do São Francisco (2022) in Pernambuco and Bahia, and Sul de Minas (2025) in Minas Gerais. Further applications, such as Jundiahy in São Paulo, are under examination. Outside the GIs, Brazilian law separates *vinho fino* (from vinifera grapes) and *vinho de mesa* (often from American or hybrid grapes).
countries.climate_soils:
Brazil's vineyards span from 31°S to 5°S, and three climatic logics coexist. In the temperate south (Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, Paraná), vines follow the normal annual cycle, but summer rain and humidity are the enemy: the Serra Gaúcha gets 1,700 mm or more, mostly during the growing season, so early-ripening grapes, trellis training and fungicides are the rule. Soils there are clays derived from basalt of the Serra Geral formation. The Campanha Gaúcha on the Uruguayan border is drier and sunnier, with sandy, granite-derived soils, and the Santa Catarina plateau (900 to 1,400 m) has cold nights and late harvests.

In the tropical north-east, the Vale do São Francisco has a semi-arid climate with intense sun, about 500 mm of rain and constant warmth; vines are irrigated from the river and can produce two harvests a year, timed by pruning. In the south-east highlands of Minas Gerais and São Paulo, summers are wet but winters dry and cool, so double pruning shifts ripening to the dry season.

grapes.name: Isabel (Isabella) and Bordô
grapes.note: American grapes that still dominate Brazilian vineyards for juice and vinho de mesa.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.note: Backbone of traditional-method sparkling wine in the Serra Gaúcha; a main variety of the Vale dos Vinhedos DO.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.note: For sparkling wine (one of the three grapes of the Altos de Pinto Bandeira DO) and increasingly still reds in Santa Catarina.

grapes.name: Riesling Itálico
grapes.note: Welschriesling, a traditional base for Brazilian sparkling wine and permitted in the Altos de Pinto Bandeira DO.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.note: The red flagship of Vale dos Vinhedos DO, ripening reliably in the humid Serra.

grapes.name: Moscato Branco and other Muscats
grapes.note: Aromatic sweet sparkling Moscatel, the speciality of Farroupilha and the São Francisco valley.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon and Tannat
grapes.note: Important reds of the Campanha Gaúcha and Serra Gaúcha.

grapes.name: Syrah
grapes.note: The leading grape of the 'winter wines' of Minas Gerais and São Paulo, made by double pruning.

grapes.name: Goethe
grapes.note: A historic American-vinifera hybrid of the Urussanga valleys in Santa Catarina, protected by its own IP.

countries.name: Peru
countries.tagline: The cradle of South American wine, where desert vineyards once supplied an empire and now feed pisco stills.

stats.note: ICEX market study 2025: about 13,000 ha of grapes for wine and pisco; production 19.2 million litres in 2024 (PRODUCE reported 19.1 million litres in 2023).

countries.overview:
Peru is where South American wine began. Within a decade of Francisco Pizarro's conquest of the Inca empire, Spanish settlers had planted vines in the irrigated desert valleys of the south coast, and by the late 16th century the valleys of Ica, Pisco, Moquegua and Arequipa held the largest vineyards in the Americas. Their wine travelled by mule to the silver mines of Potosí, in today's Bolivia, then the largest city in the Americas, where workers were partly paid in wine, and to Lima, capital of the viceroyalty. Peruvian vines also seeded Chile and, through Chile, Argentina.

That golden age ended in stages. The Spanish crown restricted wine exports from Peru to protect Spanish producers; the earthquake of 1687 destroyed the cellars and clay *botijas* of Ica and Pisco; producers turned to distilling, and by 1764 pisco made up 90% of the grape drinks of the region. The expulsion of the Jesuits in 1767 cost the vineyards their best managers, and in the 19th century cotton, booming during the American Civil War, replaced vines on the coast. Pisco, a grape brandy distilled from fresh must and named after the port of Pisco, became Peru's national spirit and its grapes' main destiny.

Today Peru has roughly 13,000 ha of grapes for wine and pisco and makes about 19 million litres of wine a year, most of it sweet or semi-sweet for the home market, dominated by Tabernero and Santiago Queirolo. A small quality scene has grown around Tacama, Ica's historic estate, Intipalka and boutique producers in Ica, Cañete (Lunahuaná), Arequipa and Moquegua. Desert conditions, almost no rain and cooling from the Humboldt Current make dry wines possible; most vines are ungrafted. Peru claims exclusive rights to the name pisco, and its 1991 pisco denomination covers Lima, Ica, Arequipa, Moquegua and parts of Tacna.

history.title: First vineyards in Ica
history.text: Spanish settlers, Francisco de Carabantes among them, plant Vitis vinifera in Ica's desert valley; the vines later spread to Chile.

history.title: Supplying the viceroyalty
history.text: Vineyards in Ica, Pisco, Nazca, Moquegua and Arequipa become the largest in the Americas, shipping wine to Lima and the silver city of Potosí.

history.title: Earthquake ends the wine boom
history.text: A great earthquake destroys Villa de Pisco and Ica, their cellars and clay jars; distilling grows in importance.

history.title: Pisco takes over; Jesuits expelled
history.text: By 1764 pisco represents 90% of grape beverages; in 1767 the Jesuits are expelled and their vineyards auctioned.

history.title: Cotton replaces vines
history.text: High cotton prices during the American Civil War push coastal growers from vineyards to cotton.

history.title: The Olaechea family buys Tacama
history.text: Manuel Pablo Olaechea acquires Hacienda Tacama in Ica; in the 20th century the family hires French consultants, including Émile Peynaud, and modernises Peruvian winemaking.

history.title: Pisco denomination of origin
history.text: Peru establishes the pisco DO covering Lima, Ica, Arequipa, Moquegua and the Tacna valleys of Locumba, Sama and Caplina.

countries.classification: Peru has no wine appellation system comparable to Chile's or Argentina's. The protected name that matters is the denomination of origin *Pisco*, established in 1991, which covers the coastal valleys of Lima, Ica, Arequipa, Moquegua and Tacna (Locumba, Sama and Caplina valleys) and specifies eight pisco grapes (Quebranta, Negra Criolla, Mollar, Uvina, Italia, Torontel, Moscatel and Albilla) and production rules. Peru contests Chile's use of the name pisco, which Chile protected in its own law in 1931; international recognition is split between the two countries. Wine labels may name valleys or regions without a formal appellation.
countries.climate_soils: Peru's wine valleys are river oases in one of the driest deserts on Earth, the coastal Atacama-Sechura desert, with almost no rain. The cold Humboldt Current cools the coast and brings morning fog, and vineyards in Ica sit at about 400 to 500 m, with sandy alluvial soils irrigated from rivers and wells. Further south, Moquegua and Arequipa's valleys (Majes, Vítor) are higher and more continental. Phylloxera has not been a significant problem in the sandy desert soils, so own-rooted vines are common.

grapes.name: Quebranta
grapes.note: Peru's emblematic pisco grape, a non-aromatic black grape born in Peru from Listán Prieto (Negra Criolla) and Mollar.

grapes.name: Negra Criolla
grapes.note: Listán Prieto, the colonial grape (Mission, País, Criolla Chica), used for pisco and traditional wine.

grapes.name: Moscatel, Italia, Torontel
grapes.note: Aromatic grapes for pisco acholado and aromático, and for sweet wines.

grapes.name: Malbec, Tannat, Petit Verdot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah
grapes.note: Grown in Ica and other valleys for modern dry reds.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
grapes.note: For dry whites in Ica's estates.

countries.name: Bolivia
countries.tagline: Some of the world's highest vineyards, where wine and singani grow above 1,600 m on the edge of the tropics.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 3,478 ha of grapes in 2024 (all uses). Tarija holds about 80 percent of Bolivia's wine industry; Correo del Sur (2021) put Tarija's grape area at about 5,000 ha. No reliable national wine-production figure; FAOSTAT carries only an outside estimate (about 8,000 t in 2023)

countries.overview:
Bolivia makes wine in a place where vines should not grow: at 21°S, inside the tropics, but high in the Andes. Almost all vineyards sit between about 1,600 and 3,000 m, so the altitude replaces latitude, nights are cold and the sunlight is fierce. That combination gives aromatic grapes and deeply coloured reds, and it is the selling point of the small modern industry centred on the Tarija valley in the south of the country.

Vines arrived from Peru with Spanish settlers and missionaries in the 16th century to supply wine for Mass and for the booming silver city of Potosí. The earliest documented vineyards are in the Tarija valley around 1589 to 1590, and in the Cinti valley of Chuquisaca, where colonial haciendas trained vines up native molle and chañar trees, a practice that survives in vineyards 100 to 200 years old. For centuries most grapes went to *singani*, a fragrant brandy distilled from Muscat of Alexandria that Bolivia protects as a denomination of origin.

Modern winemaking dates from the 1960s and 1970s, when producers such as Kohlberg and Kuhlmann moved operations to Tarija and imported European technology. Today wineries including Kohlberg, Aranjuez, Campos de Solana, La Concepción, Casa Vieja and Magnus make Tannat, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and aromatic whites, and a revival of old Criolla and Moscatel vines in Cinti has drawn attention abroad. Bolivia celebrates a national day of wine and singani on the last Friday of February.

history.title: First documented vineyards in Tarija
history.text: Documents of Luis de Fuentes y Vargas, founder of Tarija, mention vineyards in the Tarija valley, including at Tolomosa, the earliest records of vines in Bolivia.

history.title: Wine for Potosí
history.text: Vineyards in Cinti, Tarija and the valleys of Potosí department supply wine and aguardiente to the silver mines of Potosí, then one of the largest cities in the world.

history.title: First winery in Cinti
history.text: The first industrial winery is established at San Pedro near Camargo in Chuquisaca, starting with singani.

history.title: Tarija modernises
history.text: Producers such as Kuhlmann (which moves from Cinti to Tarija in 1973) and Kohlberg invest in European equipment; a national viticulture centre is created in 1986.

history.title: Singani denomination of origin
history.text: Law 1334 recognises Singani as a denomination of origin reserved for brandies made in defined valleys of Tarija, Chuquisaca, La Paz and Potosí.

history.title: National day of wine and singani
history.text: Bolivia establishes a national day of wine and singani, celebrated on the last Friday of February.

countries.classification: Bolivia's only protected wine-sector name is the denomination of origin *Singani*, recognised by Law 1334 of 4 May 1992 and reserved for grape brandy distilled from Muscat of Alexandria wines produced, distilled and bottled in defined zones: the central valley and provinces of Tarija (Cercado, Avilés, Méndez, Arce), the Nor and Sud Cinti valleys of Chuquisaca, Luribay, Sapahaqui and the Loayza and Murillo provinces of La Paz, and valleys of Potosí department such as Cotagaita and Turuchipa. 'Gran singani' must come from grapes grown above 1,600 m. Wines carry place names (Tarija, Valle de Cinti) without a formal appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Bolivian vineyards are high-altitude, subtropical and semi-arid. In Tarija's central valley (about 1,700 to 2,100 m) days are warm, nights cool and rain falls mostly in summer; winds help dry the vines. Cinti, at about 2,400 m, is a narrow canyon of red rock. Intense ultraviolet radiation thickens grape skins and builds aromatics. Soils are alluvial and colluvial, derived from erosion of the surrounding peaks, with clay and sandy loams.

grapes.name: Muscat of Alexandria (Moscatel de Alejandría)
grapes.note: The main grape, used above all for singani.

grapes.name: Tannat
grapes.note: The leading quality red of Tarija, thick-skinned and suited to altitude.

grapes.name: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Merlot
grapes.note: Modern reds from Tarija's wineries.

grapes.name: Negra Criolla (Listán Prieto) and Vischoqueña
grapes.note: Colonial grapes surviving in old Cinti vineyards trained up trees.

grapes.name: Torrontés, Chardonnay, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.note: Aromatic and fresh whites at altitude.

countries.name: Paraguay
countries.tagline: Jesuit mission vines, German settlers and a handful of hectares in the humid hills of Guairá.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 229 ha of grapes in 2022, almost all table grapes (later years are FAO estimates); wine output tiny and unrecorded by OIV

countries.overview:
Paraguay sits squarely in the humid subtropics, with hot summers and heavy rain, and has never been a natural home for the vine. Its wine history comes in three short chapters. In the Jesuit mission period, from the late 16th century, missionaries planted European grapes in the *reducciones* of the south-east to make wine for Mass, as part of self-sufficient Guaraní communities. After independence in the early 19th century, viticulture faded as Paraguayans turned to yerba mate and beer, and sacramental wine was imported.

The modern thread is German. In the early 20th century immigrant families planted vines in the hills of Guairá department; Colonia Independencia, founded in 1919 to 1920 at the foot of the Ybytyruzú range, became the centre of Paraguayan grape growing, mostly for table grapes and fruit wine, and holds a harvest festival each year. A 2016 estimate put the national vineyard at about 150 ha, with only a small share used for wine and a single known commercial winery in Colonia Independencia making a few thousand litres of Riesling and Cabernet Sauvignon. Paraguay had no active wine exports as of 2024.

history.title: Jesuit mission vines
history.text: Jesuit missionaries plant vines in the Guaraní reducciones of south-eastern Paraguay for sacramental wine, until the order's expulsion in 1767.

history.title: Wine fades
history.text: After independence, viticulture declines as yerba mate and beer dominate and Mass wine is imported.

history.title: Carlos Voigt's vineyard
history.text: Carlos Voigt, a grower of German heritage, begins growing grapes in Guairá, marking the rebirth of Paraguayan viticulture.

history.title: Colonia Independencia
history.text: The agricultural colony of Independencia is founded in Guairá; German and Paraguayan families make it the centre of the country's grape growing.

countries.classification: Paraguay has no wine appellation system or specific wine regulation comparable to its neighbours; wine is governed by general food and Mercosur rules.
countries.climate_soils: Humid subtropical climate with abundant rain (often 1,300 to 1,700 mm) and hot summers; the slightly higher, cooler hills of Guairá around the Ybytyruzú range are the only area with a grape-growing tradition.

grapes.name: American and hybrid table grapes
grapes.note: Most of the small vineyard area grows table grapes.

grapes.name: Riesling, Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.note: Grown in tiny quantities by artisanal producers in Colonia Independencia.

countries.name: Colombia
countries.tagline: Equatorial Andean vineyards above 2,000 m in Boyacá, plus a tropical wine industry in the Cauca valley.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figures: 3,003 ha of grapes in 2024, mostly table grapes in Valle del Cauca, and 2,272 t of wine in 2023. A 2026 travel survey counts about nine serious small wineries, while Casa Grajales in Valle del Cauca reports capacity of about 7 million litres a year

countries.overview:
Colombia lies on the equator, so its vineyards have no winter. Two very different wine cultures have grown up anyway. In the tropical Cauca valley around La Unión, Valle del Cauca, the Grajales family has grown table and wine grapes for more than 40 years; their Casa Grajales winery, which reports a capacity of about 7 million litres a year, makes wines from grapes adapted to the tropics, harvested more than once a year, and runs the National Grape Park.

The quality scene is in the high Andes of Boyacá, north of Bogotá, around Villa de Leyva, Sutamarchán and Sáchica in the Alto Ricaurte at about 2,000 to 2,200 m, and in the Valle del Sol near Duitama and Nobsa at about 2,500 m. Cool nights, intense equatorial light and a dry, semi-desert microclimate let growers make Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Pinot Noir and Cabernet. Viñedos Ain Karim, established in 1988 near Sutamarchán and the first to plant Sauvignon Blanc in Colombia, and Marqués de Puntalarga in Nobsa, which grows Pinot Noir and Riesling, are the pioneers. With no seasons, vines can be pruned to give two harvests a year. There is no appellation system; volumes are tiny and almost all is drunk at home.

history.title: Casa Grajales and tropical wine
history.text: The Grajales family develops tropical viticulture in La Unión, Valle del Cauca, producing wine from multiple harvests a year.

history.title: Ain Karim
history.text: Viñedos Ain Karim is established near Sutamarchán, Boyacá, and plants Colombia's first Sauvignon Blanc.

countries.classification: Colombia has no wine appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Equatorial climate with no seasons; quality vineyards rely on altitude (about 2,000 to 2,600 m in Boyacá) for cool nights, and on the dry, semi-desert microclimate of the Alto Ricaurte around Villa de Leyva, with eroded, low-fertility soils. In the Cauca valley, tropical heat allows several harvests a year.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling
grapes.note: The main whites of Boyacá's high vineyards.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah
grapes.note: Reds at altitude.

grapes.name: Tropical-adapted varieties (including Isabella and Moscatel)
grapes.note: In the Cauca valley for Casa Grajales.

countries.name: Venezuela
countries.tagline: Tropical wine in the semi-arid hills of Carora, with two harvests a year.

stats.note: FAOSTAT, official national figure: 1,293 ha of grapes in 2023 (all uses); Bodegas Pomar's vineyards at Altagracia, Lara, cover about 80 ha

countries.overview:
Venezuela's wine industry is essentially one company and one place. In 1985 the brewer Empresas Polar and the Cognac house Martell joined forces to make wine in the tropics; the brand Pomar combines their names. After experimental plantings at El Tocuyo, they settled on the semi-arid plain of Carora in Lara state, a hot, dry area at about 10°N where cacti and goats are more common than vines. Of about 20 European varieties trialled, six adapted to the climate.

Because there is no winter, Pomar's vineyards at Altagracia (about 80 ha) are pruned to produce two harvests a year, and all grapes are picked by hand. The winery makes red, white and rosé wines, traditional-method sparkling wines (its Brut Rosé has won medals abroad) and Ecclesia, the communion wine used in Venezuelan churches. Venezuela has no appellation system, and small artisanal producers aside, the country's wine is Pomar's.

Carora's terroir is a dry, hot plain at a few hundred metres, with poor soils and irrigation; the long, bright days and absence of winter mean the vine never truly rests, so vineyard management (pruning dates, water) does the work that seasons do elsewhere.

history.title: Polar and Martell found Pomar
history.text: Empresas Polar and Martell launch a wine project in Lara; after trials at El Tocuyo, vineyards are planted at Carora.

history.title: Three decades of tropical wine
history.text: Pomar marks three decades of continuous production of still and sparkling wine from twice-yearly harvests.

countries.classification: Venezuela has no wine appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Semi-arid tropical climate at about 10°N; hot all year with little rain on the Carora plain, so vines are irrigated and pruned to fruit twice a year.

grapes.name: Six European varieties adapted at Carora
grapes.note: Selected from about 20 vinifera varieties trialled in the 1980s; they make all of Pomar's red, white, rosé and sparkling wines.

countries.name: Ecuador
countries.tagline: Vineyards on the equator, from the Andes above Quito to the limestone coast of Guayas.

stats.note: Three producers reported as of 2022 (Primicias); no national statistics found.

countries.overview:
Ecuador's wine scene is tiny and improbable: vines growing almost exactly on the equator, without seasons. As of 2022 a Spanish journalist counted three producers. Chaupi Estancia, the oldest, has grown grapes for about 30 years at Yaruquí, near Quito, at about 2,400 m and only 10 km from the equator line, making Palomino, a Chardonnay and Viognier blend, Pinot Noir and experimental blends. Dos Hemisferios, the best known, began as a table-grape grower in San Miguel del Morro on the coast of Guayas and turned to wine from 2004, with limestone soils swept by sea breezes; its first wine, Paradoja (Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec), came from the 2006 harvest. Viña del Guayacán, founded in 2017 at Zapotillo in Loja near the Peruvian border, makes small lots of Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.

With no winter, vines can be harvested twice a year, but they age fast and rarely live beyond about 25 years. There is no appellation system.

history.title: Chaupi Estancia
history.text: Chaupi Estancia begins growing vines at Yaruquí near Quito, at about 2,400 m on the equator.

history.title: Dos Hemisferios
history.text: A table-grape grower in coastal Guayas turns to wine; its first wine, Paradoja, comes from the 2006 harvest.

history.title: Viña del Guayacán
history.text: A third winery is founded at Zapotillo, Loja, near the Peruvian border.

countries.classification: Ecuador has no wine appellation system.
countries.climate_soils: Equatorial: no seasons, so vines are pruned to give up to two harvests a year. The Andes give cool nights at 2,400 m near Quito; the Guayas coast is warm but cooled by the Humboldt Current, with limestone soils.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon, Malbec, Pinot Noir
grapes.note: Main reds.

grapes.name: Chardonnay, Viognier, Palomino
grapes.note: Whites from the highlands and coast.

regions.name: Atacama
regions.tagline: Desert oases of pisco and a few audacious coastal vines.
regions.summary: The northernmost viticultural region, matching the Atacama administrative region, with the Copiapó and Huasco valleys. Almost all of its vineyard serves pisco and table grapes; wine is a curiosity except for coastal experiments in Huasco.
regions.history: Copiapó's wine was a 1950s novelty; Huasco has made sweet *pajarete* since colonial times. Chile's 1931 pisco law already defined Atacama and Coquimbo as the pisco zone.
regions.terroir: Hyper-arid desert with river oases fed by Andean snowmelt; coastal fog makes a few cool sites possible near the sea.
regions.grapes: Moscatel varieties and Pedro Jiménez for pisco; Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah in coastal Huasco.
regions.styles: Pisco above all; small volumes of sweet pajarete and experimental dry wines.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Valle de Copiapó and Valle del Huasco (each = a province).

regions.name: Coquimbo
regions.tagline: Pisco country that learned to make limestone Chardonnay and high-altitude Syrah.
regions.summary: Three transverse valleys, Elqui, Limarí and Choapa, cut across this semi-arid region where Chile narrows between the Andes and the coast. Pisco still takes most of the grapes, but the coastal ends of Limarí and Elqui and the high side valleys of Elqui now produce some of Chile's most distinctive wines.
regions.history: Vines were planted here in the 16th century for wine and aguardiente; pisco became the regional spirit, and the town of La Unión renamed itself Pisco Elqui in 1936. The 1990s brought Falernia in Elqui and Tabalí and Maycas del Limarí in Limarí.
regions.terroir: Desert-edge climate with under 100 mm of rain; Pacific fog and wind near the coast; granite and alluvium, with rare limestone in Limarí's coastal hills; extreme light and cold nights at altitude.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, Pinot Noir; Moscatel and Pedro Jiménez for pisco.
regions.styles: Mineral Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, peppery Syrah, pisco.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Elqui (areas La Serena, Vicuña, Paiguano), Limarí (Ovalle, Monte Patria, Punitaqui, Río Hurtado), Choapa (Salamanca, Illapel).

regions.name: Aconcagua
regions.tagline: Warm Panquehue reds and the cold-coast whites of Casablanca and Leyda.
regions.summary: The Aconcagua viticultural region covers the Valparaíso administrative region. Inland, the Aconcagua Valley gave Chile its first great modern reds; on the coast, Casablanca and San Antonio (Leyda, Lo Abarca) made Chile a white-wine country.
regions.history: Maximiano Errázuriz planted Panquehue in 1870. Casablanca was planted from 1982 by Pablo Morandé; Leyda's vineyards date from 1998 when a pipeline brought Maipo water to the hills; Casa Marín planted Lo Abarca in 2000.
regions.terroir: Warm interior valley with alluvial and colluvial soils; coastal valleys 4 to 30 km from a cold ocean with granite, clay and occasional limestone; frost and water scarcity are the coastal challenges.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Carmenère inland; Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah on the coast.
regions.styles: Ripe Panquehue reds, saline coastal whites, cool-climate Pinot and Syrah.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Aconcagua (nine areas), Casablanca, San Antonio (zone Leyda with San Juan and Santo Domingo; areas Cartagena, Algarrobo; DO Lo Abarca), plus Marga-Marga and the area Zapallar.

regions.name: Valle Central
regions.tagline: Chile's engine room: Maipo Cabernet, Colchagua Carmenère and Maule's old vines.
regions.summary: The Central Valley region runs from the Santiago basin to southern Maule and makes more than four-fifths of Chile's DO wine. Its four subregions (Maipo, Rapel, Curicó, Maule) contain the country's historic estates, its icon Cabernets, its Carmenère heartland and its largest reserve of old dry-farmed vines.
regions.history: From 16th-century País in Maule through the 19th-century Bordeaux estates of Santiago to the export boom of the 1990s, almost every chapter of Chilean wine was written here.
regions.terroir: A tectonic trough between the Andes and coastal range; alluvial valley floors, Andean colluvial terraces and coastal granite; Mediterranean climate with rain rising southwards from about 300 to over 700 mm.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, País, Carignan, Cinsault.
regions.styles: Everything from bulk varietal wine to Chile's most collectable reds.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Maipo, Rapel (zones Cachapoal, Colchagua), Curicó (zones Teno, Lontué), Maule (zones Claro, Loncomilla, Tutuvén) > areas; plus the 2018 DOs Apalta, Los Lingues and Licantén.

regions.name: Valle del Maipo
regions.tagline: The cradle of Chilean Cabernet, from city-edge estates to Puente Alto's stony terraces.
regions.summary: Maipo covers the Metropolitan Region around Santiago. Its Andean sector, Alto Maipo (Puente Alto, Pirque, Santiago), is the source of Chile's most famous Cabernets: Don Melchor, Almaviva, Viñedo Chadwick, Santa Rita's Casa Real and Cousiño Macul.
regions.history: Silvestre Ochagavía's French vines (1851) were planted here, and the great 19th-century estates followed: Cousiño Macul 1856, Santa Carolina 1875, Santa Rita 1880, Concha y Toro 1883. Carmenère was identified at Viña Carmen in Buin in 1994.
regions.terroir: Alluvial cobbles of the Maipo at 600 to 800 m on the Andean side; warmer clay-loams in the centre; coastal granite in the west. About 300 to 350 mm of rain, cold Andean night winds.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon above all, with Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah and Cabernet Franc.
regions.styles: Structured, long-lived Cabernet and Bordeaux blends; ripe Carmenère.
regions.classification: Subregion with thirteen commune-based areas; growers also speak informally of Alto, Central and Pacific Maipo.

regions.name: Valle del Rapel
regions.tagline: Cachapoal and Colchagua: Carmenère's two homes.
regions.summary: Rapel covers the O'Higgins administrative region through its two zones. Cachapoal has Andean Cabernet and the Carmenère of Peumo; Colchagua has the hillside icons of Apalta, the Andean DO Los Lingues and a cool western frontier reaching Paredones.
regions.history: Colonial haciendas such as Los Lingues and El Huique grew wheat and País; the 1990s Apalta projects of Montes and Lapostolle made Colchagua the face of modern Chilean red wine.
regions.terroir: Andean volcanic and colluvial soils in the east, clay alluvium in the centre, granite hills in the west; warm, sunny summers moderated by sea breezes in the west.
regions.grapes: Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Malbec, Merlot, Carignan.
regions.styles: Rich reds; fresher Syrah and whites in the coastal west.
regions.classification: Subregion > zones Cachapoal (six areas) and Colchagua (twelve areas) > 2018 DOs Apalta and Los Lingues.

regions.name: Valle de Curicó
regions.tagline: Where Miguel Torres started Chile's modern era.
regions.summary: Curicó, 200 km south of Santiago, is a varied, productive valley with two zones, Teno and Lontué, plus the coastal DO Licantén.
regions.history: Torres arrived in 1979 with stainless steel; San Pedro at Molina became one of South America's largest vineyards; Valdivieso has made sparkling wine in Lontué since the 19th century.
regions.terroir: Andean piedmont in the east, alluvial valley floor, dry-farmed hills and coastal slate and clay near the Mataquito mouth.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Carmenère, Chardonnay, País.
regions.styles: Reliable varietal wines, sparkling, and old-vine País from the hills.
regions.classification: Subregion > zones Teno (Rauco, Romeral, Vichuquén) and Lontué (Molina, Sagrada Familia); DO Licantén (2018).

regions.name: Valle del Maule
regions.tagline: Chile's biggest vineyard and its deepest reserve of old dry-farmed vines.
regions.summary: Maule produces almost half of Chile's wine and contains three zones: Claro, Loncomilla and Tutuvén (Cauquenes). Beyond its bulk production, it is the home of old-vine Carignan, País and Cinsault on the granite hills of the coastal secano.
regions.history: País was planted here in the 16th century; Carignan was spread after the 1939 Chillán earthquake; VIGNO began codifying Maule Carignan around 2010.
regions.terroir: Volcanic and alluvial soils on the irrigated plain; granite, maicillo and slate on the dry-farmed coastal hills; about 700 mm of rain.
regions.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Carmenère, País, Carignan, Cinsault, Malbec.
regions.styles: Bulk varietals; earthy, juicy old-vine reds; increasingly natural-leaning País.
regions.classification: Subregion > zones Claro (six areas), Loncomilla (seven areas), Tutuvén (Cauquenes); much of the secano qualifies for the Secano Interior special DO.

regions.name: Sur
regions.tagline: Old País and Cinsault on granite, and Chardonnay in the rain.
regions.summary: The Southern region combines Itata, Bío-Bío and Malleco. Itata's dry-farmed old vines and Malleco's cool Chardonnay make it the most talked-about part of Chile for adventurous drinkers.
regions.history: The colonial heartland of Chilean wine around Concepción and Chillán; bulk wine through the 20th century; reinvented from the 2010s by small producers and natural winemakers.
regions.terroir: Rolling granite hills (maicillo) near the coast, volcanic soils inland and in Malleco; humid, with over 1,000 mm of rain and a shorter season.
regions.grapes: País, Cinsault, Moscatel de Alejandría, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.styles: Light, fragrant reds; dry and orange Moscatel; taut Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Itata (Chillán, Quillón, Portezuelo, Coelemu), Bío-Bío (Yumbel, Mulchén), Malleco (Traiguén); much of it also Secano Interior.

regions.name: Austral
regions.tagline: The lake district and the islands: Chile's southern frontier.
regions.summary: The Austral region runs from Cautín south to wherever vines will grow. It holds the Cautín and Osorno valleys and, since 2025, the Chiloé archipelago.
regions.history: Defined in 1994 with an open southern limit; Casa Silva's Lago Ranco vineyard showed the potential; Chiloé added by Decree 27 (published May 2025).
regions.terroir: Cool, wet temperate climate; volcanic soils; short growing season.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling.
regions.styles: Sparkling and high-acid whites, light Pinot Noir.
regions.classification: Region > subregions Valle del Cautín, Valle de Osorno, Chiloé.

regions.name: Mendoza
regions.tagline: Argentina's wine heartland: 142,800 ha of irrigated vines between the Andes and the desert.
regions.summary: Mendoza holds more than 70% of Argentina's vineyards and grapes. Its five broad zones are the historic Primera Zona of Luján de Cuyo and Maipú, the high Uco Valley, the warm eastern plain, the southern oasis of San Rafael and General Alvear, and the northern desert of Lavalle.
regions.history: Founded in 1561, Mendoza drank and sold wine from the colonial era, but it became the national wine province after the 1853 Quinta Normal, the 1885 railway and mass Italian and Spanish immigration. The 1990s turned it into an international fine-wine region.
regions.terroir: Alluvial fans from the Andes, stony near the mountains and sandy to the east; 500 to 1,600 m; about 200 mm of mostly summer rain; hail, frost and the Zonda wind are the main hazards.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Bonarda, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Criolla Grande, Cereza, Chardonnay, Torrontés, Pedro Giménez.
regions.styles: Red above all, plus traditional-method sparkling, Chardonnay and bulk wine.
regions.classification: Provincial IG > department IGs > district IGs; DOCs Luján de Cuyo and San Rafael.

regions.name: Luján de Cuyo and Maipú
regions.tagline: The Primera Zona: old-vine Malbec on the terraces of the Mendoza river.
regions.summary: Just south of Mendoza city, Luján de Cuyo and Maipú form the traditional first zone of Argentine fine wine, at 750 to 1,100 m along the Mendoza river. Luján holds the country's first DOC and more Malbec than any other department.
regions.history: Italian, Spanish and French families planted here from the late 19th century; Trapiche, López, Lagarde, Norton, Escorihuela and Weinert are among its historic houses, and Catena built its pyramid in Agrelo in the late 1990s.
regions.terroir: Stony alluvial soils near the river (Vistalba, Las Compuertas, Lunlunta, Drummond), deeper clay-loam to the south (Agrelo, Perdriel, Ugarteche).
regions.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bonarda, Chardonnay, Petit Verdot.
regions.styles: Classic, ripe, velvety Malbec; Cabernet blends; sparkling wine.
regions.classification: DOC Luján de Cuyo; IGs Luján de Cuyo, Agrelo, Alto Agrelo, Las Compuertas, Vistalba, Maipú, Lunlunta, Barrancas, Russel, El Paraíso.

regions.name: Valle de Uco
regions.tagline: High, cool and stony: the valley that redefined Argentine Malbec.
regions.summary: The Uco Valley spans Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos at 900 to 1,600 m, about 100 km south-west of Mendoza city. It is the most used IG in Argentina and the home of the country's most detailed terroir mapping.
regions.history: Fruit-growing country until the 1990s, when Catena's Adrianna vineyard (1992), Clos de los Siete (1998), Salentein and others proved its potential. District IGs followed from 2012, and Zuccardi's 2016 winery at Paraje Altamira became a symbol.
regions.terroir: Alluvial fans of stones, sand and calcium carbonate; cold nights, frost and hail; strong UV light.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Semillon, Sauvignon Blanc.
regions.styles: Fresh, floral, chalky Malbec; precise Chardonnay; sparkling base.
regions.classification: Interdepartmental IG Valle de Uco > departments Tupungato, Tunuyán, San Carlos > districts Gualtallary (provisional), El Peral, Los Chacayes, Vista Flores, San Pablo, Paraje Altamira, Pampa El Cepillo, Cordón del Cepillo, La Consulta.

regions.name: East Mendoza
regions.tagline: The volume engine: hot plains, old Bonarda and the Catena family's first vineyard.
regions.summary: Eastern Mendoza (San Martín, Junín, Rivadavia, Santa Rosa, La Paz) holds the largest vineyard area in Argentina on flat, hot plains at 600 to 750 m. It produces most of the country's everyday wine, juice and concentrate, and old-vine Bonarda and Malbec of real character.
regions.history: Settled by Italian and Spanish immigrants after the railway; Nicola Catena planted his first Malbec at Rivadavia in 1902.
regions.terroir: Deep sandy and silty alluvium; warmer and lower than western Mendoza.
regions.grapes: Bonarda, Malbec, Criolla Grande, Cereza, Pedro Giménez, Syrah.
regions.styles: Generous reds, bulk wine, juice.
regions.classification: Department IGs plus district IGs Distrito Medrano and Reducción.

regions.tagline: Mendoza's southern oasis, home of Argentina's second DOC.
regions.summary: The southern oasis of the Diamante and Atuel rivers at 450 to 800 m, about 230 km from Mendoza city. San Rafael has been a DOC since 2007 and is known for fresh, fairly priced reds and sparkling wines.
regions.history: French, Italian and Spanish immigrants built the oasis from the late 19th century; Valentín Bianchi's family winery dates from 1928.
regions.terroir: Alluvial soils, cooler than eastern Mendoza thanks to latitude.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bonarda, Chenin Blanc, Syrah.
regions.styles: Fruity reds, sparkling wine.
regions.classification: DOC San Rafael; IGs San Rafael and General Alvear.
