regions.name: San Juan
regions.tagline: Desert Syrah in the Tulum oasis and high-mountain wine in Calingasta and Pedernal.
regions.summary: Argentina's second wine province, about 39,700 ha, mostly in the hot Tulum valley around the capital, plus the high valleys of Pedernal, Zonda and Calingasta.
regions.history: Vines arrived in the 1560s; the province became a grape, raisin and wine powerhouse after the railway; Syrah took on a provincial identity from the 1990s; three Calingasta IGs were added in 2024.
regions.terroir: Desert climate with under 100 mm of rain; alluvial soils on the Tulum floor; stony, calcareous soils at 1,300 to 1,700 m in Pedernal and Calingasta.
regions.grapes: Syrah, Malbec, Bonarda, Cereza, Criolla, Pedro Giménez, Moscatel de Alejandría, Torrontés Sanjuanino.
regions.styles: Generous Syrah and Malbec; fresh mountain reds; raisins and juice.
regions.classification: Provincial IG > department IGs (19) > Valle del Tulum, Valle del Pedernal, Valle de Zonda, Pozo de los Algarrobos, Barreal, Tamberías, Hilario, Sorocayense.

regions.tagline: Torrontés Riojano's homeland in the Famatina valleys.
regions.summary: La Rioja's wine is concentrated in the Famatina valleys around Chilecito at 1,000 to 1,700 m, the birthplace of Torrontés Riojano. The province's IG carries 'Argentina' in its name to distinguish it from Spain's Rioja.
regions.history: Colonial vineyards for wine and aguardiente; 20th-century cooperatives, especially La Riojana in Chilecito.
regions.terroir: Arid valleys between the Famatina and Velasco ranges; alluvial soils; hot days, cool nights.
regions.grapes: Torrontés Riojano, Malbec, Bonarda, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon.
regions.styles: Aromatic Torrontés, value reds.
regions.classification: Provincial IG La Rioja Argentina > Valles del Famatina > department IGs and Valle de Chañarmuyo.

regions.tagline: High Andean oases of Criolla, Torrontés and altitude reds.
regions.summary: Catamarca's vineyards lie in the Fiambalá and Tinogasta valleys, around Belén, Pomán and in Santa María at the southern end of the Calchaquí valleys.
regions.history: Colonial vineyards and adobe wineries; a revival of home-made *vino patero* and modern altitude projects.
regions.terroir: Desert valleys at 1,200 to 2,000 m; sandy and stony soils.
regions.grapes: Torrontés Riojano, Malbec, Syrah, Criolla.
regions.styles: Traditional and modern altitude wines.
regions.classification: Provincial IG > department IGs Tinogasta, Belén, Pomán, Santa María.

regions.tagline: The Calchaquí valleys: Torrontés at Cafayate and Malbec above 3,000 m.
regions.summary: Salta's vineyards sit almost entirely in the Calchaquí valleys from Cafayate (1,700 m) to Cachi and Payogasta (over 3,000 m). Malbec covers 46% of the vineyard; Torrontés from Cafayate is the regional signature.
regions.history: Jesuits and Spanish settlers planted Criolla; Colomé was founded in 1831 and planted French Malbec and Cabernet in the 1850s; Swiss Donald Hess bought it in 2001 and planted the 3,111 m Altura Máxima vineyard.
regions.terroir: Sandy and gravelly alluvium, granite slopes; extreme UV, cold nights, under 200 mm of rain.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Torrontés Riojano, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Criolla Chica.
regions.styles: Floral Torrontés; deep, tannic altitude reds.
regions.classification: Provincial IG Salta; interprovincial Valles Calchaquíes; Valle de Cafayate, Molinos, Cachi, San Carlos, Valle de Pucará.

regions.history: A modern project scene from the 2000s around Maimará, Tilcara and Huacalera.
regions.terroir: Stony alluvial terraces, extreme altitude and light.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Merlot.

regions.summary: Tucumán's wine comes from the Tafí del Valle department on the dry western side of the Aconquija range, at Colalao del Valle and Amaicha del Valle.
regions.history: Small family and community wineries, including the Amaicha indigenous community's winery.
regions.terroir: Arid valleys at about 1,700 to 2,000 m.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Torrontés.
regions.styles: Altitude reds and aromatic whites.

regions.name: Patagonia
regions.tagline: Wind, cold nights and old vines along the Río Negro.
regions.summary: Patagonian wine is centred on the Alto Valle of the Río Negro and the San Patricio del Chañar plateau in Neuquén, with outposts in La Pampa and Chubut down to 45°S.
regions.history: Humberto Canale planted in 1909; old Malbec, Merlot and Pinot Noir vineyards of the 1930s to 1950s were rediscovered by Noemía (2001) and Chacra (2004); Neuquén's desert projects date from the late 1990s.
regions.terroir: Irrigated river valleys at 250 to 400 m; alluvial soils; constant wind, cool nights, long summer days.
regions.grapes: Malbec, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Semillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay.
regions.styles: Fresh, perfumed reds; Pinot Noir; crisp whites; sparkling wine in Chubut.
regions.classification: Interprovincial IG Patagonia; provincial IGs Neuquén and Río Negro; Alto Valle de Río Negro; department IGs; Chubut IGs Trevelin, El Hoyo, Sarmiento.

regions.summary: Córdoba's small wine area sits around Colonia Caroya and Jesús María, the Traslasierra valley and Cruz del Eje.
regions.history: Jesuit estancias made wine from the 17th century; Friulian immigrants founded Colonia Caroya in 1878.
regions.terroir: Sierras and piedmont plains with summer rain.
regions.grapes: Isabella (for Frambua), Malbec and other vinifera.
regions.styles: Traditional Frambua and small-scale vinifera wines.
regions.classification: Provincial IG Córdoba Argentina; IGs Colón, Colonia Caroya, Cruz del Eje, San Javier.

regions.history: Mostly 21st-century projects; Trapiche's coastal vineyard at Chapadmalal and IGs from 2011 (Villa Ventana) to 2024 (Tandil).
regions.terroir: Cool, humid maritime and Pampas climates; loess and stony hill soils.
regions.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Albariño, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Malbec.
regions.styles: Saline whites, light reds, sparkling wine.
regions.classification: IGs Chapadmalal, Villa Ventana, Balcarce, Tandil.

regions.grapes: Tannat, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Marselan, Sauvignon Blanc, Albariño.

regions.name: Serra Gaúcha

regions.summary: The basalt plateau of north-east Rio Grande do Sul around Bento Gonçalves, Garibaldi, Caxias do Sul, Flores da Cunha and Farroupilha makes the majority of Brazil's wine. It holds both of Brazil's DOs and four more IPs.
regions.history: Settled by Italian immigrants from 1875; cooperatives such as Aurora (1931); multinational investment in the 1970s; Brazil's first GI in 2002.
regions.terroir: Clay soils from basalt; 400 to 800 m; humid subtropical climate with heavy summer rain.
regions.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling Itálico, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Moscato, plus American Isabel and Bordô.

appellations.name: Atacama
appellations.grapes: Moscatel varieties and Pedro Jiménez (mostly for pisco); Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah
appellations.nerd_note: Huasco's traditional sweet *pajarete*, a cooked-must style from the upper valley around Alto del Carmen, is one of the oldest wine styles still made in Chile.
appellations.summary: The northernmost of Chile's six viticultural regions, matching the administrative Región de Atacama and split into the Copiapó and Huasco valleys. This is pisco country first and wine country a distant second: SAG's 2024 census counted about 560 ha of pisco grapes against under 60 ha of wine grapes. What wine there is comes from desert river oases fed by Andean snowmelt, plus a few daring coastal plantings in Huasco where the Pacific fog makes cool-climate Chardonnay and Pinot Noir possible at latitude 28°S.

appellations.name: Coquimbo
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Syrah, Pinot Noir; Pedro Jiménez and Moscatel for pisco
appellations.nerd_note: The region produced 58 million litres of DO wine in 2026, 7.4% of Chile's DO total, a share far larger than its reputation as 'pisco country' suggests.
appellations.summary: Chile's second viticultural region from the north, matching the Coquimbo administrative region and its three transverse valleys, Elqui, Limarí and Choapa. Here the Atacama Desert gives way to semi-arid scrub; the country narrows to under 200 km and the Andes and the coastal range nearly touch. Pisco still dominates the vineyard (about 8,700 ha of pisco grapes in 2024), but since the 1990s the region has become the source of some of Chile's most distinctive wines: chalk-influenced Chardonnay from Limarí's coastal hills and peppery high-altitude Syrah from Elqui.

appellations.name: Aconcagua
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.nerd_note: Zapallar and the Marga-Marga valley sit directly under the region in the decree's table, outside any subregion.
appellations.summary: The viticultural region that matches the Valparaíso administrative region. It is named after the Aconcagua river and mountain (6,961 m, the highest peak outside Asia), but its modern fame rests as much on the cool coastal valleys of Casablanca and San Antonio as on the warm inland Aconcagua Valley itself. SAG's 2024 census put its wine vineyard at about 7,760 ha, roughly two-thirds white varieties, which tells you how the coast has reshaped it.

appellations.name: Valle Central
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, País, Carignan
appellations.nerd_note: 'Valle Central' on a label is often a blend across all four subregions, the Chilean equivalent of a regional entry-level wine.
appellations.summary: The Central Valley region is the engine of Chilean wine: the long tectonic trough between the Andes and the coastal range from Santiago's Chacabuco province south to Cauquenes and Linares in Maule. It holds four subregions (Maipo, Rapel, Curicó, Maule) and, by SAG's figures, made 661.6 million litres of DO wine in 2026, 83.7% of the national total. The name covers everything from Puente Alto's Cabernet terraces to 19th-century País vines on the Maule dry-farmed hills, so on a serious bottle you will almost always see a subregion, zone or area instead.

appellations.name: Sur
appellations.grapes: País, Cinsault, Moscatel de Alejandría, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling
appellations.nerd_note: SAG counted 10,323 ha of wine grapes in Ñuble alone in 2024, more than the entire Metropolitan Region that holds the Maipo.
appellations.summary: The Southern region (Región del Sur) runs from the Ñuble river country to Malleco in Araucanía and contains the Itata, Bío-Bío and Malleco valleys. It is where Chile's colonial viticulture survived most intact: dry-farmed, head-trained País, Cinsault and Moscatel on granite hills that never saw the 1980s modernisation. Rainfall is higher (often over 1,000 mm), summers shorter, and the new wave of growers has turned it into the most exciting source of old-vine and cool-climate wine in the country.

appellations.name: Austral
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Gewürztraminer
appellations.nerd_note: The only Chilean region whose southern limit is not a line on a map but a viticultural condition written into the decree.
appellations.summary: Chile's southernmost viticultural region, defined in 1994 as running from Cautín province 'as far south as soil and climate allow the vine to grow'. It began with the Cautín and Osorno valleys; in 2025 a decree added the Chiloé archipelago as a third subregion, explicitly justified by climate change pushing viable viticulture south. Vineyards are tiny (a few dozen hectares across Araucanía, Los Ríos and Los Lagos in 2024) and focus on Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling with high natural acidity.

appellations.name: Valle de Copiapó
appellations.grapes: Moscatel varieties, Pedro Jiménez
appellations.summary: Subregion matching Copiapó province, a desert river oasis at about 27°S where table grapes and pisco grapes vastly outnumber wine vines. Wine production here was a 1950s novelty around the city of Copiapó and remains marginal; the valley matters to the atlas as the northern edge of Chile's DO system.

appellations.name: Valle del Huasco
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah; Moscatel for pisco and pajarete
appellations.nerd_note: Tara's coastal vineyard gets almost no rain at all: the vines live on fog, drip lines and stubbornness.
appellations.summary: Subregion matching Huasco province, where the Huasco river cuts from the Andes to the sea past Vallenar and Freirina. The upper valley around Alto del Carmen is pisco and *pajarete* country (a traditional sweet wine made from concentrated must); the coastal end has become a laboratory for desert-coast viticulture, where Viña Ventisquero's Tara project grows Chardonnay and Pinot Noir on saline, calcareous soils a few kilometres from the Pacific.

appellations.name: Valle del Elqui
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Carmenère, Sauvignon Blanc, Pedro Jiménez; Moscatel and Pedro Jiménez for pisco
appellations.terroir: Granite and colluvial soils on steep valley sides; strong UV, very low humidity and big day-night swings at altitude; the coastal end is cooled by the Pacific fog called *camanchaca*.
appellations.nerd_note: Falernia's founders came from Trentino in Italy and named the estate after Falernian, the most famous wine of ancient Rome.
appellations.summary:
The Elqui Valley, about 500 km north of Santiago, is one of the clearest skies on Earth (hence its observatories) and the spiritual home of Chilean pisco. Vineyards climb from the coast near La Serena to around 2,000 m in the side valleys above Vicuña and Paiguano, and since Viña Falernia began bottling in the late 1990s the valley has shown that Syrah grown in intense light and cold nights can be peppery, floral and fresh rather than jammy. Rainfall is under 100 mm a year, so every vine is drip-irrigated with snowmelt from the Elqui river.

Most of the valley's grapes still go to pisco, especially Moscatel and Pedro Jiménez, and the town of Pisco Elqui renamed itself in 1936 to stake Chile's claim in the long dispute with Peru over the name. For wine drinkers the interest lies in the extremes: Sauvignon Blanc and Syrah from wind-cooled sites near the coast, and high-altitude Syrah, Garnacha and Carignan from the granitic slopes of Paiguano and Alcohuaz.

appellations.name: La Serena
appellations.summary: Area matching La Serena commune at the mouth of the Elqui, the valley's coastal end. Morning fog and sea breezes make it the coolest part of Elqui, suited to Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay, though vineyards are scattered among the city's sprawl and farms. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Vicuña
appellations.summary: Area matching Vicuña commune, the heart of the middle Elqui valley and home of Viña Falernia, where wide valley-floor vineyards sit at around 500 to 700 m between bare granite mountains. Syrah and Carmenère ripen easily in the intense sun; the nights, cooled by air draining off the Andes, keep the wines aromatic. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Paiguano
appellations.nerd_note: The decree spells it Paiguano; road signs and most maps say Paihuano.
appellations.summary: Area matching Paiguano commune (also spelled Paihuano), the upper Elqui where the Claro river valley climbs past Pisco Elqui towards Alcohuaz. Small terraced vineyards at 1,500 to around 2,000 m give some of the highest-altitude wines in Chile, mostly Syrah, Garnacha, Carignan and Malbec, alongside traditional pisco grapes. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Valle del Limarí
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Syrah
appellations.terroir: Calcareous clays and limestone in the coastal hills (Talinay, Quebrada Seca), alluvial terraces along the river, granite inland; persistent morning fog, strong afternoon winds and almost no rain.
appellations.nerd_note: Quebrada Seca, Limarí's best-known Chardonnay site, was refused its own DO in 2018 because it is not a recognised named locality, only a dry gully.
appellations.summary:
Limarí, about 400 km north of Santiago, holds something almost unique in Chile: limestone. Calcium carbonate deposits in the coastal hills of Talinay and Quebrada Seca, a rarity in a country of granite and alluvium, give Limarí Chardonnay a salty, chalky tension that winemakers compare to Chablis without blushing. The Pacific is only 20 to 30 km away and the morning *camanchaca* fog rolls up the valley daily, so this desert edge (under 100 mm of rain) behaves like a cool-climate region.

Vines were planted here in colonial times, but the modern story begins in the 1990s with Tabalí, Concha y Toro's Maycas del Limarí project and De Martino scouting for new terroir. Chardonnay is the headline, with Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and cool, savoury Syrah close behind. Inland, in Monte Patria and Río Hurtado, the valley is warmer and drier and still mostly devoted to pisco and table grapes.

appellations.name: Ovalle
appellations.summary: Area matching Ovalle commune, the lower Limarí valley that includes the limestone hills of Talinay and Quebrada Seca near the coast. This is where Limarí's reputation for mineral Chardonnay and Pinot Noir is made, by Tabalí, Concha y Toro and others. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Monte Patria
appellations.summary: Area matching Monte Patria commune in the upper Limarí basin, where the Grande and Huatulame rivers come down from the Andes. Warm, dry and high, it grows mainly pisco and table grapes, with some Syrah and Cabernet for wine. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Punitaqui
appellations.summary: Area matching Punitaqui commune, a small inland basin south of Ovalle between the coastal and Andean ranges. Vineyards are few and mostly for pisco and bulk wine. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Río Hurtado
appellations.summary: Area matching Río Hurtado commune, a narrow Andean side valley of the Limarí known for dark skies and small fruit farms. Its few vineyards serve pisco and local wine. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Valle del Choapa
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: The Choapa Valley, about 400 km north of Santiago, is where Chile is narrowest and the Andes and coastal range almost touch. It has two areas, Illapel and Salamanca, few vineyards and almost no wineries of its own; grapes grown on rocky foothill soils here, mainly Syrah and Cabernet Sauvignon, are trucked south to wineries elsewhere, prized for high acidity and low pH.

appellations.name: Salamanca
appellations.summary: Area matching Salamanca commune in the upper Choapa valley, an Andean foothill zone of stony soils and mining country. Syrah and Cabernet from here go mostly to wineries outside the valley. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Illapel
appellations.summary: Area matching Illapel commune in the Choapa valley, around the provincial capital. Vineyards are scattered and small, part of a mixed farming landscape of table grapes and fruit. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Valle del Aconcagua
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Syrah, Merlot; Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir near the coast
appellations.terroir: Alluvial and colluvial soils on the warm valley floor at Panquehue; granite and schist hillsides; coastal sites near Zapallar and Quillota with clay over schist and a strong Pacific influence.
appellations.nerd_note: 'Aconcagua Costa' and 'Aconcagua Andes' on Errázuriz labels are the 2011 complement terms in action, not separate appellations.
appellations.summary:
The Aconcagua Valley is where Chile's fine-wine revival found its first great red. In 1870 Maximiano Errázuriz planted French vines at Panquehue, about 100 km north of Santiago, on the warm inland floor of a valley that funnels Andean snowmelt from Aconcagua mountain to the sea at Concón. Panquehue's heat, which in the 1990s produced the Cabernet-Carmenère blend Seña and the Don Maximiano Founder's Reserve, made Aconcagua synonymous with dense, sun-built reds.

The valley is more varied than that. It runs from the Andean foothills (Calle Larga, San Esteban, Santa María), through the warm central basin of Panquehue, Catemu and Llaillay, to the coastal hills of Quillota, Hijuelas and Zapallar. Since 2005 Errázuriz has planted its Manzanar vineyard about 12 km from the Pacific, labelled Aconcagua Costa, where schist and clay soils give taut Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Seña moved its own vineyard to the Ocoa hills of Hijuelas, a biodynamic hillside between the two climates.

Taste the contrast: Panquehue Cabernet and Syrah are broad and ripe, Aconcagua Costa whites are saline and lean, and the 2004 Berlin Tasting, where Viñedo Chadwick 2000 and Seña 2001 beat first-growth Bordeaux blind, put the whole valley on the world map.

appellations.name: Panquehue
appellations.summary: Area matching Panquehue commune, the warm heart of the inland Aconcagua valley and home of Viña Errázuriz since 1870, with its Max Viñedo hillside vineyard and the Don Maximiano estate. Long, hot summer afternoons give ripe, structured Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Carmenère. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Quillota
appellations.summary: Area matching Quillota commune in the lower Aconcagua valley, famous for avocados and cherimoyas. Its vineyards benefit from the coastal influence and suit Syrah and cooler-climate reds. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Hijuelas
appellations.summary: Area matching Hijuelas commune between Quillota and Llaillay. It includes the Ocoa hills where Seña planted its biodynamic hillside vineyard in 1998, after the wine's early vintages were sourced from Panquehue. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Catemu
appellations.summary: Area matching Catemu commune, a warm side basin of the Aconcagua valley with mixed fruit farming and some vineyards for red varieties. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Llaillay
appellations.summary: Area matching Llaillay commune (Llay-Llay on many maps), a windy gap where the Aconcagua valley narrows; vineyards here are few and mostly red. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: San Felipe
appellations.summary: Area matching San Felipe commune, the provincial capital of the upper Aconcagua valley, warm and irrigated, with plantings of Cabernet Sauvignon and Syrah among fruit orchards. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Santa María
appellations.summary: Area matching Santa María commune in the upper Aconcagua, at the foot of the Andes. Cool mountain air at night helps reds keep freshness. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Calle Larga
appellations.summary: Area matching Calle Larga commune near Los Andes, on the Andean piedmont where stony soils and mountain breezes shape fresher reds. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: San Esteban
appellations.summary: Area matching San Esteban commune, the highest part of the Aconcagua valley. Viña San Esteban's In Situ project farms here, beside petroglyph-covered rocks of Paidahuen hill that recall the valley's pre-Hispanic people. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Zapallar
appellations.summary: Area matching Zapallar commune on the Pacific coast north of Valparaíso, listed in the decree directly under the Aconcagua region. A handful of new coastal vineyards here grow Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah in fog and sea wind; it marks the northern edge of Aconcagua's coastal frontier. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Valle del Marga-Marga
appellations.summary: A small coastal subregion matching Quilpué commune, inland from Viña del Mar, listed directly under the Aconcagua region. It is cool, hilly and close to the sea, with only a few vineyards, mostly for white wine and Pinot Noir. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Valle de Casablanca
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah, Gewürztraminer
appellations.terroir: Granitic hills with clay-loam and sandy topsoils on the valley floor; marine fog and afternoon winds; frequent spring frost; no river irrigation, so wells and reservoirs.
appellations.nerd_note: Casablanca is the exception to Chile's ungrafted-vine story: nematodes in its sandy soils make rootstocks a sensible choice here.
appellations.summary:
Casablanca turned Chile into a white-wine country. In 1982 Pablo Morandé planted vines in this flat, frost-prone valley halfway between Santiago and Valparaíso, against the advice of almost everyone, because the Pacific 20 to 30 km away pushes cold fog and wind through gaps in the coastal range every afternoon. The result was the first truly cool-climate wine region in a country that had only known the warm Central Valley: crisp Sauvignon Blanc, citrus-and-butter Chardonnay and, as growers moved up the slopes, Pinot Noir and cool Syrah.

The valley rises gently from about 200 m in the east to 400 m near the coast, and the western end (Lo Ovalle, Las Dichas, Tapihue) is markedly cooler than the eastern Lo Vásquez end along Ruta 68. Spring frost is the great hazard, and water is scarce: there is no Andean river, so growers rely on wells and reservoirs. Casablanca is also one of the few Chilean regions where grafting is common, because its sandy soils host nematodes.

In the glass, good Casablanca Sauvignon shows grapefruit, herbs and a salty finish; Chardonnay is fresher than Central Valley versions; Pinot Noir and Syrah from Matetic-style slopes are peppery and red-fruited. The entire commune is one subregion with no internal areas, and labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Valle de San Antonio
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Syrah
appellations.terroir: Granite and decomposed granite with clay topsoils, calcareous patches at Lo Abarca; 4 to 15 km from the Pacific; morning fog, cold breezes, low rainfall and water scarcity.
appellations.nerd_note: Matetic's estate straddles the border with Casablanca, and its Rosario valley vineyards sit in San Antonio's Cartagena area.
appellations.summary:
The San Antonio Valley, matching San Antonio province on the coast west of Santiago, is the sharpest of Chile's cool-climate frontiers. The first vines went in only in the late 1990s and 2000: Viña Leyda's founders piped water 8 km from the Maipo river to plant the Leyda hills in 1998, and María Luz Marín planted her vineyard at Lo Abarca, 4 km from the sea, in 2000. Cold Humboldt Current water offshore keeps summers cool, and sites sit 4 to 15 km from the Pacific on granitic hills, some with a cap of clay and patches of limestone.

The wines are thrillingly tense: Sauvignon Blanc with crushed-rock salinity and passion fruit, Chardonnay with high acidity, savoury Pinot Noir and some of Chile's most peppery Syrah. The subregion contains the Valle de Leyda zone (San Juan and Santo Domingo areas), the areas of Cartagena and Algarrobo, and since 2018 the tiny Lo Abarca DO. Labels from all of it may carry the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Valle de Leyda
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Syrah
appellations.summary: Leyda is a zone of the San Antonio Valley, made of the San Juan (San Antonio commune) and Santo Domingo areas, and the name most cool-climate fans know. Its gently rolling hills sit 8 to 15 km from the Pacific; the decisive moment came in 1998 when the Fernández family ran an 8 km pipeline from the Maipo to irrigate Viña Leyda. Today Leyda Sauvignon Blanc is a benchmark of saline, citrus-driven Chilean white, with Pinot Noir and Chardonnay close behind.

appellations.name: San Juan
appellations.summary: Area of the Valle de Leyda zone defined by San Antonio commune, covering much of the Leyda hills around the village of Leyda itself. Viña Leyda and Amayna farm here on granite with clay, a few kilometres from the sea. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Santo Domingo
appellations.summary: Area of the Valle de Leyda zone defined by Santo Domingo commune, south of the port of San Antonio near the Maipo river mouth. Coastal vineyards here are among the coolest in the zone. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Cartagena
appellations.summary: Area matching Cartagena commune on the San Antonio coast. It includes the village of Lo Abarca (which became its own DO in 2018) and Matetic's Rosario valley vineyards, a few kilometres inland. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Algarrobo
appellations.summary: Area matching Algarrobo commune on the northern coast of San Antonio province, a beach-resort town with a few cool vineyards in the hills behind it. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Lo Abarca
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir, Syrah
appellations.nerd_note: Casa Marín's single-vineyard names (Cipreses, Laurel, Miramar) map individual slopes of this one hillside DO.
appellations.summary: Lo Abarca is Chile's tiniest DO, about 44.5 ha around a hamlet 4 km from the Pacific in the San Antonio Valley, and in practice it is one producer's vineyard: Casa Marín, planted from 2000 by María Luz Marín against every adviser's warning. Created by decree in 2018 (one of the first DOs not tied to a commune), it has calcareous and granitic slopes, cold fog and wind, and produces Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir and Syrah of startling salinity. Labels carry the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Valle del Maipo
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah, Cabernet Franc; some Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.terroir: Stony alluvial terraces of the Maipo river (Puente Alto's 'piedmont' gravels), colluvial fans at the foot of the Andes, warmer clay-loams in the centre and granitic coastal hills in the west; Mediterranean climate, about 300 to 350 mm of winter rain, cold Andean night winds.
appellations.nerd_note: 'Alto Maipo' is not a legal name: on labels the Andean sector shows up through the area names Puente Alto and Pirque, or through the complement *Andes*.
appellations.summary:
Maipo is the historic heart of Chilean fine wine and the home of its most famous Cabernet Sauvignon. When Santiago's 19th-century mining and banking aristocracy came home from Paris, they planted Bordeaux varieties on their estates at the city's edge: Silvestre Ochagavía imported French vines and a French winemaker in 1851, Cousiño Macul was founded in 1856, Santa Carolina in 1875, Santa Rita in 1880 and Concha y Toro at Pirque in 1883. Those estates, a short carriage ride from the capital, defined the Chilean style for a century.

The subregion covers the whole Metropolitan Region, from the Andean foothills to the coastal range, and growers split it three ways. Alto Maipo, on the Andean piedmont at 600 to 800 m (Puente Alto, Pirque, Santiago's Macul and Peñalolén), has stony alluvial terraces of the Maipo river and cold mountain air at night; it gives Chile's classic Cabernet, with cassis, graphite and the hint of mint or eucalyptus locals call the Maipo signature. Central Maipo (Buin, Paine, Isla de Maipo, Talagante) is warmer and flatter, a source of generous Cabernet and Carmenère. Pacific Maipo, towards Melipilla and Alhué, feels the sea breeze and is the newest frontier.

The wines to know come mostly from a 10 km stretch of Puente Alto: Don Melchor (first vintage 1987), Almaviva (the 1997 Concha y Toro and Baron Philippe de Rothschild joint venture) and Viñedo Chadwick, whose 2000 vintage won the 2004 Berlin Tasting. Maipo Cabernet is firmer and more savoury than Napa's, more sun-filled than Bordeaux, and among the best-value long-agers in the world.

appellations.name: Santiago
appellations.summary: Area defined in the decree by the communes of Peñalolén and La Florida, on Santiago's eastern edge. It holds the last city-fringe vineyards of the 19th-century estates: Cousiño Macul's original Macul vineyard (founded 1856, now much reduced by housing) and Viña Aquitania, founded in 1990 by Bruno Prats and Paul Pontallier of Bordeaux. Alluvial gravels under the Andes give firm, classic Cabernet. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Pirque
appellations.summary: Area matching Pirque commune, on the south bank of the Maipo where the river leaves the Andes. Concha y Toro founded its winery here in 1883 at the Subercaseaux family's country house, and the commune also holds Haras de Pirque (a horse-stud estate turned winery) and William Fèvre Chile. Cold air pouring out of the Maipo canyon at night keeps Cabernet fresh and structured. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Puente Alto
appellations.nerd_note: Viñedo Chadwick was a polo field until Eduardo Chadwick planted it in 1992 at his family's Puente Alto property.
appellations.summary: Area matching Puente Alto and La Pintana communes on the north bank of the Maipo: the most valuable Cabernet terroir in Chile. On a stony alluvial terrace at about 650 m sit Concha y Toro's Don Melchor vineyard, Almaviva and Viñedo Chadwick, side by side. Deep, free-draining river cobbles, cool mountain nights and a long dry season give Cabernet of fine tannin, cassis and graphite that ages for decades. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Buin
appellations.summary: Area defined by Buin, Paine and San Bernardo communes, the Central Maipo heartland south of Santiago. It includes Alto Jahuel, home of Santa Rita (founded 1880), and Viña Carmen, where in 1994 Jean-Michel Boursiquot identified Carmenère among the vines Chileans called Merlot. Warm days and alluvial soils give rich Cabernet and Carmenère. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Isla de Maipo
appellations.summary: Area matching Isla de Maipo commune, an island-like tract between arms of the Maipo river in central Maipo. De Martino and Tarapacá are based here; the warm, alluvial valley floor produces ripe Cabernet, Carmenère and Syrah. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Talagante
appellations.summary: Area defined by Talagante, Peñaflor, El Monte and Padre Hurtado communes, west of Santiago. Undurraga, founded here in 1885 by Francisco Undurraga, still has its historic winery and park at Santa Ana. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Melipilla
appellations.summary: Area defined by Melipilla and San Pedro communes, the western 'Pacific Maipo' sector, where sea breezes reach through the coastal range. Newer plantings of Cabernet, Syrah and some whites experiment with this cooler fringe. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Alhué
appellations.summary: Area matching Alhué commune, a secluded valley in the coastal range at the south-western edge of the Metropolitan Region, with a few vineyards among old haciendas. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: María Pinto
appellations.summary: Area matching María Pinto commune, in the hills west of Santiago between Curacaví and Melipilla, a minor source of red grapes. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Colina
appellations.summary: Area matching Colina commune north of Santiago, Chacabuco province. Vineyards are few and squeezed by suburban growth. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Calera de Tango
appellations.summary: Area matching Calera de Tango commune, a small farming district south-west of Santiago with some Cabernet and other reds. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Til Til
appellations.summary: Area matching Til Til commune in the far north of the Metropolitan Region, a dry, warm basin with scattered vineyards. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Lampa
appellations.summary: Area matching Lampa commune north-west of Santiago; minor vineyard area in a rapidly urbanising basin. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Valle del Rapel
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Merlot, Syrah, Malbec, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: The Rapel subregion covers the O'Higgins administrative region, named after the Rapel river that forms where the Cachapoal and Tinguiririca join. It contains two zones, Cachapoal to the north and Colchagua to the south, and SAG figures show O'Higgins making about 282 million litres of DO wine in 2026, second only to Maule. 'Valle del Rapel' alone on a label usually means a blend across both zones; serious bottles name Cachapoal, Colchagua or an area.

appellations.name: Valle del Cachapoal
appellations.grapes: Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah
appellations.summary:
Cachapoal is the northern zone of Rapel, following the Cachapoal river from the Andes past Rancagua to Lake Rapel. Its east, under the mountains (Requínoa, Machalí, Rengo), is Cabernet country, home to Altaïr and the Andes-side vineyards of Viña San Pedro. Its west, around Peumo, Pichidegua and Las Cabras, is the warm, sheltered bowl where Chilean Carmenère reaches its fullest, ripest form: Concha y Toro's Carmín de Peumo and Terrunyo Carmenère come from here.

Before 1994 Chileans called the late-ripening vine here 'Merlot Peumal' after the Peumo valley, and the name stuck as a nickname for Carmenère. The area also hides Vik in Millahue, a showpiece estate with a winery built over water. In the glass, Peumo Carmenère is plush and spicy with dark fruit, and Andes-side Cabernet is firmer and fresher.

appellations.name: Rancagua
appellations.summary: Area defined by Rancagua, Graneros, Mostazal, Codegua and Olivar communes around the O'Higgins capital, the northern gateway of Cachapoal, with mixed red plantings. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Requínoa
appellations.summary: Area matching Requínoa commune at the foot of the Andes in east Cachapoal. Altaïr, the San Pedro project created with Château Dassault in the early 2000s, and other Andes-side estates grow structured Cabernet blends on stony colluvial slopes. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Rengo
appellations.summary: Area defined by Rengo, Malloa and Quinta de Tilcoco communes in central Cachapoal, with Torreón de Paredes and Misiones de Rengo among its wineries. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Peumo
appellations.nerd_note: Before Boursiquot's 1994 identification, Chilean growers called this vine 'Merlot Peumal', after Peumo.
appellations.summary: Area defined by Peumo, Pichidegua, Las Cabras and San Vicente communes in west Cachapoal: Chile's Carmenère grand cru in all but name. Clay-rich alluvial soils near the Cachapoal river, a warm sheltered bowl and a long autumn let the late-ripening grape lose its green pyrazines. Concha y Toro's Carmín de Peumo and Terrunyo Carmenère come from its Peumo vineyard; Vik sits in the Millahue valley of San Vicente. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Machalí
appellations.summary: Area matching Machalí commune, a large Andean commune east of Rancagua reaching into the high cordillera; its vineyards sit on the piedmont near the Cachapoal canyon. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Coltauco
appellations.summary: Area matching Coltauco commune in west Cachapoal, a mixed farming district with some red plantings. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Valle de Colchagua
appellations.grapes: Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Malbec, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Carignan; Sauvignon Blanc near the coast
appellations.terroir: Clay-loam and alluvium on the valley floor, decomposed granite on the hillsides (Apalta, Marchigüe), volcanic soils towards the Andes; Mediterranean climate with about 600 mm of rain, warm days and cooler coastal west.
appellations.summary:
Colchagua is Chile's red-wine showcase, the southern zone of Rapel running from the Andes past San Fernando and Santa Cruz to the Pacific at Pichilemu along the Tinguiririca river. Its colonial haciendas (Los Lingues, Huique) grew País and wheat for centuries; the transformation began in the 1990s, when Aurelio Montes, Alexandra Marnier-Lapostolle and others bet on the granite hillsides of Apalta, and Robert Parker's praise for Montes Alpha M and Clos Apalta made the valley a brand. Santa Cruz grew into Chile's wine-tourism capital, with its Colchagua Museum and wine train.

The zone splits three ways. The eastern Andes side (San Fernando, Chimbarongo, Los Lingues) is cooler, with volcanic and colluvial soils. The centre (Nancagua, Santa Cruz, Palmilla, Peralillo and the Apalta horseshoe) is warm and sunny, the classic home of rich Carmenère, Cabernet, Syrah and Malbec. The west (Marchigüe, Lolol, Pumanque, Paredones, La Estrella, Litueche) is the 2000s frontier, where coastal breezes and granite give fresher Syrah, Cabernet and even Sauvignon Blanc at Paredones, 10 km from the sea.

Colchagua's house style is generous: ripe black fruit, soft tannins, sweet spice. The best hillside wines balance that sunshine with granite-born freshness.

appellations.name: San Fernando
appellations.summary: Area matching San Fernando commune, the eastern, Andes-side gateway to Colchagua. It contains the historic Hacienda Los Lingues (now its own DO), Casa Silva's Angostura winery and cool piedmont vineyards whose volcanic soils give firmer, fresher reds. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Chimbarongo
appellations.summary: Area matching Chimbarongo commune in east Colchagua, known for wicker crafts as well as vineyards on the Andean side of the valley. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Nancagua
appellations.summary: Area defined by Nancagua and Placilla communes on the Colchagua valley floor, warm alluvial land with large vineyards of Cabernet, Carmenère and Merlot. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Santa Cruz
appellations.summary: Area defined by Santa Cruz and Chépica communes, the tourist heart of Colchagua. It includes the Apalta horseshoe (now its own DO) and the town's Colchagua Museum; valley-floor vineyards here give generous Carmenère and Cabernet. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Palmilla
appellations.summary: Area matching Palmilla commune in central Colchagua, which includes the colonial Hacienda El Huique; Montgras and others farm warm valley vineyards nearby. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Peralillo
appellations.summary: Area matching Peralillo commune, home of Los Vascos, the estate bought in 1988 by Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite), one of the first foreign investments of Chile's modern wine boom. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Lolol
appellations.summary: Area matching Lolol commune in west Colchagua, a valley of old adobe houses and newer hillside vineyards where coastal influence cools Syrah, Cabernet and Rhône varieties. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Marchigüe
appellations.summary: Area matching Marchigüe commune, the west Colchagua frontier planted from the late 1990s, notably by Montes and Montgras. Rolling granite hills, a breeze from the Pacific and low rainfall give Syrah, Cabernet and Carmenère with freshness and grip. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Litueche
appellations.summary: Area matching Litueche commune in Cardenal Caro province near the coast, a cool frontier with a handful of vineyards. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: La Estrella
appellations.summary: Area matching La Estrella commune in the western hills of Colchagua, with granitic soils and limited, recent plantings. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Paredones
appellations.summary: Area matching Paredones commune, Colchagua's coastal end about 10 to 15 km from the Pacific. Casa Silva and others planted here in the 2000s and showed that the warm-red zone of Colchagua can also make saline Sauvignon Blanc and taut Pinot Noir on granite and schist. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Pumanque
appellations.summary: Area matching Pumanque commune in the west of Colchagua, a rural district of old haciendas with small coastal-influenced plantings. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Apalta
appellations.grapes: Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Merlot, Malbec, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Carignan
appellations.terroir: Decomposed granite on steep slopes, deeper alluvial clay on the horseshoe floor; south-facing amphitheatre with shortened direct sun hours and morning mist.
appellations.nerd_note: Montes Folly was the first Syrah planted on Apalta's steepest slopes in the 1990s; locals thought it mad, hence the name.
appellations.summary:
Apalta is the most famous hillside in Chile: a horseshoe of granite slopes opening south onto the Tinguiririca river near Santa Cruz in Colchagua, recognised as its own DO in 2018 with about 1,007 ha of vineyards. The hills shelter it on three sides, so morning mist lingers and direct sun arrives late and leaves early, slowing ripening in what would otherwise be a hot valley. Valley floor clay suits Cabernet and Carmenère; the poorer granitic slopes, terraced since the 1990s, increasingly carry Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre and Carignan.

The names are legendary: Lapostolle's Clos Apalta, a Carmenère-led blend from vines planted in the early 20th century, made in a gravity winery dug into the hill; Montes Alpha M and the steep Syrah of Montes Folly; and Neyen, an old adobe estate with Carmenère and Cabernet over a century old. Apalta wines are dense and dark but carry a fresh, granite-edged finish. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Los Lingues
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenère, Syrah, Cabernet Franc, Petit Verdot
appellations.nerd_note: Koyle, founded by members of the Undurraga family, has about 80 ha planted inside the DO.
appellations.summary: Los Lingues is a 492 ha Andes-side DO in San Fernando commune, east Colchagua, created by Supreme Decree 56 of 2017 and published in 2018. It takes its name from the colonial Hacienda Los Lingues, one of the oldest estates in Chile, and its vineyards (Koyle, Casa Silva, Siegel) sit on volcanic and colluvial soils with basalt rocks at the foot of the cordillera, where cool mountain breezes give firmer, fresher Cabernet, Carmenère and Syrah than the warm valley floor. In June 2026 Chile's Supreme Court upheld the DO against a trademark holder who had registered 'Los Lingues' brands since 1983, confirming that a denomination of origin can coexist with an earlier trademark. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Valle de Curicó
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Carmenère, Chardonnay, País
appellations.nerd_note: Valdivieso, based in Lontué, has made traditional-method sparkling wine since the 1880s, among the oldest in South America.
appellations.summary:
Curicó, about 200 km south of Santiago, is where Chile's modern wine era began. In 1979 the Catalan producer Miguel Torres bought land here and brought stainless steel tanks and temperature-controlled fermentation, technologies that spread through the country in the following decade. The subregion covers Curicó province plus Río Claro commune and has two zones: Teno in the north and Lontué in the south.

It is a workhorse valley with more grape varieties than anywhere else in Chile, best known for reliable Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc, and home to big producers such as San Pedro at Molina, whose vineyard is among the largest single blocks in South America. Its edges are where the action is now: the dry-farmed hills of Rauco and Sagrada Familia (part of the Secano Interior), and the coastal Licantén DO near the mouth of the Mataquito.

appellations.name: Valle del Teno
appellations.summary: Teno is the northern zone of Curicó, along the Teno river and the Mataquito towards the coast: Teno, Romeral, Rauco, Hualañé and Vichuquén communes. It runs from Andean piedmont at Romeral through warm valley floor to coastal hills near Lake Vichuquén.

appellations.name: Rauco
appellations.summary: Area defined by Rauco and Hualañé communes, west of Curicó city, with dry-farmed hills that qualify for the Secano Interior special DO for País and Cinsault. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Romeral
appellations.summary: Area defined by Romeral and Teno communes, the Andes side of Curicó, where cool mountain breezes favour Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Vichuquén
appellations.summary: Area matching Vichuquén commune on the coast around Lake Vichuquén, with new cool-climate plantings of Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Valle del Lontué
appellations.summary: Lontué is the southern zone of Curicó, along the Lontué river: Curicó, Molina and Sagrada Familia communes plus Río Claro in Talca province. It is the valley's productive centre, with large estates around Molina and Lontué.

appellations.name: Molina
appellations.summary: Area defined by Molina, Río Claro and Curicó communes. It holds San Pedro's vast estate at Lontué and Miguel Torres's winery near Curicó, where Torres began modernising Chilean winemaking in 1979. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Sagrada Familia
appellations.summary: Area matching Sagrada Familia commune, south-west of Curicó, where valley floor gives way to dry-farmed hills with old País; part of the Secano Interior. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Licantén
appellations.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Carmenère
appellations.summary: Licantén is a small coastal DO of about 124 ha in the Mataquito valley of Curicó, created in 2018. Its only producer, La Ronciere, planted the Idahue vineyard in 2012 about 24 km from the sea, entirely to red varieties, on four soil types including llicorella-like slate, lutites, gravel and clay. Cool Pacific air gives Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Carmenère a fresher, more tensile profile than the inland Curicó style. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Valle del Maule
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc, Merlot, Carmenère, Chardonnay, País, Carignan, Cinsault, Malbec
appellations.terroir: Volcanic and alluvial soils on the irrigated valley floor; granite, decomposed granite (*maicillo*) and slate on the dry-farmed coastal hills; cooler and wetter than the Maipo, with about 700 mm of rain.
appellations.nerd_note: VIGNO wines must be at least 65% Carignan from dry-farmed vines over 30 years old in Maule's secano and spend at least two years ageing before release; the rules are a private association's, not part of Decree 464.
appellations.summary:
Maule is Chile's biggest wine subregion by far. SAG's 2024 census put 48,565 ha of wine grapes in the Maule administrative region (which also contains Curicó), 41.5% of the national total, and in 2026 that administrative region made 452 million litres, about 48% of all Chilean wine. Much of that is bulk Cabernet, Sauvignon Blanc and Merlot from irrigated valley floor; but Maule also holds the country's deepest well of history. Spanish settlers planted País here in the 16th century, and on the dry-farmed granite hills of the coastal range, the *secano*, head-trained bush vines of País, Carignan and Cinsault, some well over a century old, survived every modernisation simply because nobody bothered to rip them out.

The decree splits Maule into three zones. Claro (around Talca) runs from Andean San Clemente to coastal Empedrado and Curepto, where slate soils give rare mineral reds. Loncomilla (Linares, San Javier, Parral, Villa Alegre, Colbún) is the warm central valley plus the old Carignan of the dry hills. Tutuvén is the single area of Cauquenes, the epicentre of dry-farmed País and Carignan.

Since about 2010 the VIGNO (Vignadores de Carignan) association has defined a Maule Carignan style from old, dry-farmed bush vines, and a new generation (Bouchon, Gillmore, González Bastías, Garage Wine Co, De Martino and many more) bottles País and Cinsault that taste of wild strawberry, earth and dust. Maule is where Chile reconnects with its first four centuries of wine.

appellations.name: Valle del Claro
appellations.summary: Claro is the northern zone of Maule, named after the river through Talca: Talca, San Clemente, Pencahue, Maule, Pelarco, San Rafael, Empedrado and Curepto communes. It runs from Andean San Clemente to the coastal slate of Empedrado.

appellations.name: Talca
appellations.summary: Area defined by Talca, Maule and Pelarco communes around Maule's capital, with irrigated valley vineyards and dry-farmed hills that qualify for Secano Interior. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Pencahue
appellations.summary: Area matching Pencahue commune west of Talca, warm and relatively dry, known for ripe reds and dry-farmed old vines. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: San Clemente
appellations.summary: Area matching San Clemente commune, a huge Andean commune east of Talca stretching to the Argentine border; vineyards on the piedmont give fresh Cabernet and Sauvignon Blanc. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: San Rafael
appellations.summary: Area matching San Rafael commune north of Talca (not to be confused with Argentina's San Rafael DOC), a farming district with red plantings. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Empedrado
appellations.summary: Area matching Empedrado commune in Maule's coastal range, one of the few slate terroirs in Chile. Miguel Torres planted a vineyard on its schist slopes in the 2000s, producing a rare, mineral Pinot Noir. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Curepto
appellations.summary: Area matching Curepto commune near the Mataquito mouth, in the coastal secano, with old dry-farmed País and newer coastal plantings. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Valle del Loncomilla
appellations.summary: Loncomilla is the central zone of Maule, along the Loncomilla river: San Javier, Villa Alegre, Retiro, Parral, Linares, Yerbas Buenas, Colbún and Longaví communes. It mixes large irrigated estates with the old dry-farmed Carignan and País of the western hills around San Javier and Villa Alegre.

appellations.name: San Javier
appellations.summary: Area matching San Javier commune, the hub of Maule's old-vine revival. Gillmore at Villavicencio and the Bouchon family at Mingre farm dry-farmed Carignan, País and Cabernet in the coastal hills, and many VIGNO Carignans come from here. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Villa Alegre
appellations.summary: Area matching Villa Alegre commune south of Talca, with vineyards on the Loncomilla plain and old secano vines nearby. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Parral
appellations.summary: Area matching Parral commune, birthplace of Pablo Neruda, in southern Maule; mixed irrigated and dry-farmed vineyards. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Linares
appellations.summary: Area defined by Linares and Yerbas Buenas communes, a large valley-floor vineyard zone with some old vines in the surrounding hills. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Colbún
appellations.summary: Area matching Colbún commune on the Andean side of Maule, near the Colbún reservoir; piedmont vineyards give fresher reds. Labels may add the complement *Andes*.

appellations.name: Longaví
appellations.summary: Area matching Longaví commune in southern Maule. The brand Longaví, from the Garcés Silva family's young winemakers, takes its name from the volcano. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Retiro
appellations.summary: Area matching Retiro commune in southern Maule, irrigated farmland with vineyards for Cabernet and País. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Valle del Tutuvén
appellations.summary: Tutuvén is Maule's southern-coastal zone, consisting only of Cauquenes commune, named after the Tutuvén river. It is the heart of Chile's dry-farmed old-vine country.

appellations.name: Cauquenes
appellations.grapes: País, Carignan, Cinsault, Malbec
appellations.nerd_note: The Lomas de Cauquenes cooperative still crushes grapes from hundreds of small dry-farm growers.
appellations.summary: Cauquenes is the epicentre of Chile's rediscovered heritage. On the granite hills of the coastal range, bush-trained, dry-farmed País and Carignan up to 100 to 200 years old grow without irrigation, ploughed by horse, picked into wooden boxes. For decades the grapes went to cheap *pipeño* and jug wine; since the late 2000s VIGNO Carignan, Miguel Torres's sparkling País (Estelado) and a crowd of small natural-leaning producers have turned the commune into a source of juicy, earthy, low-alcohol reds. It is the single area of the Valle del Tutuvén zone and part of the Secano Interior. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Valle del Itata
appellations.grapes: País, Cinsault, Moscatel de Alejandría, Carignan, Semillon, Corinto (Chasselas)
appellations.terroir: Decomposed granite (*maicillo*) and red clay on rolling coastal hills; humid Mediterranean climate with 1,000 mm or more of winter rain; dry-farmed, own-rooted bush vines.
appellations.nerd_note: Itata's Moscatel is the same Muscat of Alexandria distilled into pisco further north; here it is fermented dry, often on its skins.
appellations.summary:
Itata is where Chilean wine began in earnest and where its oldest living vineyards remain. Spanish settlers and Jesuits planted vines around Concepción and Chillán in the mid-16th century, and by the colonial era the Itata and Ñuble river country supplied wine to Concepción and beyond; one shipment of 5,000 *botijas* went from Concepción to Lima in 1795. Phylloxera never came, so head-trained País, Moscatel de Alejandría and Cinsault still grow on their own roots on granite hills a few kilometres from the Pacific.

For most of the 20th century Itata sold cheap bulk wine to the big Central Valley houses. That changed in the 2010s, when De Martino, Carmen, Pedro Parra, Roberto Henríquez, Leonardo Erazo and many small farmers started bottling dry-farmed Cinsault and País of real charm: bright red fruit, light body, granite-dust freshness. Moscatel became a fragrant dry white and the base of skin-contact orange wines. The 2018 creation of the Ñuble administrative region gave Itata a political identity too, and SAG's 2024 census counted about 10,300 ha of wine grapes in Ñuble.

The subregion covers coastal and central Ñuble plus Florida commune; its four areas are Chillán, Quillón, Portezuelo and Coelemu. Much of it is also covered by the Secano Interior special DO for País and Cinsault, and in 2022 Itata growers protested a plan to open those two grapes to every Chilean DO, fearing they would lose the one advantage they had.

appellations.name: Chillán
appellations.summary: Area defined by Chillán, Bulnes, San Carlos, Chillán Viejo and Ñiquén communes, the inland Itata around the capital of Ñuble. Valley-floor vineyards and some old País and Moscatel on the surrounding hills. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Quillón
appellations.summary: Area defined by Quillón, Ránquil and Florida communes in southern Itata, where the Itata river runs between granite hills dotted with old Moscatel and Cinsault. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Portezuelo
appellations.summary: Area defined by Portezuelo, Ninhue, Quirihue and San Nicolás communes, the north-western coastal hills of Itata with some of its oldest dry-farmed País and Cinsault. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Coelemu
appellations.summary: Area defined by Coelemu and Treguaco communes near the mouth of the Itata. It includes Guarilihue, the granite hamlet where De Martino and others source century-old Cinsault and Moscatel for wines fermented in clay *tinajas*. Labels may add the complement *Costa*.

appellations.name: Valle del Bío-Bío
appellations.grapes: País, Moscatel de Alejandría, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: The Bío-Bío subregion follows Chile's second-longest river in the old frontier country of southern Chile: Yumbel, Nacimiento, Mulchén, Negrete and Laja communes. For centuries it made País and Moscatel for local consumption; since the 1990s cooler, wetter conditions (well over 1,000 mm of rain) have drawn Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling, Gewürztraminer and Sauvignon Blanc. Its two areas are Yumbel and Mulchén. In July 2026 the Secano Interior special DO was extended to seven Biobío communes, including Nacimiento, Los Ángeles and Laja, in recognition of the region's peasant wine tradition.

appellations.name: Yumbel
appellations.summary: Area defined by Yumbel and Laja communes on the north bank of the Bío-Bío, an old frontier town famous for its San Sebastián pilgrimage; dry-farmed País here qualifies for Secano Interior. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Mulchén
appellations.summary: Area defined by Mulchén, Nacimiento and Negrete communes, cool and rainy, planted to Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and aromatic whites. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Valle del Malleco
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.terroir: Volcanic soils (trumao) of sand and clay, well drained despite heavy rain; cool, short season with big day-night swings.
appellations.nerd_note: Aquitania's founding partners included Bordeaux's Bruno Prats and Paul Pontallier, so Chile's southern Chardonnay pioneer has Médoc roots.
appellations.summary: Malleco, about 550 km south of Santiago in Araucanía, is the subregion that proved southern Chile could make world-class white wine. In the mid-1990s Felipe de Solminihac of Viña Aquitania planted Chardonnay near Traiguén on well-drained volcanic soils; the resulting Sol de Sol Chardonnay, first released around 2000, showed a nervy, citrus-and-flint style no one expected from Chile. Rainfall reaches about 1,300 mm a year, the season is short and frost is a constant threat, so yields are tiny. Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc follow the same cool logic. The single defined area is Traiguén.

appellations.name: Traiguén
appellations.summary: Area matching Traiguén commune in Malleco, where Viña Aquitania planted the Sol de Sol Chardonnay vineyard in the 1990s and Baettig and others have followed with taut Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. Labels may add the complement *Entre Cordilleras*.

appellations.name: Valle del Cautín
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc
appellations.summary: Cautín, matching Perquenco and Galvarino communes in Araucanía, is a small, very cool subregion where a few producers grow Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc on volcanic soils under heavy rainfall. It is part of the push of Chilean viticulture into the lake district.

appellations.name: Valle de Osorno
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling
appellations.summary: Osorno covers Osorno, San Pablo and Purranque communes in Los Lagos plus La Unión and Futrono in Los Ríos, near 40°S. Casa Silva's vineyard on the shores of Lake Ranco at Futrono, planted in the 2000s, makes sparkling wine, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir with piercing acidity, proving that the lake district can ripen grapes in warm years.

appellations.name: Chiloé
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling
appellations.nerd_note: The same 2025 decree created a DO for Rapa Nui (Easter Island), 3,700 km out in the Pacific.
appellations.summary: Chiloé became a Chilean DO subregion in 2025: Decree 27 of November 2024, published on 14 May 2025, added the whole archipelago of Chiloé province to the Austral region. The decree's own reasoning is striking: climate change has widened the latitude where vines can grow, and the islands' insular conditions now produce distinctive quality wine. Plantings near 42°S are minuscule, mainly cool-climate whites and Pinot Noir, and the DO is one of the southernmost legally defined wine areas anywhere, though Argentina's Chubut IGs reach further south.

appellations.name: Rapa Nui - Isla de Pascua
appellations.nerd_note: Rapa Nui is the only Chilean DO not attached to any viticultural region or subregion.
appellations.summary: Almost certainly the most remote wine appellation in the world: Easter Island, about 3,700 km off the Chilean coast in the South Pacific, became a Chilean DO area through Decree 27 (signed November 2024, published May 2025). It covers the island's entire commune and sits outside every viticultural region, listed on its own as numeral 7 of article 1. The government's stated aim was to give the island's handful of subtropical vineyards the same labelling rights as mainland wine; volumes are tiny and the subtropical, humid climate makes any wine here an experiment.

appellations.name: Secano Interior
match: Denominación de Origen Especial Secano Interior
appellations.grapes: País (Mission, Criolla), Cinsault
appellations.nerd_note: The decree formally recognises Mission and Criolla as accepted synonyms of País, linking Chile's grape to California's Mission and Argentina's Criolla Chica (all Listán Prieto).
appellations.summary:
Secano Interior ('dry interior') is a special denomination of origin for wines made only from País and Cinsault grown on unirrigated land in the coastal hills and interior of Maule, Ñuble and Biobío. It rescues a category the 1994 law had effectively excluded: País was not even on the list of varieties allowed for DO wine. The decree names the qualifying areas (Rauco, Romeral, Molina, Sagrada Familia, Talca, Pencahue, San Clemente, San Rafael, San Javier, Villa Alegre, Parral, Linares, Cauquenes, Chillán, Quillón, Portezuelo, Coelemu and Yumbel) plus further communes; in July 2026 Decree 4 added Hualqui, Nacimiento, Los Ángeles, Laja, San Rosendo, Santa Juana and Tomé in Biobío.

The label can read 'Secano Interior' followed by the subregion, zone or area. SAG recorded 5.4 million litres under this DO in 2026, small but symbolic: it gives legal standing to the dry-farmed, own-rooted, often centenarian bush vines that are now Chile's hottest wine story.

appellations.name: Cuyo
appellations.grapes: Malbec, Bonarda, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cereza, Criolla Grande, Torrontés, Pedro Giménez
appellations.summary: Cuyo is the interprovincial IG covering Mendoza, San Juan and San Luis, the historic western heartland that makes the vast majority of Argentine wine. The name comes from the Huarpe word for 'sandy land' or 'desert country', and the region is exactly that: an irrigated oasis economy at the foot of the Andes. As an IG it is rarely seen on serious labels, which prefer a province or a district.

appellations.name: Mendoza
appellations.grapes: Malbec (39,856 ha in 2024), Bonarda, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cereza, Criolla Grande, Syrah, Chardonnay, Torrontés, Pedro Giménez
appellations.terroir: Alluvial fans of Andean rivers: stony, calcareous gravels near the mountains, deep sandy and silty soils on the eastern plain; continental desert climate with hail ('la piedra') and the hot, dry Zonda wind as the main hazards.
appellations.nerd_note: Mendoza's first vines were planted shortly after the city's founding by Pedro del Castillo on 2 March 1561.
appellations.summary:
Mendoza is the province that is Argentine wine to most of the world: about 142,800 ha of vines in 2024 (INV), more than 70% of the national vineyard and of the 2026 grape harvest. The vineyards are irrigated oases strung along the Mendoza, Tunuyán, Diamante and Atuel rivers, fed by Andean snowmelt through a canal network that began with Huarpe and Inca irrigation and was expanded by the Spanish from the 1560s. Rain is scarce (around 200 mm), sunshine abundant, and altitude does the cooling: vineyards run from about 500 m in the east to over 1,500 m in the Uco Valley.

The province has five broad zones. The Primera Zona of Luján de Cuyo and Maipú, just south of the city, is the historic fine-wine heart. The Uco Valley, 80 to 120 km south-west at 900 to 1,600 m, is the modern star. The East (San Martín, Junín, Rivadavia, Santa Rosa, La Paz) is the volume engine. San Rafael and General Alvear in the south form their own oasis, and Lavalle in the north grows mostly for bulk wine and grape juice. As an IG, 'Mendoza' on a label means the grapes come from anywhere in the province, the usual choice for blends and good-value Malbec.

appellations.name: San Juan
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Malbec, Bonarda, Cereza, Criolla Grande, Pedro Giménez, Moscatel de Alejandría, Torrontés
appellations.nerd_note: Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, who later brought Pouget and Malbec to Mendoza's Quinta Normal, was born in San Juan in 1811.
appellations.summary: San Juan is Argentina's second wine province, about 39,700 ha of vines in 2024 (INV) and roughly a quarter of the national harvest. It is hotter, drier and lower than Mendoza: the Tulum valley around the provincial capital is a desert oasis growing grapes for wine, raisins, juice and table fruit. Its fine-wine story lives at the edges, in the high Andean valleys of Calingasta and Pedernal and the cooler Zonda valley, and in Syrah, which has had a strong San Juan identity since the 1990s.

appellations.name: San Luis
appellations.summary: San Luis is the third Cuyo province and a minor wine producer, with about 100 ha of vines (INV 2024). Its IG, recognised in 2019, covers the whole province; small projects around the capital and in the Sierras de San Luis grow Malbec and other reds at moderate altitude.

appellations.name: La Rioja Argentina
appellations.grapes: Torrontés Riojano, Malbec, Bonarda, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.nerd_note: Torrontés Riojano is a natural cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Listán Prieto (Criolla Chica), born in the New World.
appellations.summary: La Rioja's provincial IG carries 'Argentina' in its name to avoid any confusion with Spain's Rioja. The province has about 7,000 ha of vines (INV 2024), concentrated in the Famatina valley around Chilecito, and is the homeland of Torrontés Riojano, the most aromatic and widely planted of Argentina's three Torrontés grapes. Large cooperatives such as La Riojana dominate production.

appellations.name: Catamarca
appellations.grapes: Torrontés Riojano, Malbec, Syrah, Criolla, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: Catamarca's provincial IG covers about 2,700 ha of vines (INV 2024) in high Andean valleys: Fiambalá and Tinogasta in the west, Belén and Santa María in the north (where the Calchaquí valleys begin), and Pomán. Old Criolla and Torrontés vines, home-made *vino patero* and new altitude Malbec and Syrah share the landscape.

appellations.name: Salta
appellations.grapes: Malbec, Torrontés Riojano, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Criolla Chica
appellations.summary: Salta is Argentina's altitude province: about 3,700 ha of vines (INV 2024), almost all in the Calchaquí valleys between 1,700 and 3,100 m. Malbec covers 46% of the provincial vineyard, but Salta's signature is Torrontés from Cafayate, floral and fresh, and Malbec and Tannat of deep colour and thick skins built by intense sunlight. The provincial IG appears on blends from across the valleys.

appellations.name: Jujuy
appellations.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Franc, Syrah, Merlot, Criolla
appellations.summary: Jujuy, Argentina's northernmost wine province, has only about 70 ha of vines (INV 2024) but some of the most spectacular: terraces in the Quebrada de Humahuaca, a UNESCO World Heritage valley, at 2,300 to over 3,000 m. Since 2025 a second IG, Valles Templados, covers the lower, temperate valleys around San Salvador and Perico.

appellations.name: Tucumán
appellations.summary: Tucumán's provincial IG covers a small wine area of about 145 ha (INV 2024), almost all in the Tafí del Valle department on the Calchaquí side of the mountains, at Colalao del Valle and Amaicha del Valle, where Malbec and Torrontés grow at about 1,700 to 2,000 m.

appellations.name: Córdoba Argentina
appellations.summary: Córdoba's provincial IG (with 'Argentina' added to separate it from Spain's Córdoba) covers about 240 ha of vines (INV 2024). The province's wine history is Jesuit and Italian: the Jesuit estancias of the 17th and 18th centuries made wine, and Friulian immigrants at Colonia Caroya still make Frambua from American hybrid grapes.

appellations.name: Neuquén
appellations.summary: Neuquén's provincial IG covers about 1,500 ha (INV 2024), most of it created from scratch since the late 1990s on the desert plateau of San Patricio del Chañar, north of the city of Neuquén, where large irrigation projects turned steppe into vineyard for Bodega del Fin del Mundo, Familia Schroeder and NQN. Strong winds, cool nights and long sun make dense, fresh Malbec, Pinot Noir and Merlot.

appellations.name: Río Negro
appellations.summary: Río Negro's provincial IG covers about 1,300 ha (INV 2024), most along the irrigated Alto Valle of the Río Negro, an apple-and-pear valley where Humberto Canale planted vines in 1909. It is the source of some of Argentina's oldest Malbec, Merlot and Semillon and of Pinot Noir that convinced Italian and Danish investors (Chacra, Noemía) to settle here.

appellations.name: Patagonia
appellations.grapes: Malbec, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Semillon, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay
appellations.summary: The Patagonia IG is an interprovincial umbrella for Neuquén, Río Negro, La Pampa, Chubut and the rest of southern Argentina. It is one of the most used IGs on export labels (13% of IG wine sold in 2022, per INV), because it carries an image of cold, wind and purity. The vineyards cluster in irrigated river valleys of the Negro, Neuquén and Colorado, plus a scatter of new sites as far south as Chubut's Sarmiento at 45°S.

appellations.name: Luján de Cuyo
appellations.created: DOC 1989/1993 (sources differ); registered by INV Res. C.15/2005
appellations.grapes: Malbec (8,920 ha of the department's 15,210 ha in 2024), Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Petit Verdot
appellations.terroir: Alluvial terraces of the Mendoza river, stony near the river in the north, deeper clay-loam over gravel to the south; 850 to 1,100 m; about 200 mm of rain, wide day-night swings.
appellations.nerd_note: Luján de Cuyo holds about 22% of all Malbec in Mendoza, more than any other department (INV 2025 Malbec report).
appellations.summary:
Luján de Cuyo is Argentina's first denomination of origin and the historic home of fine Malbec. The department lies just south of Mendoza city on the first terrace of the Mendoza river at 850 to 1,100 m, and from the late 19th century its districts (Vistalba, Las Compuertas, Chacras de Coria, Mayor Drummond, Perdriel, Agrelo, Ugarteche) were planted by Italian, Spanish and French families. Many vineyards are 60 to over 100 years old and own-rooted.

The DOC was pushed through by local producers in the late 1980s and early 1990s to defend Malbec's reputation; INV registered it under the 1999 national law in 2005. It is the only Argentine DOC in regular use: INV reported 382,866 litres exported and 511,537 litres sold domestically under the DOC in 2022. Its terroir divides north to south. The northern districts near the river (Vistalba, Las Compuertas, Chacras, Drummond) have stony alluvial soils and give perfumed, elegant Malbec. The southern districts of Perdriel, Agrelo and Ugarteche have deeper clay-loam and give broader, darker wines. Agrelo, Las Compuertas, Vistalba and Alto Agrelo also have their own IGs.

Luján Malbec is the classic Argentine style: plum, violet and mocha, ripe and velvety, built for ageing in the best old-vine cuvées.

appellations.name: Luján de Cuyo (IG)
appellations.summary: Alongside the DOC, the department of Luján de Cuyo is also registered as a plain IG with identical limits. The IG lets producers name the department without meeting the DOC's extra rules, and most Luján wines on export shelves use it this way.

appellations.name: Agrelo
appellations.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay
appellations.nerd_note: The pyramid at Catena Zapata, designed by Pablo Sánchez Elía and built in the late 1990s, was inspired by Mayan temples.
appellations.summary: Agrelo, a district in southern Luján de Cuyo at 950 to 1,100 m, is one of the most planted fine-wine zones in Argentina and the home of Catena Zapata's pyramid winery and its La Pirámide vineyard (planted 1983). Deeper clay-loam soils with stones below give dense, dark, plush Malbec and good Cabernet Sauvignon; frost and hail are risks on the open plain. Agrelo was the eighth most used IG for exports in 2022 (INV).

appellations.name: Alto Agrelo
appellations.summary: Alto Agrelo became Argentina's newest Luján de Cuyo IG in July 2025, at the request of Grupo Avinea, whose 232-ha organic estate there is the source of Argento's estate Malbecs. It covers the higher, western part of Agrelo towards the Andean foothills, where stonier soils and cooler nights give fresher Malbec than the classic Agrelo plain. It joins Luján de Cuyo, Agrelo, Las Compuertas and Vistalba as the fifth IG within the department.

appellations.name: Las Compuertas
appellations.nerd_note: 'Las Compuertas' means 'the floodgates', after the colonial sluices that diverted the Mendoza river into irrigation canals.
appellations.summary: Las Compuertas, at about 1,050 m on the north side of Luján de Cuyo by the Mendoza river, holds some of Argentina's oldest Malbec vineyards, many planted in the early 20th century and still own-rooted. Poor, stony alluvial soils and the cooling effect of the river's canyon give fragrant, fine-grained Malbec. Cheval des Andes and many old-vine cuvées source here.

appellations.name: Vistalba
appellations.summary: Vistalba, a small district at about 1,000 m beside Las Compuertas on the north bank of the Mendoza river, was recognised as an IG in 2022. Old Malbec on stony soils gives refined, perfumed wines; Carlos Pulenta's Vistalba estate and Fabre Montmayou are based here.

appellations.name: Maipú
appellations.summary: Maipú, east of Luján de Cuyo along the Mendoza river at 750 to 1,000 m, is the other half of Mendoza's historic Primera Zona. It is where the 19th-century wine industry concentrated after the 1885 railway arrived: Trapiche, López, Giol's La Colina de Oro and the national wine museum are here.
