Its riverside districts (Lunlunta, Cruz de Piedra, Barrancas, Russell) have old vineyards on stony alluvium and give classic, ripe Malbec, Cabernet and old-vine Bonarda.

appellations.name: Lunlunta
appellations.summary: Lunlunta is a riverside district of Maipú, on high terraces above the Mendoza river at about 900 m. Old Malbec here, including Catena's Angélica vineyard planted in the 1920s, grows on stony alluvium and gives deep but fresh wines.

appellations.name: Barrancas
appellations.summary: Barrancas, in eastern Maipú on the banks of the Mendoza river, is a warm district of old vineyards known for ripe Malbec, Syrah and Bonarda. It was among the first Maipú districts registered as an IG, and among the most exported of small IGs in 2022.

appellations.name: Russel
appellations.summary: Russell (registered as 'Russel') is a district of Maipú with deep soils and long-established vineyards for Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon.

appellations.name: El Paraíso
appellations.summary: El Paraíso is a small IG in Maipú's Fray Luis Beltrán area, along the Mendoza river, recognised in 2007 for its traditional red-wine vineyards.

appellations.name: Godoy Cruz
appellations.summary: Godoy Cruz, now part of Greater Mendoza, was a 19th-century wine town. It keeps historic wineries such as Escorihuela Gascón (founded 1884) and Bodega Arizu, though the IG's vineyards have almost all given way to the city.

appellations.name: Guaymallén
appellations.summary: Guaymallén, on the eastern side of Mendoza city, is a historic wine department now largely urban; under 500 ha of vines remain (INV 2024), mostly Malbec and Criolla.

appellations.name: Las Heras
appellations.summary: Las Heras stretches from Mendoza city north-west into the high Andes along the road to Chile. Its vineyards (about 1,300 ha in 2024) lie near the city; the separate Canota IG covers a higher piedmont site.

appellations.name: Canota
appellations.nerd_note: The site sits near the Canota monument, which marks where San Martín's Army of the Andes split its columns in 1817.
appellations.summary: Canota (Valle de Canota) is a small piedmont IG in Las Heras, north-west of Mendoza city on the old road to Villavicencio, recognised in 2020. Vineyards here at over 1,000 m sit on alluvial fans of the pre-cordillera, a cooler, stonier frontier for Malbec.

appellations.name: Lavalle
appellations.created: 2002 (INV Res. C.32/2002; synonym Desierto de Lavalle 2009)
appellations.summary: Lavalle, north of Mendoza city, is the province's driest and lowest wine department (around 600 m), with about 12,300 ha of vines (INV 2024) for bulk wine, juice and grape concentrate. The synonym 'Desierto de Lavalle' was added in 2009 for wines from its sandy, desert vineyards.

appellations.name: San Martín
appellations.summary: San Martín is the largest vineyard department in Argentina, about 25,800 ha in 2024 (INV), the heart of the Eastern Mendoza oasis along the Mendoza and Tunuyán rivers at 650 to 750 m. Hot, flat and fertile, it produces much of Argentina's everyday wine, grape juice and concentrate, with Criolla Grande, Cereza, Bonarda and Pedro Giménez.

appellations.name: Junín
appellations.summary: Junín, in Eastern Mendoza, has about 10,800 ha of vines (INV 2024) and a reputation for generous Bonarda and Malbec from warm, sandy soils.

appellations.name: Rivadavia
appellations.summary: Rivadavia, in Eastern Mendoza along the Tunuyán river, has about 13,900 ha of vines (INV 2024). Nicola Catena planted his first Malbec here at La Libertad in 1902, and old-vine Bonarda from the East has become a cult value wine.

appellations.name: Distrito Medrano
appellations.summary: Medrano, straddling Rivadavia and Junín in Eastern Mendoza, was recognised as an IG in 2014. Its stony soils near the Tunuyán river give more structured Malbec and Bonarda than the typical eastern plain.

appellations.name: Reducción
appellations.summary: La Reducción is a district of Rivadavia in Eastern Mendoza, recognised as an IG in 2020. Its name recalls a colonial *reducción*, a settlement where indigenous Huarpe people were gathered; it grows traditional reds.

appellations.name: Santa Rosa
appellations.summary: Santa Rosa, at the south-eastern edge of the Eastern oasis along the Tunuyán river, has about 7,900 ha of vines (INV 2024), mostly for everyday wine.

appellations.name: La Paz
appellations.summary: La Paz is Mendoza's easternmost wine department, hot and dry on the border with San Luis, with only about 135 ha of vines (INV 2024).

appellations.name: Valle de Uco
appellations.grapes: Malbec (16,584 ha across its three departments in 2024), Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon
appellations.terroir: Alluvial fans from the Andes with river stones, sand and calcium carbonate crusts; 900 to 1,600 m; cool continental climate, about 300 mm of summer rain, frequent hail and spring frost.
appellations.nerd_note: The three Uco departments together hold 41.6% of all Malbec in Mendoza (INV 2025).
appellations.summary:
The Uco Valley is where Argentine wine went uphill and found its future. It is a long depression at 900 to 1,600 m between the Andes and a low pre-cordillera, 80 to 120 km south-west of Mendoza city, covering the departments of Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos and watered by the Tunuyán river and Andean streams. Historically it grew fruit, potatoes and some Criolla; the turn came in the 1990s, when Nicolás Catena planted the Adrianna vineyard at about 1,450 m in Gualtallary (1992) and a wave of French, Dutch and Argentine investors followed: Clos de los Siete, Salentein, Andeluna, O. Fournier, and later Zuccardi's winery at Paraje Altamira.

The valley's soils are alluvial fans pushed out from the Andes: stony and often calcareous near the mountains, with sand and silt further east. Each fan and each terrace behaves differently, so Uco has spawned more district IGs than anywhere else in Argentina (Los Chacayes, Paraje Altamira, San Pablo, Pampa El Cepillo, Vista Flores, La Consulta, El Peral, Cordón del Cepillo, with Gualtallary pending), and producers increasingly label single 'parajes'. The climate is cool for Argentina, with frost and hail as real threats.

Uco Malbec is fresher and more floral than Luján's, with violet, red fruit, firm chalky tannins and high natural acidity; Cabernet Franc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir excel too. Valle de Uco is by far Argentina's most used IG: 41% of all IG wine sold in 2022 and 45% of IG exports (INV).

appellations.name: Tupungato
appellations.created: 2002 (INV Res. C.32/2002; synonym Valle de Tupungato 2006)
appellations.summary: Tupungato is the northernmost Uco department, named after the 6,570-m Tupungato volcano that looms over it. About 10,600 ha of vines (INV 2024) climb from 900 m to over 1,500 m in Gualtallary. Chandon, in Argentina since 1959, was an early investor here for sparkling base wine; Catena's Adrianna vineyard (1992) showed that the high north-west could make world-class Malbec and Chardonnay.

appellations.name: Gualtallary
appellations.created: Provisional ('mención precaria'), INV; definitive status unconfirmed
appellations.grapes: Malbec, Chardonnay, Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir
appellations.nerd_note: In 2022 wines labelled Gualtallary exported 438,207 litres at an average US$7.1 per litre, ninth among Argentine IGs (INV).
appellations.summary:
Gualtallary, a district of Tupungato rising from about 1,200 to 1,600 m, is the closest thing Argentina has to a grand cru. Nicolás Catena's Adrianna vineyard, planted in 1992 at about 1,450 m when everyone said the site was too cold, gave the world-famous Adrianna Malbecs and White Bones and White Stones Chardonnays. Soils are shallow alluvial gravels and sand over limestone (calcium carbonate) crusts, sometimes with fossil-bearing caliche; the light is intense and the nights cold.

Gualtallary wines are electric: violet-scented, chalk-textured Malbec, taut Chardonnay, and Cabernet Franc with herbal lift. Zuccardi, El Enemigo, SuperUco and Huentala all farm here. Its IG application ran into disputes over the boundary; INV's 2023 statistics list it as a 'mención precaria' (a provisional authorisation to label) and I found no confirmation of definitive registration as of October 2026.

appellations.name: El Peral
appellations.summary: El Peral is a district of Tupungato at about 1,100 to 1,300 m, recognised as an IG at the request of Bodegas Chandon. Chandon grows sparkling-base Chardonnay and Pinot Noir here; cool nights and stony soils also give fresh Malbec.

appellations.name: Tunuyán
appellations.summary: Tunuyán is the central Uco department, about 10,200 ha of vines (INV 2024), from the Tunuyán river plain to the Andean foothills. It contains the IGs of Los Chacayes, Vista Flores and San Pablo, and the area of Los Árboles, where Bodegas Salentein built its cross-shaped winery at the end of the 1990s.

appellations.name: Los Chacayes
appellations.summary: Los Chacayes is an alluvial fan at 1,100 to 1,600 m in western Tunuyán, recognised as an IG in 2017. Its soils are among the stoniest in Uco, with big river boulders and little fine material, and the vines struggle: Malbec here is dark, tannic and mountain-fresh. François Lurton's Bodega Piedra Negra and Corazón del Sol are among the estates here.

appellations.name: Vista Flores
appellations.summary: Vista Flores is the Tunuyán district around which Michel Rolland and partners created Clos de los Siete from 1998: a block of about 850 ha divided among several wineries (Monteviejo, Cuvelier, DiamAndes, Rolland), each making its own wine and contributing to the shared Clos de los Siete blend. At about 1,000 to 1,200 m, sandy-loam and stony soils give plush, polished Malbec.

appellations.name: San Pablo
appellations.summary: San Pablo, recognised in 2019, is Uco's highest IG, a cold alluvial terrace in Tunuyán at roughly 1,300 to 1,700 m, where frost and snow are real risks. Its limits were drawn by geology and climate rather than politics. Wines are taut and aromatic: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and Malbec with very high acidity. Salentein and Zuccardi are among the growers.

appellations.name: San Carlos
appellations.summary: San Carlos is the southern Uco department, about 8,800 ha of vines (INV 2024), two-thirds of them Malbec. It holds Paraje Altamira, Pampa El Cepillo, Cordón del Cepillo and La Consulta, and a long tradition of growers' cooperatives and old Malbec around La Consulta and Eugenio Bustos.

appellations.name: Paraje Altamira
appellations.grapes: Malbec, Cabernet Franc, Semillon, Chardonnay
appellations.nerd_note: In 2022 Paraje Altamira wines exported at US$20.4 per litre on average, four times the national IG average (INV).
appellations.summary:
Paraje Altamira is the alluvial fan of the Tunuyán river in San Carlos, at about 1,000 to 1,150 m, and Argentina's most studied terroir. Its recognition in 2013 followed five years of work including some 200 soil pits; the first zone of 4,790 ha (1,400 ha of vineyard) was later enlarged to about 9,290 ha with 2,800 ha of vines. The legal name carries 'Paraje' because 'Altamira' was a registered trademark.

The soils are a jumble of rounded river stones coated in white calcium carbonate, over sand and silt, which drain fast and push Malbec to small berries and fine, chalky tannin. Zuccardi built its Valle de Uco winery here in 2016 out of the same stones, and its Piedra Infinita Malbec comes from the fan. Catena's Nicasia vineyard and Achával-Ferrer's Finca Altamira are among the other landmarks. Paraje Altamira wines command among the highest average export prices of any Argentine IG.

appellations.name: Pampa el Cepillo
appellations.summary: Pampa El Cepillo, recognised in 2019, is the plain south of Paraje Altamira in San Carlos, around 1,000 to 1,100 m. It is cold, frost-prone and windswept, with stony, calcareous alluvium; Malbec and Cabernet Franc ripen slowly into firm, fresh wines. Its limits were drawn on geological and climatic criteria.

appellations.name: Cordón el Cepillo
appellations.summary: Cordón del Cepillo, recognised in 2022, is a higher piedmont zone in San Carlos along the Cepillo range, west of Pampa El Cepillo. It is one of the newest Uco frontiers, with very stony soils and cool conditions.

appellations.name: La Consulta
appellations.summary: La Consulta, a district of San Carlos at about 950 to 1,100 m, is old Malbec country: dozens of growers farm vineyards planted in the mid-20th century on deep alluvial soils. It was recognised in 2014 at the request of Leoncio Arizu, and many of the region's best old-vine Malbecs are sourced here.

appellations.name: San Rafael
appellations.summary:
San Rafael is Mendoza's southern oasis, an irrigated plain at 450 to 800 m on the Diamante and Atuel rivers, about 230 km south of the city, with about 11,500 ha of vines (INV 2024). French, Italian and Spanish immigrants built it into a fruit-and-wine district from the late 19th century; the Bianchi, Suter and Goyenechea houses are long-standing names. It became Argentina's second DOC in 2007, though the denomination is little used.

San Rafael is cooler than eastern Mendoza thanks to its southern latitude, and its wines are fresh, fruity and fairly priced: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Bonarda, Chenin Blanc and sparkling wines. The Cañón del Atuel and the 'Valle Grande' reservoir make it a tourism hub as well.

appellations.name: San Rafael (IG)
appellations.summary: The department of San Rafael is also registered as a plain IG with the same limits as the DOC; producers usually label this simpler designation.

appellations.name: General Alvear
appellations.summary: General Alvear, east of San Rafael on the Atuel river, is Mendoza's southernmost wine department, with about 3,100 ha (INV 2024) of mostly traditional varieties and everyday wine.

appellations.name: Valle del Tulum
appellations.summary: The Tulum valley is the central irrigated oasis of San Juan around the provincial capital, at 600 to 700 m along the San Juan river. Hot and sunny with under 100 mm of rain, it grows most of the province's grapes: Cereza, Criolla, Pedro Giménez and Moscatel for wine, juice and raisins, alongside Syrah, Malbec and Bonarda for fine wine. Departments such as Pocito, Rawson, Caucete, 25 de Mayo, Sarmiento and San Martín lie within it.

appellations.name: 25 de Mayo
appellations.summary: Veinticinco de Mayo is one of San Juan's largest vineyard departments, south-east of the capital in the Tulum valley, about 7,700 ha of vines in 2024 (INV), much of it for bulk wine and juice.

appellations.name: 9 de Julio
appellations.summary: Nueve de Julio is a Tulum-valley department east of San Juan city with about 2,800 ha of vines (INV 2024), mostly traditional varieties.

appellations.name: Albardón
appellations.summary: Albardón, just north of San Juan city along the river, has about 1,400 ha of vines (INV 2024), many for table grapes and raisins.

appellations.name: Angaco
appellations.summary: Angaco, north-east of San Juan city, has about 2,100 ha of vines (INV 2024) in the Tulum oasis.

appellations.name: Caucete
appellations.summary: Caucete, east of the San Juan river, is one of the province's big vineyard departments (about 6,700 ha in 2024, INV) and second only to Sarmiento for Malbec in San Juan.

appellations.name: Chimbas
appellations.summary: Chimbas, on the northern edge of San Juan city, is a small, largely urban wine department with about 700 ha of vines (INV 2024).

appellations.name: Iglesia
appellations.summary: Iglesia is a high Andean department in north-western San Juan, around 1,600 to 1,900 m, with only a few hectares of vines (INV 2024) in an oasis landscape of poplars and adobe villages.

appellations.name: Jáchal
appellations.summary: Jáchal, in northern San Juan, is a historic agricultural oasis at about 1,150 m known for onions and wine; vineyards are now small.

appellations.name: Pocito
appellations.summary: Pocito, south of San Juan city in the Tulum valley, has about 2,900 ha of vines (INV 2024) and several of the province's established wineries.

appellations.name: Rawson
appellations.summary: Rawson, a Tulum-valley department on the southern edge of San Juan city, has about 1,250 ha of vines (INV 2024).

appellations.name: Santa Lucía
appellations.summary: Santa Lucía, east of San Juan city, has about 900 ha of vines (INV 2024), mostly traditional.

appellations.name: Sarmiento
appellations.summary: Sarmiento, in southern San Juan, is the province's leading Malbec department (932 ha of Malbec of about 7,000 ha of vines, INV 2024) and contains the high Pedernal valley.

appellations.name: Ullum
appellations.summary: Ullum, west of San Juan city around the Ullum reservoir, has about 1,200 ha of vines (INV 2024) on stony soils in the pre-cordillera.

appellations.name: Valle Fértil
appellations.summary: Valle Fértil, in the eastern San Juan hills, is a green valley with almost no vineyard today; its IG dates from the 2002 national list.

appellations.name: Zonda
appellations.summary: Zonda is the department west of San Juan city, in a valley between pre-cordillera ranges that gave its name to the Zonda wind. About 1,000 ha of vines (INV 2024) with a reputation for fresher Syrah and Malbec.

appellations.name: Rivadavia (San Juan)
appellations.summary: Rivadavia in San Juan (not to be confused with Mendoza's Rivadavia) is a mostly urban department west of the provincial capital with under 200 ha of vines (INV 2024).

appellations.name: San Martín (San Juan)
appellations.summary: San Martín in San Juan, east of the capital in the Tulum valley, has about 3,600 ha of vines (INV 2024). Not to be confused with Mendoza's much larger San Martín.

appellations.name: Valle de Zonda
appellations.summary: Valle de Zonda, recognised in 2015, is a narrower IG for the vineyards of the Zonda valley itself, a pre-cordillera basin west of San Juan city where cooler nights and stony soils give fresher reds than the Tulum oasis.

appellations.name: Valle del Pedernal
appellations.summary: Pedernal is San Juan's high-altitude showcase: a narrow valley at about 1,250 to 1,500 m in Sarmiento department, between pre-cordillera ranges, where calcareous, stony soils and cold nights produce Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Chardonnay with real freshness. Pyros and Viñas de Segisa are among its producers.

appellations.name: Pozo de los Algarrobos
appellations.summary: Pozo de los Algarrobos is a small IG in Caucete department, east of the San Juan river, recognised in 2015 for the vineyards of this desert locality.

appellations.name: Calingasta
appellations.created: 2002 (INV Res. C.32/2002; synonym Valle de Calingasta 2013)
appellations.summary: Calingasta is San Juan's spectacular Andean valley, a north-south trough at 1,350 to 1,700 m between the main cordillera and the pre-cordillera, reached by a mountain road from San Juan. Only about 250 ha of vines (INV 2024), two-thirds of them Malbec, grow around Calingasta, Tamberías and Barreal on stony soils with huge day-night swings, giving deep-coloured, fresh reds. Since 2024 the valley has three more sub-IGs, Tamberías, Hilario and Sorocayense.

appellations.name: Barreal
appellations.summary: Barreal, at about 1,650 m at the southern end of the Calingasta valley under the Mercedario peak, is one of the highest IGs in Cuyo. Cara Sur makes light, mountain Criolla and Bonarda here from old vines trained on parral.

appellations.name: Tamberías
appellations.summary: Tamberías is a village at about 1,500 m in the Calingasta valley, recognised as an IG at the request of the Calingasta municipality, together with Hilario and Sorocayense. Its name refers to Inca *tambos* (waystations) on the trail along the valley.

appellations.name: Hilario
appellations.summary: Hilario is a small locality in the Calingasta valley, recognised as an IG together with Tamberías and Sorocayense in early 2024 to protect the names of the valley's distinct high-altitude terroirs.

appellations.name: Sorocayense
appellations.summary: Sorocayense (Paraje Sorocayense) is a locality in the Calingasta valley, recognised as an IG together with Tamberías and Hilario in 2024.

appellations.name: Valles del Famatina
appellations.grapes: Torrontés Riojano, Malbec, Bonarda, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon
appellations.summary: The Famatina valleys, between the Famatina range (6,100 m) and the Velasco hills in La Rioja, are the province's wine heartland, with Chilecito at the centre at about 1,000 to 1,400 m. This is the home of Torrontés Riojano, grown for generations on high pergolas and made into aromatic, floral whites, and of the giant La Riojana cooperative. Valles del Famatina was Argentina's third most used IG in 2022 and second for exports by volume (INV), mostly as good-value Torrontés and Malbec.

appellations.name: Chilecito
appellations.summary: Chilecito is La Rioja's wine capital and the core of the Famatina valleys, with about 580 ha of Malbec and much more Torrontés Riojano; La Riojana cooperative is based here, and the town still has the cableway built in 1904 to carry ore from the Famatina mines.

appellations.name: Famatina
appellations.summary: Famatina department, north of Chilecito under the snow-capped Famatina range, grows Torrontés and Malbec at 1,400 to 1,700 m; it contains the Valle de Chañarmuyo IG.

appellations.name: Arauco
appellations.summary: Arauco, around Aimogasta in northern La Rioja, is olive country first; its IG covers small vineyards of traditional varieties.

appellations.name: Castro Barros
appellations.summary: Castro Barros, in the valleys north of La Rioja city, has about 70 ha of Malbec among small traditional vineyards (INV 2024).

appellations.name: Felipe Varela
appellations.summary: Coronel Felipe Varela department, around Villa Unión in western La Rioja, grows grapes in an arid basin near the Talampaya canyon.

appellations.name: General Lamadrid
appellations.summary: General Lamadrid is a remote high department in western La Rioja with a few hectares of vines.

appellations.name: San Blas de los Sauces
appellations.summary: San Blas de los Sauces, in northern La Rioja, is a string of small oasis villages with traditional vineyards.

appellations.name: Sanagasta
appellations.summary: Sanagasta, a hill valley north of La Rioja city, has a small wine tradition and a few hectares of Malbec.

appellations.name: Vinchina
appellations.summary: Vinchina, in the far west of La Rioja near the Andes, is a high, arid department with tiny vineyards for local wine.

appellations.name: Valle de Chañarmuyo
appellations.summary: Chañarmuyo is a high valley at about 1,700 m in Famatina department where Bodega Chañarmuyo planted a modern estate in the 2000s. Recognised in 2014, it gives altitude Malbec, Cabernet and Torrontés of more freshness than the lower Famatina floor.

appellations.name: Tinogasta
appellations.summary: Tinogasta, around Fiambalá and Tinogasta towns in western Catamarca at 1,200 to 1,700 m, is the province's main wine area, with old Torrontés and Criolla vines, adobe wineries and home-made *vino patero*, plus modern altitude Syrah and Malbec.

appellations.name: Belén
appellations.summary: Belén, in central-western Catamarca, grows grapes in small Andean oases such as Hualfín and Londres at 1,200 to 1,800 m.

appellations.name: Pomán
appellations.summary: Pomán, at the foot of the Ambato range in Catamarca, has a few traditional vineyards around Saujil and Mutquín.

appellations.name: Santa María
appellations.summary: Santa María, in the north of Catamarca at about 1,900 m, is the southern end of the Calchaquí valleys system, with about 220 ha of Malbec and old Torrontés vines (INV 2024).

appellations.name: Valles Calchaquíes
appellations.grapes: Malbec, Torrontés Riojano, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat, Cabernet Franc, Criolla Chica
appellations.terroir: Sandy and gravelly alluvium on valley terraces, granite and schist slopes; 1,700 to 3,100 m; high UV, cold nights, under 200 mm of rain.
appellations.summary:
The Calchaquí valleys form one of the highest wine regions on Earth: a 270-km chain of arid valleys along the Calchaquí river and its tributaries, crossing Salta, Tucumán and Catamarca from Cachi and Payogasta in the north to Cafayate and Santa María in the south. Vineyards sit between about 1,700 m at Cafayate and over 3,000 m around Payogasta, under the Andes' eastern ranges. The Jesuits and Spanish settlers brought Criolla vines in the colonial era; the Isasmendi and Dávalos families planted French Malbec and Cabernet at Colomé in the 1850s.

Altitude defines the wine. Strong ultraviolet light thickens grape skins, giving Malbec, Tannat and Cabernet Sauvignon deep colour and firm tannin; nights are cold, so acidity stays high. Torrontés Riojano reaches its most perfumed and best-balanced style at Cafayate. Soils are sandy and stony alluvium with low organic matter, and rainfall is under 200 mm. The IG was the fourth most used Argentine IG in 2022 (INV).

appellations.name: Valle de Cafayate
appellations.created: 2002 (INV Res. C.32/2002; only 'Valle de Cafayate' allowed since 2005)
appellations.summary: Cafayate is the wine town of the Calchaquí valleys, at about 1,700 to 2,000 m, with roughly 2,765 ha of vines (INV 2024), three-quarters of Salta's total. Its sandy, wind-scoured terraces under the red sandstone of the Quebrada de las Conchas give Argentina's best Torrontés, aromatic yet dry, and dense, sun-built Malbec, Cabernet and Tannat. Wineries such as El Esteco, Etchart, El Porvenir and Michel Rolland's Yacochuya line the town. Because 'Cafayate' is a registered trademark, INV ruled in 2005 that only the form 'Valle de Cafayate' may be used on labels.

appellations.name: Molinos
appellations.summary: Molinos is a colonial village in the middle Calchaquí valley at about 2,000 m. Its department includes Colomé, founded in 1831 and one of Argentina's oldest working wineries, whose vineyards climb from 2,300 to 3,111 m, and the small high estate of Tacuil. Malbec covers 69% of its 133 ha (INV 2024).

appellations.name: Cachi
appellations.summary: Cachi, in the upper Calchaquí valley at about 2,300 to 3,000 m under the Nevado de Cachi, has about 117 ha of vines (INV 2024), 73% Malbec. Vineyards at Cachi Adentro and Payogasta are among the highest in the world.

appellations.name: San Carlos (Salta)
appellations.summary: San Carlos department in Salta, between Cafayate and Molinos along the Calchaquí river, includes Angastaco and Animaná, with about 670 ha of vines (INV 2024). It contains the Valle de Pucará IG.

appellations.name: Valle de Pucará
appellations.summary: Valle de Pucará, recognised in March 2025 at the request of Finca de los Viñedos Imposibles, is a high side valley west of Angastaco in San Carlos department, at well over 2,000 m. Its name (from the Quechua for 'fortress') recalls pre-Hispanic hilltop sites; local growers make Malbec and Criolla of extreme concentration.

appellations.name: Quebrada de Humahuaca
appellations.summary: The Quebrada de Humahuaca, a UNESCO World Heritage valley of coloured mountains in Jujuy, has a tiny modern wine scene on terraces between about 2,300 and 3,300 m around Maimará, Tilcara, Huacalera and Uquía. Fernando Dupont, Bodega Kindgard and others make Malbec, Cabernet Franc, Syrah and Merlot of intense colour and freshness. It is one of the highest IGs in the world.

appellations.name: Valles Templados
appellations.summary: Valles Templados ('temperate valleys'), recognised in August 2025 at the request of Jujuy's provincial government, covers the lower, greener valleys of Jujuy around San Salvador, El Carmen and Perico, where a subtropical-montane climate allows a small but growing wine production.

appellations.name: Tafí
appellations.summary: Tafí (Tafí del Valle department) is Tucumán's wine IG, taking in Colalao del Valle and Amaicha del Valle on the Calchaquí side of the Aconquija range at about 1,700 to 2,000 m, where Malbec and Torrontés grow. Amaicha's indigenous community runs its own community winery, Los Amaichas.

appellations.name: Alto valle de Río Negro
appellations.summary: The Alto Valle is the irrigated upper valley of the Río Negro from the Neuquén-Limay confluence east past General Roca, an apple-and-pear oasis at about 250 to 300 m. Humberto Canale planted vines here in 1909, and old Malbec, Merlot, Pinot Noir and Semillon from mid-20th-century plantings now attract fine-wine producers. Cool nights, constant wind and long summer days give fresh, perfumed wines.

appellations.name: General Roca
appellations.summary: General Roca department is the core of Río Negro wine, along the Alto Valle with about 215 ha of Malbec (INV 2024); it includes Mainqué, home of Noemía and Chacra.

appellations.name: Avellaneda
appellations.summary: Avellaneda department, in the middle Río Negro valley around Choele Choel, grows pears, apples and a little wine; about 58 ha of Malbec (INV 2024).

appellations.name: General Conesa
appellations.summary: General Conesa, on the lower Río Negro, is a small irrigated area with a few vineyards.

appellations.name: Pichimahuida
appellations.summary: Pichi Mahuida, on the Río Colorado at the north-eastern edge of Río Negro province, has a few small vineyards.

appellations.name: Añelo
appellations.summary: Añelo department in Neuquén contains San Patricio del Chañar, where from the late 1990s irrigation turned desert plateau into vineyards for Bodega del Fin del Mundo, Familia Schroeder and NQN; it holds 89% of Neuquén's Malbec (INV 2024).

appellations.name: Confluencia
appellations.summary: Confluencia, the department around Neuquén city where the Neuquén and Limay rivers meet, has small vineyards near Plottier and Centenario.

appellations.name: Sarmiento (Chubut)
appellations.summary: Sarmiento, in central Chubut near lakes Musters and Colhué Huapi at about 45.5°S, is one of the southernmost wine IGs in the world, recognised in 2023. Small vineyards of cool-climate varieties grow in a cold, windy steppe oasis.

appellations.name: Trevelin
appellations.summary: Trevelin, a town founded by Welsh settlers in the Andean foothills of Chubut at about 43°S, became an IG in 2020. Vineyards near the Futaleufú river, among the southernmost in the Americas, grow Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling for crisp, low-alcohol wines.

appellations.name: El Hoyo
appellations.summary: El Hoyo, a pre-Andean valley in the far north of Chubut near El Bolsón at only about 300 m, became an IG in September 2023 at the request of Patagonian Wines, the estate founded by Bernardo Weinert. Its roughly 28 ha grow Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling and Gewürztraminer at latitude 42°S.

appellations.name: Colón
appellations.summary: Colón department, north of Córdoba city, contains Colonia Caroya and Jesús María, the historic core of Córdoba wine.

appellations.name: Colonia Caroya
appellations.nerd_note: The nearby Estancia Jesuítica de Caroya, part of a UNESCO World Heritage site, made wine for the Jesuit college of Córdoba from the 17th century.
appellations.summary: Colonia Caroya was settled in 1878 by immigrants from Friuli, who planted vines on land of the former Jesuit estancia of Caroya. They still make Frambua, a sweetish red from the American hybrid Isabella, alongside vinifera wines, and celebrate a harvest festival each year.

appellations.name: Cruz del Eje
appellations.summary: Cruz del Eje, in north-western Córdoba, is a warm valley with a small grape-growing tradition.

appellations.name: San Javier
appellations.summary: San Javier department, in the Traslasierra valley west of the Córdoba hills around Villa Dolores, has small vineyards at the foot of the Comechingones range.

appellations.name: Chapadmalal
appellations.summary: Chapadmalal, on the Atlantic coast south of Mar del Plata, is Argentina's maritime wine experiment: Trapiche planted vineyards here around 2010 a few kilometres from the sea, and the IG followed in 2014. Cool, humid, windy conditions on loess soils give Sauvignon Blanc, Albariño, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir with real salinity, sold as Costa & Pampa.

appellations.name: Balcarce
appellations.summary: Balcarce, in the Tandilia hills of south-eastern Buenos Aires province, was recognised in 2022 at the request of the area's one significant winery. It is cool, humid Pampas country suited to Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and sparkling base.

appellations.name: Tandil
appellations.summary: Tandil, in the granite hills of the Tandilia system, became an IG in July 2024, the third in the Buenos Aires hills. Better known for salami and cheese, it now has a few vineyards on rocky slopes.

appellations.name: Villa Ventana
appellations.summary: Villa Ventana, in the Sierra de la Ventana hills of south-western Buenos Aires province, was recognised in 2011. A handful of small wineries grow cool-climate varieties on stony slopes.

appellations.name: Victoria, Entre Ríos
appellations.summary: Victoria, on the Paraná river delta in Entre Ríos, revives a wine tradition that flourished in the province in the late 19th and early 20th centuries before 1930s national regulation favoured Cuyo and many vineyards were uprooted. Recognised in 2021, it grows small volumes of red wine in a humid, temperate climate.

appellations.name: Canelones
appellations.grapes: Tannat, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Marselan, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Albariño, Muscat Hamburg
appellations.terroir: Rolling hills of heavy clay and clay-calcareous soils; humid maritime climate with about 1,000 mm of rain; sea breezes from the River Plate.
appellations.nerd_note: Uruguay grows nearly a third of the world's Tannat, by INAVI and University of Adelaide estimates, and most of it is in Canelones.
appellations.summary: Canelones, immediately north of Montevideo, is Uruguay's wine heartland: by most accounts more than 60% of national production, with Montevideo together over three-quarters of the vineyard. Its gently rolling hills of heavy clay and clay-calcareous soils (around Las Piedras, Progreso, Juanicó, Canelón Chico, Las Violetas and Melilla's edge) are home to the historic family wineries of Italian, Basque and Spanish descent: Pisano, Pizzorno, Carrau, Stagnari, Juanicó, Marichal, Toscanini, De Lucca, Varela Zarranz. Tannat is king, making structured, ageable reds whose tannins are tamed by the maritime humidity, alongside Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Marselan, Sauvignon Blanc and a growing range of Italian and Spanish varieties. INAVI itself is headquartered in Las Piedras.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Montevideo
appellations.summary: Montevideo department holds the historic suburban vineyards of the capital, at Melilla, Colón, Peñarol and Carrasco. Francisco Vidiella made the first harvest of European vines at Colón in 1883, and Bodega Bouza, Carrau's Colón winery, Bodega Santa Rosa and others keep the tradition alive within city limits. Conditions mirror Canelones: clay soils, river-moderated climate, Tannat, Merlot and Albariño.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: San José
appellations.summary: San José, west of Canelones, is pastoral cattle country with a significant vineyard (about 500 ha in 2013) on the gentle hills around Libertad, Ecilda Paullier and Rincón del Pino. Conditions are similar to Canelones, slightly more influenced by the River Plate.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Maldonado
appellations.grapes: Albariño, Tannat, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Franc, Sauvignon Blanc, Marselan
appellations.terroir: Granite, gneiss and decomposed 'balasto' rock on hills up to a few hundred metres; strong Atlantic winds; cooler summers.
appellations.nerd_note: Garzón's vineyard is split into a large number of small blocks to follow the patchwork of granite and soil depth.
appellations.summary:
Maldonado is Uruguay's fastest-growing and most glamorous wine region, on granite hills between Punta del Este, José Ignacio and the sierras inland. Nobody planted here until Alto de la Ballena in 2001, because the rocky, poor soils gave low yields; that is exactly what attracted the quality pioneers. The ocean is close, winds are strong and summers fresher, so Tannat comes out brighter and Albariño, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Franc shine.

Bodega Garzón, built near Pueblo Garzón by Argentine billionaire Alejandro Bulgheroni and opened in 2016, put the department on the world map with hundreds of small vineyard blocks on granite and ballast-like decomposed rock. Viña Edén, Bodega Oceánica José Ignacio, Familia Deicas's Atlántico Sur and Cerro del Toro are among the others.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Rocha
appellations.summary: Rocha, the easternmost coastal department towards the Brazilian border, is Uruguay's newest wine frontier, with a handful of small vineyards in windswept coastal and sierra sites.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Lavalleja
appellations.summary: Lavalleja, inland from Maldonado in the eastern sierras, has few vineyards, but Familia Deicas farms an extreme site on the volcanic outcrop of Cerro del Guazuvirá, a rare volcanic terroir in Uruguay.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Colonia
appellations.summary: Colonia, on the River Plate opposite Buenos Aires, has the oldest commercial winery in Uruguay, Los Cerros de San Juan (1854), and a hub of wineries around Carmelo, including Irurtia, Narbona and the Zubizarreta family. The warmer river influence and sedimentary soils make Tannat fuller and riper here.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Soriano
appellations.summary: Soriano, on the Uruguay river north of Colonia, has a small vineyard area among the grain farms around Dolores and Mercedes.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Salto
appellations.nerd_note: Uruguayans called Tannat 'Harriague' in the founder's honour for decades.
appellations.summary: Salto, on the Uruguay river in the north-west, is where Pascual Harriague planted Tannat around 1870 and where the grape's Uruguayan story began. Today its vineyards are small (about 60 ha in 2013), in a warmer, more continental climate.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Paysandú
appellations.summary: Paysandú, on the Uruguay river, has about 170 ha of vines (2013) on sedimentary soils in a warm, continental climate; Tannat and Cabernet ripen fully here.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Artigas
appellations.summary: Artigas, the northernmost department, grows grapes around Bella Unión on the Brazilian border, in Uruguay's warmest climate (about 115 ha in 2013).
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Durazno
appellations.summary: Durazno, in the centre of the country, has a small, experimental wine scene led by Bodega El Capricho, an early planter of Verdejo and Mencía in Uruguay. Supple reds from warmer inland conditions.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Florida
appellations.summary: Florida department, north of Canelones, has a few dozen hectares of vines (about 50 ha in 2013).
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Tacuarembó
appellations.summary: Tacuarembó, in the north-central interior, has small emerging plantings (about 30 ha in 2013).
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Rivera
appellations.summary: Rivera, on the Brazilian border, is Uruguay's most distinctive northern terroir: deep, red, sandy soils derived from sandstone, very free-draining in a warmer, sunnier climate. The Carrau family pioneered here from the 1970s with the Cerro Chapeu vineyard; the wines, notably Tannat and Cabernet, are fragrant and juicy with silky tannins.
appellations.classification: Uruguay has no legal appellations; geographic indications on labels follow the 19 departments.

appellations.name: Vale dos Vinhedos
appellations.grapes: DO: Merlot (main red), Chardonnay (main white); complementary Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat, Pinot Noir, Riesling Itálico. IP: 12 red and 11 white vinifera varieties.
appellations.terroir: Basalt-derived clays and some sandier soils on hillsides at 400 to 700 m; humid subtropical climate with summer rain.
appellations.nerd_note: Grape prices in the DO rose from about R$2.50 to R$12 per kilo after certification, by the producers' association's account.
appellations.summary:
Vale dos Vinhedos ('valley of the vineyards') is the cradle of Brazilian fine wine and its first appellation, a valley of about 82 km² of rolling hills shared by Bento Gonçalves, Garibaldi and Monte Belo do Sul in the Serra Gaúcha. Italian families settled here from 1875, and their descendants (Valduga, Miolo, Pizzato, Don Laurindo and others) turned small farms into Brazil's most visited wine valley. In 2002 it received Brazil's first geographical indication of any kind, an IP, and in 2012 the first wine DO.

The DO is built on two grapes: Merlot, which ripens reliably in the humid climate, for reds, and Chardonnay for whites and sparkling wine, with Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat, Pinot Noir and Riesling Itálico as permitted partners. Reds must age 12 months before release, and every lot is tasted by a regulatory council. About 11 wineries were certified to use the DO seal in 2025, while the older IP remains in force for a wider range of grapes. Expect supple, fresh Merlot with soft tannins and bright acidity, and some of Brazil's best traditional-method sparkling wine.

appellations.name: Altos de Pinto Bandeira
appellations.grapes: Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Riesling Itálico
appellations.nerd_note: The producers' association, Asprovinho, began work on the DO in 2016 and won it in 2022, twelve years after the area's IP.
appellations.summary: Altos de Pinto Bandeira is Brazil's second wine DO and one of the very few appellations anywhere reserved exclusively for traditional-method sparkling wine. Its 65 km² lie mostly in Pinto Bandeira (77%), with slivers of Farroupilha and Bento Gonçalves, on basalt plateaus at 520 to 770 m. Only Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Riesling Itálico are allowed, from vineyards trained on espalier or 'Y' trellises with a yield cap of 12 t/ha, and the whole process (base wine, second fermentation and ageing in bottle) must happen inside the area. Each bottle carries a numbered seal; the first DO wines reached the market in 2023. Producers such as Cave Geisse, founded by the Chilean Mario Geisse in 1979, made Pinto Bandeira's reputation for crisp, toasty, long-aged sparkling wine.

appellations.name: Pinto Bandeira
appellations.summary: Pinto Bandeira's IP (2010) covers about 7,960 ha on the high basalt plateau north-east of Bento Gonçalves and allows red, white and sparkling wines from eight red and twelve white vinifera varieties, with at least 85% of grapes from the area and sparkling wine by the traditional method only. It remains in force alongside the stricter sparkling-only DO Altos de Pinto Bandeira.

appellations.name: Altos Montes
appellations.summary: Altos Montes covers about 174 km² of high country in Flores da Cunha and Nova Pádua, among the highest parts of the Serra Gaúcha (often above 800 m). Its IP (2012) covers still and sparkling wines from varieties including Tannat, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Cabernet Franc. Flores da Cunha, settled by Venetians, is one of Brazil's leading wine-producing municipalities.

appellations.name: Monte Belo
appellations.summary: Monte Belo (Monte Belo do Sul), a 56 km² municipality next to the Vale dos Vinhedos, received its IP in 2013 for still and sparkling wines from a network of small family wineries descended from Italian settlers. Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat and Chardonnay are prominent.

appellations.name: Farroupilha
appellations.grapes: Moscato Branco, Moscato Giallo, Moscatel Nazareno, Malvasia de Cândia and other Muscats
appellations.nerd_note: The pilgrimage sanctuary of Nossa Senhora de Caravaggio in Farroupilha hosted the IP's founding mass in 2015.
appellations.summary: Farroupilha, near Caxias do Sul, is Brazil's Moscato capital, and its 2015 IP is unusual worldwide: it protects only Muscat-based products, including fine white Moscatel, Moscatel espumante (sweet, fragrant sparkling), frisante, licoroso, mistela and Moscatel brandy. The town grows most of Brazil's Moscato Branco, and its sparkling Moscatel, low in alcohol and fresh, is a national favourite.

appellations.name: Campanha Gaúcha
appellations.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat, Merlot, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir
appellations.summary: The Campanha Gaúcha is Brazil's second wine region by volume, a sunny, rolling grassland (the pampa) on the Uruguayan and Argentine borders between 29°S and 32°S. Modern vineyards date from the 1970s, when Almadén planted at Santana do Livramento; by 2019 about 1,512 ha supplied 31% of Brazilian fine-wine production. Its 2020 IP covers 14 municipalities and 18 wineries, with up to 36 vinifera varieties allowed. Drier, sunnier conditions and sandy, granite-derived soils give riper reds than the Serra: Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat and Merlot, plus Chardonnay for whites and sparkling.

appellations.name: Vinhos de Altitude de Santa Catarina
match: Vinhos de Altitude de Santa Catarina
appellations.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Malbec
appellations.summary: This IP covers wines from vineyards at least 900 m above sea level across 29 municipalities of Santa Catarina's high plateau, around São Joaquim, Urubici, Campos Novos and Caçador, about a fifth of the state. Nearly 300 ha of vines produce about a million bottles a year; the rules cap yields at 7,000 litres per hectare and require blind tasting. Cold winters (São Joaquim sees snow), late ripening into April and cool nights give Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and sparkling wines with high acidity.

appellations.name: Vales da Uva Goethe
appellations.grapes: Goethe (and Goethe Primo)
appellations.summary: Vales da Uva Goethe, in the valleys around Urussanga in southern Santa Catarina, protects wines from Goethe, a 19th-century American hybrid grape brought by Italian immigrants. The IP (2012) covers dry and off-dry whites, light wines, sparkling wines by traditional and Charmat methods, and licorosos, a rare case of a GI built on a hybrid.

appellations.name: Bituruna
appellations.summary: Bituruna, in southern Paraná, was granted an IP in 2022 for its *casca dura* ('hard skin') white wines, made from a pink, thick-skinned local grape long grown by Italian-descended families. The dry, aromatic wines of four wineries (Sanber, Bertoletti, Di Sandi and Dell Mont) were the first certified; Bituruna calls itself Paraná's wine capital.

appellations.name: Vale do São Francisco
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tempranillo, Touriga Nacional, Chenin Blanc, Moscato Canelli, Muscats
appellations.nerd_note: Embrapa's Jorge Tonietto called it the first region of tropical wines in the world to hold a GI with EU-style production standards.
appellations.summary: The world's first tropical wine region with a geographical indication, recognised by INPI on 1 November 2022. It covers five municipalities along the São Francisco river: Lagoa Grande, Petrolina and Santa Maria da Boa Vista in Pernambuco, and Casa Nova and Curaçá in Bahia, at about 9°S in the semi-arid sertão. Irrigation from the river turned caatinga scrub into vineyards from the 1960s. Because the vines never go dormant, growers prune to schedule successive harvests, often two a year. The IP covers fine still wines, sparkling wines and Muscat sparkling wines; fruity Syrah, Tempranillo, Chenin Blanc and Moscato are typical.

appellations.name: Sul de Minas
match: Vinhos de Inverno do Sul de Minas
appellations.grapes: Syrah, Sauvignon Blanc, Cabernet Franc, Merlot
appellations.nerd_note: The technique was developed in the 2000s by the Minas Gerais agricultural research company Epamig and spread to São Paulo, Goiás and the Federal District.
appellations.summary: Sul de Minas, granted in February 2025, is Brazil's 13th wine GI and protects 'vinhos de inverno', winter wines. Vines are pruned twice (*dupla poda*): once to grow the plant through the rainy summer and again to set fruit that ripens in the dry, cool winter, with harvest required between 1 June and 21 September. The area covers ten municipalities around Três Corações and Três Pontas (São João da Mata, Cordislândia, São Gonçalo do Sapucaí, Três Corações, Três Pontas, Campos Gerais, Boa Esperança, Bom Sucesso, Ibituruna and Ijaci). Syrah is the star, with Sauvignon Blanc and Cabernet Franc.

appellations.name: Ica
appellations.nerd_note: Ica's Huacachina oasis, a lagoon among giant dunes 5 km from the city, is the tourist centre of Peru's wine route.
appellations.summary: Ica, about 300 km south of Lima, is the heart of Peruvian wine and pisco: a desert valley with roughly half the country's production, about 400 to 500 m above sea level, irrigated by the Ica river and wells. It holds the colonial-era Hacienda Tacama, Viña Ocucaje (1898), Santiago Queirolo's estate and Intipalka, and the Tabernero group is based in nearby Chincha. Hot days and cool, foggy nights give ripe reds such as Malbec, Tannat and Petit Verdot, while Quebranta and the aromatic grapes go to pisco.

appellations.name: Lima
appellations.summary: Lima region's wine and pisco valleys lie south of the capital in Cañete, around Lunahuaná and Azpitia, where small producers make pisco, artisanal wine and *cachina* (young, partly fermented grape wine) on terraces along the Cañete river.

appellations.name: Arequipa
appellations.summary: Arequipa's wine valleys (Majes, Vítor, Caravelí) were colonial vineyards supplying the mines of Upper Peru; today they produce pisco and a revival of traditional wines from old Negra Criolla vines in desert valleys at 500 to 1,800 m.

appellations.name: Moquegua
appellations.nerd_note: Archaeological surveys have documented dozens of colonial winery sites, with their clay botijas, in the Moquegua valley.
appellations.summary: Moquegua was one of the great wine valleys of the viceroyalty; archaeologists have mapped dozens of colonial *bodegas* with clay jars in its desert valley. It is a pisco DO region with small, traditional producers.

appellations.name: Tacna
appellations.summary: Tacna, on the Chilean border, has pisco DO status in the Locumba, Sama and Caplina valleys, with small vineyards for pisco and local wine.

appellations.name: Valle Central de Tarija
appellations.grapes: Tannat, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Merlot, Moscatel de Alejandría, Torrontés
appellations.nerd_note: Tarija's Concepción valley in Uriondo is the hub of Bolivia's wine route, with adobe wineries and Casa Vieja's traditional cellar.
appellations.summary: The central valley of Tarija, at about 1,600 to 2,150 m, holds most of Bolivia's vineyards and wineries around the city of Tarija, Concepción (Uriondo), Santa Ana and La Pintada. A mild, semi-arid climate with summer rain, winds and cool nights favours Tannat, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah and Muscat for singani. Kohlberg, Aranjuez, Campos de Solana, Casa Vieja, La Concepción and Magnus are based here.

appellations.name: Valle de Cinti
appellations.grapes: Negra Criolla, Moscatel de Alejandría, Vischoqueña
appellations.nerd_note: About 300 ha of vineyard in Cinti include around 30 vineyards with vines trained up living trees.
appellations.summary: The Cinti valley in Chuquisaca, around Camargo and Villa Abecia at about 2,400 m, is the spiritual home of Bolivian traditional winemaking. Its colonial vineyards, some 100 to 250 years old, climb native molle and chañar trees in a narrow red-rock canyon, a training system found almost nowhere else. Old Negra Criolla, Moscatel and Vischoqueña vines make singani and small-batch wines that have attracted a new generation of producers since 2000.

appellations.name: Samaipata
appellations.summary: Samaipata, in the Andean foothills of Santa Cruz department at about 1,700 m, is a young wine area near a famous pre-Inca site. Small wineries such as Uvairenda (Vinos 1750) and Landsuá make fresh reds and whites in a more humid climate.

appellations.name: Cotagaita and Vitichi
appellations.summary: Neighbouring valleys in Potosí department, with about 250 ha of vines (2008), roughly a tenth of Bolivia's vineyard, mostly traditional grapes for singani and local wine.

sites.name: Viña Concha y Toro, Pirque
sites.text: Founded in 1883 by Melchor de Concha y Toro and his wife Emiliana Subercaseaux at their country house in Pirque, on the south bank of the Maipo. Today it is Latin America's largest wine company, and the historic park, house and the 'Casillero del Diablo' cellar (named for a legend the founder spread to scare off thieves) are Chile's most visited wine attraction.

sites.name: Don Melchor vineyard
sites.text: A Cabernet vineyard of about 127 ha on the alluvial terrace of the Maipo at Puente Alto, source of Don Melchor since its first vintage in 1987. Farmed in soil-defined blocks of river stones and sandy loam, it is the benchmark for Puente Alto Cabernet: cassis, cedar and graphite with fine, firm tannin. Now run as an independent winery within the Concha y Toro group.

sites.name: Almaviva
sites.text: Created in 1997 by Concha y Toro and Baron Philippe de Rothschild (Mouton) to make one Bordeaux-style blend from Puente Alto, with Carmenère as a distinctive minor partner. The wine's name, from Count Almaviva of Beaumarchais and Mozart's *Le nozze di Figaro*, and its single-wine focus signalled Chile's arrival among the great Cabernet terroirs.

sites.name: Viñedo Chadwick
sites.text: Eduardo Chadwick planted this 15-ha Cabernet vineyard in 1992 on his father's former polo field in Puente Alto. Its 2000 vintage beat Lafite, Margaux and Latour in the 2004 Berlin Tasting, and its 2014 vintage became the first Chilean wine to receive a perfect 100-point score from James Suckling.

sites.name: Viña Santa Rita, Alto Jahuel
sites.text: Founded in 1880 by Domingo Fernández Concha in Alto Jahuel, Buin. During the War of Independence its hacienda sheltered 120 soldiers of Bernardo O'Higgins, celebrated in the '120' wine range. The estate keeps a colonial house, chapel, park and the Andean Museum of pre-Columbian art.

sites.name: Viña Cousiño Macul, Peñalolén
sites.text: Founded in 1856 by Matías Cousiño, whose family fortune came from coal and silver, on land at the foot of the Andes in what is now Santiago's Peñalolén. Its 19th-century brick cellars are among the oldest in Chile; urban growth has shrunk the vineyard, and most production moved to Buin, but the historic winery still operates inside the city.

sites.name: Viña Carmen, Alto Jahuel
sites.text: Chile's oldest wine brand (1850) and the place where, on 24 November 1994, the French ampelographer Jean-Michel Boursiquot noticed that some of the 'Merlot' vines were in fact Carmenère, a grape thought lost after phylloxera. Viña Carmen's neighbouring estate sits in Alto Jahuel, Buin, close to Santa Rita.

sites.name: Viña Santa Carolina, Macul
sites.text: Founded in 1875 by Luis Pereira and named after his wife Carolina Íñiguez. Its 19th-century cellars, built with lime and egg-white mortar, survive inside Santiago's Macul district and are a national monument; Macul lies just outside the decree's 'Santiago' area, within the wider Maipo subregion.

sites.name: Viña Aquitania, Peñalolén
sites.text: Founded in 1990 by Bordeaux's Bruno Prats (Cos d'Estournel) and Paul Pontallier (Château Margaux) with Chilean Felipe de Solminihac, on the last Andean foothill vineyards inside Santiago. Its Lazuli Cabernet comes from here; its Sol de Sol Chardonnay from Malleco.

sites.name: Haras de Pirque
sites.text: A thoroughbred horse stud turned winery in Pirque, its horseshoe-shaped gravity cellar set among hillside Cabernet vineyards at the mouth of the Maipo canyon. Italy's Antinori family, first its partner in the Albis blend, later took control of the estate.

sites.name: Antiyal, Paine
sites.text: Álvaro Espinoza's family estate in Paine, one of Chile's pioneers of biodynamic farming from the late 1990s. A tiny vineyard of Carmenère, Cabernet and Syrah tended with cows, compost and lunar calendars.

sites.name: De Martino, Isla de Maipo
sites.text: The De Martino family winery (founded 1934) led Chile's 2010s turn away from ripeness and new oak. Its Viejas Tinajas wines from Itata, fermented in old clay jars, and its single-vineyard Legado range map terroirs from Limarí to Malleco.

sites.name: Viña Undurraga, Talagante
sites.text: Francisco Undurraga founded the winery in 1885 at Santa Ana, Talagante, where its historic house and landscaped park survive. Undurraga says it was the first Chilean winery to export to the United States, in 1903.

sites.name: Viña Errázuriz, Panquehue
sites.text: Maximiano Errázuriz planted the Aconcagua Valley's first fine-wine vineyard here in 1870. Today the Chadwick family's Errázuriz runs the historic bodega, the hillside Max Viñedo, the Don Maximiano Founder's Reserve vineyard and a modern icon winery built in 2010.

sites.name: Max Viñedo (Errázuriz)
sites.text: The terraced hillside vineyard above Errázuriz's Panquehue bodega, source of Don Maximiano and the Max range. Colluvial slopes on the warm north side of the Aconcagua valley give ripe but structured Cabernet, Carmenère and Syrah.

sites.name: Seña
sites.text: Conceived in 1995 by Eduardo Chadwick and Robert Mondavi as Chile's first icon blend. After early vintages from Panquehue, the wine moved to its own biodynamic hillside vineyard in the Ocoa hills of Hijuelas, planted from 1998. Seña 2001 finished second in the 2004 Berlin Tasting.

sites.name: Manzanar vineyard, Aconcagua Costa
sites.text: Errázuriz's coastal vineyard about 12 km from the Pacific, planted from 2005 on schist and clay slopes. Labelled Aconcagua Costa, its Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Syrah turned a valley famous for heat into a source of saline, cool-climate wine.

sites.name: Viña Veramonte, Casablanca
sites.text: Founded in 1990 by Agustín Huneeus at the eastern gateway of the Casablanca Valley on Ruta 68. One of the valley's first large estates, now farmed organically, known for Sauvignon Blanc and the Primus red blend.

sites.name: Casas del Bosque, Casablanca
sites.text: Founded in 1993 by the Cúneo family in the cooler western part of Casablanca, a few kilometres closer to the ocean than Ruta 68. Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir from frost-prone, granite-and-clay slopes.

sites.name: Kingston Family Vineyards
sites.text: The Kingston family, Americans who came to Chile to prospect for gold in the early 1900s, ran cattle in western Casablanca before planting vines in 1998. Their hillside Pinot Noir and Syrah sit among the coolest sites in the valley, in the western hills closest to the Pacific.

sites.name: Viña Leyda
sites.text: In 1998 the Fernández family ran an 8 km pipeline from the Maipo river to irrigate the dry hills of Leyda and planted the first vines in what became the Valle de Leyda zone. Leyda Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir now define the San Antonio coast's saline style.

sites.name: Casa Marín, Lo Abarca
sites.text: María Luz Marín planted vines 4 km from the Pacific at Lo Abarca in 2000, told by everyone that grapes would never ripen. Her single-slope Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Gewürztraminer, Pinot Noir and Syrah gave the hamlet its own DO in 2018, practically a one-producer appellation.

sites.name: Matetic
sites.text: The Matetic family's biodynamic estate in the Rosario valley straddles the Casablanca and San Antonio boundary. Its EQ Syrah, from cool granite slopes, helped prove Chile could make peppery, Rhône-like Syrah.

sites.name: Viña Falernia, Vicuña
sites.text: Founded in 1998 by Aldo Olivier Gramola and his cousin Giorgio Flessati, Trentino natives, beside the Puclaro reservoir in the Elqui Valley. Falernia showed that the pisco valley could make serious wine, above all a peppery, high-altitude Syrah.

sites.name: Pisco Elqui
sites.text: A village in the upper Elqui (Paiguano) that changed its name from La Unión to Pisco Elqui in 1936 to assert Chile's claim to the word pisco in the long dispute with Peru. Distilleries and small vineyards of Moscatel and Pedro Jiménez line the river.

sites.name: Alcohuaz
sites.text: A hamlet at the top of the Claro valley in Paiguano where Viñedos de Alcohuaz farms terraced granite vineyards at roughly 1,700 to 2,200 m, among the highest in Chile. Syrah, Garnacha, Malbec and Petite Sirah are fermented in open stone lagares.

sites.name: Viña Tabalí, Limarí
sites.text: Tabalí's winery stands among petroglyphs in the Valle del Encanto near Ovalle. In the coastal hills of Talinay, about 12 km from the sea, its vineyards grow on limestone, a geological rarity in Chile, giving taut, salty Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Talinay hills, Limarí
sites.text: The coastal Altos de Talinay, where Tabalí planted on calcium carbonate soils in the 2000s. The limestone and the daily camanchaca fog make this one of the few places in South America where Chardonnay tastes of chalk.

sites.name: Quebrada Seca, Limarí
sites.text: A dry gully in the lower Limarí with calcareous soils, source of Concha y Toro's Maycas del Limarí and other mineral Chardonnays. It was proposed as a DO in 2018 but refused because it is not a recognised named locality.

sites.name: Clos Apalta (Lapostolle)
sites.text: Alexandra Marnier-Lapostolle (of the Grand Marnier family) and Cyril de Bournet founded Lapostolle in 1994. Its Clos Apalta, a Carmenère-led blend from old vines in the Apalta horseshoe, is made in a multi-level gravity winery cut into the granite hill, completed in 2005.

sites.name: Viña Montes, Apalta
sites.text: Aurelio Montes and partners founded Montes in 1987 and built a feng-shui-inspired gravity winery in Apalta, where Gregorian chant plays to barrels. Montes Alpha M (1996) and Folly, Chile's first Syrah from Apalta's steepest slopes, made the hillside famous.

sites.name: Montes Folly vineyard
sites.text: The steep upper slopes of Apalta where Montes planted Syrah in the 1990s, against local advice that vines could not be farmed on 45-degree granite. The 'folly' produced Chile's first icon Syrah, Montes Folly.

sites.name: Neyen, Apalta
sites.text: An old adobe estate in the eastern Apalta horseshoe with Carmenère and Cabernet vines over a century old. Its single blend, Espíritu de Apalta, shows the valley's dark fruit and granite freshness.

sites.name: Viña Ventisquero, Apalta
sites.text: Ventisquero's Apalta vineyard produces Pangea Syrah, created with the Australian winemaker John Duval, formerly of Penfolds Grange. The same company runs the pioneering Tara desert-coast project in the Huasco valley of Atacama.

sites.name: Museo de Colchagua, Santa Cruz
sites.text: Chile's largest private museum, founded by Carlos Cardoen in Santa Cruz in 1995, with collections from pre-Columbian ceramics to colonial winemaking tools, wine presses and huaso culture. It anchors the Colchagua wine route.

sites.name: Hacienda Los Lingues
sites.text: One of Chile's oldest colonial estates, granted in the 16th century and owned by the same family for centuries, famous for its Aculeo horses and old manor. It gave its name to the 492-ha Los Lingues DO, upheld by Chile's Supreme Court in June 2026.

sites.name: Casa Silva, Angostura
sites.text: The Silva family, which traces its Colchagua winemaking to a French ancestor in the 1890s, runs this estate near San Fernando with its own polo field and hotel. Casa Silva pioneered coastal Paredones and the far-south Lago Ranco vineyard in Osorno.

sites.name: Los Vascos, Peralillo
sites.text: A colonial Basque-founded estate bought in 1988 by Domaines Barons de Rothschild (Lafite), one of the first foreign investments of Chile's modern era. Its Le Dix blend marked the tenth anniversary of the partnership.

sites.name: Viña Vik, Millahue
sites.text: Norwegian-Uruguayan Alexander Vik's estate in the Millahue valley of Cachapoal, chosen after a lengthy terroir study. The winery sits beneath a stretched fabric roof over a water-covered cellar, next to a dramatic hilltop hotel.

sites.name: Concha y Toro Peumo vineyard
sites.text: The Peumo vineyard on the Cachapoal river, source of Carmín de Peumo and Terrunyo Carmenère. Clay-rich alluvial soils and a warm, sheltered bowl let Carmenère ripen fully, which is why Chilean growers once called the grape 'Merlot Peumal'.

sites.name: Miguel Torres, Curicó
sites.text: Miguel A. Torres bought land in Curicó in 1979, the first foreign winery investment of Chile's modern era. Stainless steel and temperature-controlled fermentation followed, and today Torres also works with Maule's País and Empedrado's slate.

sites.name: Viña San Pedro, Molina
sites.text: Founded in 1865, San Pedro farms one of the largest single vineyard blocks in South America at Lontué, Molina. It anchors the VSPT group and the 1865 and Altaïr labels.

sites.name: Viña Gillmore, San Javier
sites.text: A family estate in Villavicencio, San Javier, in the dry-farmed hills of Loncomilla, with old Carignan, Cabernet Franc and País. Gillmore is a member of VIGNO and a strong voice for Maule's old vines.

sites.name: J. Bouchon, Mingre
sites.text: The Bouchon family, from Bordeaux in the 1890s, farms Maule's coastal secano at Mingre, where they rescued wild País vines climbing trees and dry-farmed old Carignan and Semillon.

sites.name: Cauquenes secano vineyards
sites.text: The granite hills around Cauquenes hold Chile's densest concentration of dry-farmed, head-trained País and Carignan, many vines a century or more old, ploughed by horse and never irrigated. This is the heartland of VIGNO and of the Secano Interior special DO.

sites.name: Guarilihue, Itata
sites.text: A granite hamlet in Coelemu, 20 km from the sea, with own-rooted Cinsault and Moscatel planted generations ago. De Martino's Viejas Tinajas and many small producers' Cinsaults come from here, fermented in old clay tinajas.

sites.name: Traiguén (Sol de Sol vineyard)
sites.text: Viña Aquitania planted Chardonnay near Traiguén in Malleco in the mid-1990s, in a cool, rainy corner of Araucanía. The result, Sol de Sol, was the first wine to show southern Chile's potential for tense, ageable Chardonnay.

sites.name: Lago Ranco vineyard (Casa Silva)
sites.text: Casa Silva's vineyard on the shore of Lake Ranco at Futrono, near 40°S, one of the southernmost in Chile. The lake moderates frost; Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir and sparkling base wines carry very high natural acidity.

sites.name: Bodega Catena Zapata
sites.text: The Catena family's pyramid in Agrelo, built in the late 1990s to a Mayan-inspired design by Pablo Sánchez Elía, overlooks the La Pirámide vineyard planted in 1983. Nicolás Catena's research on high-altitude Malbec, continued by his daughter Laura's Catena Institute of Wine, transformed Argentina's image. Named World's Best Vineyard in 2023.

sites.name: Adrianna Vineyard, Gualtallary
sites.text: Planted by Nicolás Catena in 1992 at about 1,450 m in Gualtallary, Tupungato, where locals said grapes would never ripen. Its parcels on calcareous gravels give the Adrianna Malbecs (Mundus Bacillus Terrae, Fortuna Terrae, River Stones) and the White Bones and White Stones Chardonnays, among the most acclaimed wines of South America.

sites.name: Achával-Ferrer
sites.text: Founded in 1998 by Santiago Achával and Manuel Ferrer with Italian winemaker Roberto Cipresso among the partners, Achával-Ferrer helped prove that old, low-yielding Malbec vineyards could each make a distinct single-vineyard wine: Finca Altamira, Finca Bella Vista and Finca Mirador. Its winery stands by the Mendoza river in Perdriel.

sites.name: Zuccardi Valle de Uco
sites.text: Opened in 2016 at Paraje Altamira, the Zuccardi winery is built from the rounded, lime-coated stones of its own vineyards, and works largely with concrete fermenters and untoasted casks. Sebastián Zuccardi's parcel-by-parcel approach made it the World's Best Vineyard in 2019, 2020 and 2021.

sites.name: Finca Piedra Infinita
sites.text: Zuccardi's estate vineyard at Paraje Altamira, named for the 'infinite stone' of its soils: river cobbles coated in calcium carbonate over sand. Its Malbecs, including Finca Piedra Infinita and Gravascal, are made by soil type rather than variety.

sites.name: Bodega Noemía
sites.text: Founded in 2001 in Mainqué, Río Negro, by Italian Countess Noemi Marone Cinzano and Danish winemaker Hans Vinding-Diers, around a Malbec vineyard planted in 1932. Biodynamically farmed, flood-irrigated old vines in the Patagonian wind give some of Argentina's most perfumed Malbec.

sites.name: Bodega Chacra
sites.text: Piero Incisa della Rocchetta, of the family behind Sassicaia, founded Chacra in Mainqué in 2004 around ungrafted Pinot Noir planted in 1932 and 1955, naming wines after the planting years (Treinta y Dos, Cincuenta y Cinco). Biodynamic farming and Burgundian restraint made it Patagonia's reference for Pinot Noir.

sites.name: Bodega Humberto Canale
sites.text: Founded in 1909 by engineer Humberto Canale near General Roca, the pioneer winery of Patagonia. Still family-owned, it keeps old Semillon, Malbec and Merlot vineyards in the Alto Valle among apple and pear orchards.

sites.name: Bodega Colomé
sites.text: Founded in 1831 by the governor of Salta, Nicolás Severo de Isasmendi, Colomé is one of Argentina's oldest working wineries; French Malbec and Cabernet were brought in 1854. Swiss collector Donald Hess bought it in 2001, planted vineyards from 2,300 to 3,111 m and opened a James Turrell museum on the estate.

sites.name: Altura Máxima vineyard
sites.text: Colomé's vineyard at 3,111 m near Payogasta in the upper Calchaquí valley, among the highest commercial vineyards in the world. Frost, wind and extreme ultraviolet light make yields tiny; the Malbec and Pinot Noir sold as Altura Máxima are deeply coloured yet fresh.

sites.name: El Esteco, Cafayate
sites.text: A winery founded in 1892 by the Michel brothers at the edge of Cafayate, long known as Michel Torino. Today El Esteco keeps old Torrontés and Criolla vines, makes the Old Vines range, and its colonial estate houses the Patios de Cafayate hotel.

sites.name: Bodega Weinert
sites.text: Bernardo Weinert, born in Brazil, founded the winery in 1975 in a late 19th-century cellar in Carrodilla, Luján de Cuyo. Weinert is famous for ageing reds for years in large, old oak casks, the Cavas de Weinert style, a living link to Argentina's pre-1990s tradition.

sites.name: Cheval des Andes
sites.text: A joint venture launched in 1999 by Château Cheval Blanc and Terrazas de los Andes, with its own winery in Las Compuertas. The blend of old-vine Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon, flood-irrigated as in Mendoza tradition, is a Saint-Émilion view of the Andes.

sites.name: Terrazas de los Andes
sites.text: LVMH's Argentine still-wine house, founded in 1999 and housed in a restored late 19th-century winery in Perdriel. Its name refers to the vineyard 'terraces' at different altitudes chosen for each variety, a founding idea of the high-altitude movement.

sites.name: Bodega Chandon
sites.text: Moët & Chandon's first winery outside France, established in Argentina in 1959 in Agrelo. It built the country's sparkling-wine industry and planted early vineyards in the Uco Valley; the El Peral IG (2022) was granted at its request.

sites.name: Bodegas Salentein
sites.text: Dutch businessman Mijndert Pon founded Salentein in Los Árboles, Tunuyán, in the late 1990s. Its cross-shaped winery with a circular barrel cellar, the Killka art gallery and a chapel became icons of the Uco Valley boom; vineyards reach up to about 1,700 m in San Pablo.

sites.name: Clos de los Siete
sites.text: A block of about 850 ha on the western edge of Vista Flores, Tunuyán, bought from 1998 by Michel Rolland and French partners and shared among several wineries (Monteviejo, Cuvelier Los Andes, DiamAndes, Rolland). Each makes its own wines and contributes to the shared Clos de los Siete blend.

sites.name: Bodega Trapiche (Espejo de Trapiche)
sites.text: Trapiche, founded in 1883 and owned by governor Tiburcio Benegas, who pushed for the 1885 railway, is one of Argentina's founding wine brands. Its Florentine-style 1912 winery in Maipú, built beside the railway line with its own rail spur, was restored and reopened in 2008.

sites.name: Bodega Norton
sites.text: Founded in 1895 by the English engineer Edmund James Palmer Norton, who came to Argentina to build the Transandine railway. Owned since 1989 by the family of Austrian Gernot Langes-Swarovski, it farms large estates in Perdriel.

sites.name: Bodegas López
sites.text: Founded in 1898 by José López Rivas, a Spanish immigrant from Málaga, in Maipú. Still family-run, López keeps the traditional style of long ageing in huge old oak foudres, and its Château Vieux and Montchenot reds are released with years of bottle age.

sites.name: Club Tapiz
sites.text: A historic estate house of 1890 in Russell, Maipú, now an inn and restaurant belonging to the Tapiz group, which farms high vineyards in San Pablo in the Uco Valley.

sites.name: Bodega La Rural (Museo del Vino San Felipe)
sites.text: Founded in 1885 by Felipe Rutini, an immigrant from the Marche, at Coquimbito in Maipú. Its wine museum displays thousands of objects from Mendoza's past, from cowhide presses to early bottling machines; the Rutini brand now makes wine mostly from Tupungato.

sites.name: Museo Nacional del Vino y la Vendimia
sites.text: The national wine and harvest museum in Maipú, housed in the early 20th-century villa of Juan Giol, whose La Colina de Oro winery was once among the largest in the world. It tells the story of Mendoza's harvest festival and industrial wine age.

sites.name: Escorihuela Gascón
sites.text: Founded in 1884 by Spanish immigrant Miguel Escorihuela Gascón in Godoy Cruz, now inside the city. Its old cellars and park house the restaurant 1884, opened by chef Francis Mallmann.

sites.name: Bodega Lagarde
sites.text: Founded in 1897 in Mayor Drummond, Luján de Cuyo, Lagarde is one of Mendoza's oldest wineries still working in its original buildings, with old Malbec and an early Argentine planting of Viognier.

sites.name: Familia Schroeder
sites.text: A winery on the San Patricio del Chañar plateau in Neuquén. During its construction in the early 2000s workers found dinosaur fossils, later described as the titanosaur *Panamericansaurus schroederi* and displayed in the cellar; the winery's Saurus label celebrates them.

sites.name: Bodega del Fin del Mundo
sites.text: Planted from the late 1990s on desert plateau in San Patricio del Chañar, Neuquén, with water piped from the Neuquén river; one of the projects that put northern Patagonia on the wine map.

sites.name: Patagonian Wines (Weinert), El Hoyo
sites.text: Bernardo Weinert's estate in the pre-Andean valley of El Hoyo, Chubut, near El Bolsón at about 300 m and 42°S. Its roughly 28 ha of Merlot, Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Riesling and Gewürztraminer led to the El Hoyo IG in 2023.

sites.name: Estancia Jesuítica de Caroya
sites.text: A 17th-century Jesuit estancia north of Córdoba that supplied the Jesuit college with food and wine until the order's expulsion in 1767. Part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the Jesuit Block and Estancias of Córdoba; its lands were later settled by Friulian vine growers in 1878.

sites.name: Área Fundacional, Mendoza
sites.text: The site of Mendoza's foundation by Pedro del Castillo in 1561, destroyed by the earthquake of 1861. A museum over the excavated ruins of the old cabildo shows the colonial city whose irrigation canals and vineyards began Argentine wine country.

sites.name: Quebrada de Humahuaca vineyards (Maimará)
sites.text: Terraced vineyards at 2,300 to over 2,500 m around Maimará and Tilcara in the UNESCO-listed Quebrada de Humahuaca, below the multicoloured hills of the Paleta del Pintor. Producers such as Fernando Dupont make intense Malbec, Cabernet Franc and Syrah.

sites.name: Costa & Pampa, Chapadmalal
sites.text: Trapiche's Atlantic experiment, a vineyard a few kilometres from the sea south of Mar del Plata, planted around 2010. Its Albariño, Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, salty and taut, led to the Chapadmalal IG in 2014.

sites.name: Bodega Garzón
sites.text: Opened in 2016 near Pueblo Garzón, about 18 km from the Atlantic, by Argentine energy magnate Alejandro Bulgheroni. A sustainability-certified winery among granite hills, with vineyards split into many small blocks; its Albariño and Tannat made Maldonado famous, and Wine Enthusiast named it New World Winery of the Year in 2018.

sites.name: Pueblo Garzón
sites.text: A near-abandoned railway village that was revived when Argentine chef Francis Mallmann opened his hotel and restaurant in the old general store in 2003. Bodega Garzón's vineyards stretch over the surrounding hills.

sites.name: Alto de la Ballena
sites.text: Planted in 2001 on the Sierra de la Ballena, a granite ridge overlooking the Atlantic near Punta Ballena. The first modern vineyard in Maldonado, it proved that the rocky coastal hills could ripen Tannat, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Viognier.

sites.name: Viña Edén
sites.text: An estate in the hills near Pueblo Edén, Maldonado, with a winery set among granite boulders. Known for unoaked, bright Tannat and traditional-method sparkling wine.

sites.name: Bodega Bouza, Melilla
sites.text: The Bouza family's winery in Melilla, on Montevideo's rural edge, in a restored early 20th-century building. Bouza planted Uruguay's first commercial Albariño in the early 2000s and makes single-parcel Tannat (Parcela Única); it also displays a collection of vintage cars and planes.

sites.name: Bodegas Carrau, Colón
sites.text: The Carrau family, winemakers in Catalonia since the 18th century, settled in Uruguay in the 1930s. Their Colón winery in Montevideo makes classic Tannat and pioneered both the Cerro Chapeu vineyard in Rivera and Petit Manseng in Uruguay.

sites.name: Cerro Chapeu, Rivera
sites.text: A vineyard area in Rivera near the Brazilian border, on deep red sandy soils, pioneered by the Carrau family from the 1970s. Its wines, notably Tannat, are fragrant with fine tannins, quite different from the clay-grown Tannat of Canelones.
