sites.name: Establecimiento Juanicó
sites.text: A historic estate in Juanicó, Canelones, with an underground cellar built in the colonial era, owned by the Deicas family since 1979. Familia Deicas makes the Preludio blend and extreme-terroir wines from Maldonado and Lavalleja.

sites.name: Pizzorno Family Estates
sites.text: Founded in 1910 by the Italian immigrant Próspero Pizzorno in Canelón Chico, Canelones. Four generations on, the family makes Tannat-based reds and sparkling wines from its estate vineyards.

sites.name: Pisano, Progreso
sites.text: The Pisano family, of Italian origin, farm vineyards around Progreso in Canelones. Brothers Daniel, Eduardo and Gustavo Pisano helped take Uruguayan Tannat to export markets from the 1990s with wines such as the RPF (Reserva Personal de la Familia) range.

sites.name: Los Cerros de San Juan
sites.text: Founded in 1854 in Colonia department, Los Cerros de San Juan is Uruguay's oldest commercial winery. Its estate of stone buildings and old cellars sits by the San Juan river near the River Plate.

sites.name: Carmelo wine route
sites.text: The river port of Carmelo in Colonia is the hub of a small wine route of family wineries (Irurtia, Narbona, El Legado and others) facing the Paraná delta and Buenos Aires across the water.

sites.name: Harriague's Tannat, Salto
sites.text: Near Salto, around 1870, the Basque immigrant Pascual Harriague planted Tannat on an estate north of the city, using cuttings brought from Concordia across the Uruguay river. It was the beginning of Uruguay's national grape.

sites.name: Colón, Vidiella's vineyard
sites.text: At Colón, now a Montevideo suburb, Francisco Vidiella planted European vines and held his first harvest on 25 February 1883, celebrated as Uruguay's first harvest festival. The grape he grew, Folle Noire, became known locally as 'Vidiella'.

sites.name: INAVI, Las Piedras
sites.text: The headquarters of the Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura, created in 1987, in Las Piedras, the historic wine town of Canelones. INAVI regulates the industry, sets the minimum grape price and runs Uruguay Wine's promotion.

sites.name: Miolo, Vale dos Vinhedos
sites.text: The Miolo family, descendants of Giuseppe Miolo who arrived from Veneto in 1897, sold grapes for decades before launching their own winery in the late 1980s. Miolo Wine Group is now Brazil's largest fine-wine producer, with estates in the Campanha Gaúcha and the São Francisco valley; its Vale dos Vinhedos winery is a tourism hub.

sites.name: Casa Valduga, Vale dos Vinhedos
sites.text: Founded by the Valduga family, descendants of Trentino immigrants who arrived in 1875, Casa Valduga built one of Brazil's first wine-tourism complexes in the Vale dos Vinhedos and is known for traditional-method sparkling wine aged in deep cellars.

sites.name: Vinícola Salton, Tuiuty
sites.text: Founded in 1910 by the sons of the Italian immigrant Antonio Domenico Salton in Bento Gonçalves, Salton is one of Brazil's oldest and largest wineries, especially for sparkling wine, now with a large modern winery at Tuiuty.

sites.name: Cooperativa Vinícola Aurora
sites.text: Founded in 1931 by 16 families in Bento Gonçalves, Aurora is Brazil's largest wine cooperative, with more than a thousand grower families. Its downtown winery offers tours through vast cellars of Brazilian wine history.

sites.name: Cave Geisse, Pinto Bandeira
sites.text: Chilean winemaker Mario Geisse came to Brazil in the 1970s to run Moët & Chandon's operation and founded his own sparkling-wine house at Pinto Bandeira in 1979. Long-aged traditional-method Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the basalt plateau made it the reference for the Altos de Pinto Bandeira DO.

sites.name: Bento Gonçalves
sites.text: Founded as the Italian colony of Dona Isabel in 1875, Bento Gonçalves is Brazil's wine capital, home to Embrapa Uva e Vinho, the Aurora cooperative and dozens of wineries, and the gateway to the Vale dos Vinhedos.

sites.name: Flores da Cunha
sites.text: A hill town settled by Venetian immigrants in the 1870s and long the leading grape and wine municipality of the Serra Gaúcha. Its high vineyards, often above 800 m, form the heart of the Altos Montes IP, known for Tannat, Merlot and sparkling wine.

sites.name: Villa Francioni, São Joaquim
sites.text: A pioneering high-altitude winery near São Joaquim, Santa Catarina, on the plateau above 1,000 m, built in the early 2000s. Its Sauvignon Blanc, rosé and red blends helped launch the Vinhos de Altitude movement.
sites.appellation: Vinhos de Altitude de Santa Catarina

sites.name: Rio Sol, Lagoa Grande
sites.text: A large estate on the São Francisco river in Lagoa Grande, Pernambuco, founded with Portuguese investment. Irrigated vines produce more than one harvest a year in the tropical sertão, making Syrah, Touriga Nacional and sparkling wines.

sites.name: Guaspari, Espírito Santo do Pinhal
sites.text: A São Paulo state estate on former coffee land in the Mantiqueira foothills and a pioneer of winter wines by double pruning. Its Syrah, harvested in the dry winter, helped build the 'vinho de inverno' category and won international recognition.

sites.name: Santana do Livramento
sites.text: A border town facing Rivera in Uruguay, where Almadén planted vineyards in the 1970s and launched the modern Campanha Gaúcha. Cordilheira de Sant'Ana and Almadén (now part of Miolo) farm the pampa here.

sites.name: Hacienda Tacama
sites.text: An estate in the upper Ica valley with roots claimed back to the 1540s, when Francisco de Carabantes planted the first vines in the valley. Owned by the Olaechea family since 1889, its pink colonial hacienda and chapel make it Peru's best-known winery; French consultants including Émile Peynaud advised it from the mid-20th century.

sites.name: Viña Ocucaje
sites.text: Founded in 1898 in the desert south of Ica, Ocucaje is one of Peru's oldest working wineries, known for pisco and traditional sweet and fortified wines. Its estate and hotel sit amid dunes famous for marine fossil beds.

sites.name: Santiago Queirolo, Ica
sites.text: The Queirolo family, of Italian origin, founded their winery in Lima's Pueblo Libre in 1880; it is now one of Peru's two dominant producers. Its Ica estate at San José de los Molinos grows grapes for pisco and for the Intipalka fine-wine brand.

sites.name: Huacachina oasis
sites.text: A lagoon among giant sand dunes 5 km from Ica, the symbol of Peru's desert wine country and the hub for visits to the valley's wineries and pisco makers.

sites.name: Port of Pisco
sites.text: The colonial port that gave its name to Peru's grape brandy, from which aguardiente from the Ica valley was shipped to Lima and beyond. The town was devastated by earthquakes in 1687 and 2007.

sites.name: Moquegua colonial bodegas
sites.text: The Moquegua valley holds the remains of many colonial wineries with huge clay *tinajas*, evidence of a 17th and 18th century industry that shipped wine and aguardiente to Potosí's silver mines.

sites.name: Bodegas Kohlberg
sites.text: A family winery founded in Tarija by Julio Kohlberg, one of the pioneers of Bolivia's modern wine and singani industry. It is among the country's largest producers, with vineyards in the central valley.

sites.name: Bodegas Aranjuez
sites.text: A family winery on the outskirts of Tarija, Aranjuez is best known for Tannat grown at high altitude in the central valley. Its Tannat-based wines, notably the Juan Cruz label, helped bring Bolivian wine its first international recognition.

sites.name: Campos de Solana
sites.text: A Tarija winery on the road south to Padcaya, belonging to a family with a long singani tradition. Its wines include Tannat, Malbec and aromatic whites from vineyards in the central valley.

sites.name: Bodegas La Concepción, Uriondo
sites.text: A winery in the Concepción valley of Uriondo, south of Tarija, with vineyards at around 1,800 to 2,000 m, making high-altitude reds, whites and singani.

sites.name: La Casa Vieja, Concepción
sites.text: A traditional adobe winery in the village of Concepción, Uriondo, where wine is still made in old style and visitors eat under the vines; a centre of Tarija's wine route and harvest festivals.

sites.name: Villa Abecia, Cinti valley
sites.text: A village in the Cinti canyon of Chuquisaca where colonial-era vines climb native molle trees. Some vineyards here are over a century old, part of a landscape of adobe haciendas and singani stills.

sites.name: San Pedro, Camargo
sites.text: Site of Bolivia's first industrial winery, established in 1925 near Camargo in the Cinti valley by the Ortiz and Patiño families, which began with singani.

sites.name: Colonia Independencia
sites.text: A farming town in Guairá department, founded in 1919 to 1920 at the foot of the Ybytyruzú hills, settled in part by German families. It is the centre of Paraguay's small grape-growing tradition and hosts an annual grape and wine festival; a 2016 report counted a single commercial winery here producing about 1,200 litres a year.

sites.name: Viñedos Ain Karim
sites.text: Established in 1988 on the road from Villa de Leyva to Santa Sofía, near Sutamarchán in Boyacá, at about 2,000 m. Ain Karim planted Colombia's first Sauvignon Blanc and makes red, white and rosé wines from its own vineyards, aged in an underground cellar.

sites.name: Marqués de Puntalarga
sites.text: A vineyard in the Valle del Sol near Nobsa, Boyacá, at about 2,500 m, between Duitama and Belencito. It grows Pinot Noir and Riesling (made dry and sweet) and hosts the Valle del Sol Vid y Vino event each December.

sites.name: Casa Grajales and National Grape Park
sites.text: Colombia's pioneering commercial winery in La Unión, Valle del Cauca, founded more than 40 years ago by the Grajales family, with a reported capacity of around 7 million litres a year from tropical-adapted grapes. Its National Grape Park and grape and wine museum explain viticulture in the tropics.

sites.name: Bodegas Pomar, Carora
sites.text: Founded in 1985 by Empresas Polar and Martell, Pomar makes Venezuela's best-known wines from about 80 ha of vineyards at Altagracia near Carora, Lara. With no winter, vines are pruned for two harvests a year, picked by hand, and turned into still wines, traditional-method sparkling wines and communion wine.

sites.name: Dos Hemisferios
sites.text: Ecuador's best-known winery, in San Miguel del Morro, Guayas, near the Pacific. A former table-grape grower, it made its first wine, Paradoja, from the 2006 harvest; sea breezes and limestone soils, plus two harvests a year, shape its reds and whites.

sites.name: Chaupi Estancia, Yaruquí
sites.text: Ecuador's oldest wine estate, planted about 30 years ago at Yaruquí in the Quito district, at about 2,400 m and roughly 10 km from the equator. It makes Palomino, a Chardonnay and Viognier blend and Pinot Noir in a land of 'eternal spring'.
